items.stem: The diagram shows double-slit fringes formed by light of wavelength 450 nm on a screen 2.2 m from two narrow parallel slits. The slit separation is 0.24 mm and each slit has width 0.06 mm. Determine the full linear width between the two first-order minima of the central diffraction envelope.
items.workedSolution: The first single-slit diffraction minima lie at θ = ±λ / b, so the full width of the central diffraction envelope on the screen is w_env = 2λD / b = (2 × 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.2) / 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.0330 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w_env = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0330 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the adjacent interference fringe spacing λD / d instead of the diffraction envelope width 2λD / b.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes slit separation d in place of individual slit width b, computing 2λD / d.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the half-width λD / b from the centre to one minimum instead of the full width 2λD / b.

items.stem: Which pair of practical technologies directly relies on the Doppler effect to measure motion?
items.workedSolution: Medical Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow velocity in arteries from the frequency shift of reflected waves. Traffic and weather radar measure vehicle or storm speed in the same way.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that measuring blood flow velocity in arteries and vehicle speed from the frequency shift of reflected waves.

items.stem: The distance between rigid supports is 1.5 m for a guitar string with wave speed 192 m s⁻¹. Work out the frequency of mode n = 6.
items.workedSolution: Fixed-end mode n = 6: λ_n = 2L / n = 2(1.5) / 6 = 0.500 m. Dividing speed by wavelength gives f_n = v / λ_n = 192 / 0.500 = 384 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f_n = nv / (2L) to obtain 384 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic frequency v / (2L) instead of multiplying by harmonic number n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the closed-one-end pipe formula nv / (4L) instead of fixed-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n, computing f = nv / L.

items.stem: Sound moves through still air at 343 m s⁻¹. As a moving detector travels directly away from a stationary loudspeaker emitting 460 Hz, the received pitch is 380 Hz. Determine the observer's speed.
items.workedSolution: From f′ = f(v − v_o) / v, rearrange directly: v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 343 × |380 / 460 − 1| = 60.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 60.0 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.distractorRationale: Divides the speed by 2 as if solving a two-way pulse-echo Doppler shift.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the moving-source algebra v|1 − f / f'| instead of the moving-observer relation v|f' / f − 1|.

items.stem: On a flat card 3.4 m past two narrow parallel slits (0.35 mm separation), 420 nm light forms bright bands. What distance separates the central bright fringe (n = 0) and the n = 4 bright fringe?
items.workedSolution: Each interval = λD / d = 4.08 × 10⁻³ m; from central n = 0 to n = 4: y_4 = 4 × λD / d = 0.0163 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates single adjacent fringe spacing λD / d instead of multiplying by order n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies destructive half-integer factor (n − ½) instead of constructive integer order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Counts one extra interval, multiplying fringe spacing by (n + 1) fringes instead of n intervals from n = 0.

items.stem: A progressive wave travels along a long stretched rope at a speed of 2.56 m s⁻¹. From its displacement–position graph, the amplitude is 0.03 m and the wavelength is 0.32 m. Determine the frequency of oscillation.
items.workedSolution: Using f = v / λ with wave speed v = 2.56 m s⁻¹ and wavelength λ = 0.32 m gives f = 2.56 / 0.32 = 8.00 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges v = fλ to obtain f = v / λ = 8.00 Hz (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the oscillation period T = λ / v instead of the frequency f = v / λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength (vλ) instead of dividing v by λ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Mistakes two full cycles for one wavelength, halving the calculated frequency.

items.stem: Spanning 0.66 m, a cylindrical pipe open at both ends sustains harmonic mode n = 5 (with ideal open-end conditions). Taking sound speed as 330 m s⁻¹, determine the frequency.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the first-harmonic frequency f₁ instead of the n-th harmonic.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n.

items.stem: An optics bench sets a screen 2.1 m past a 400 lines mm⁻¹ grating. Coherent 460 nm light strikes normally; study order n = 3.
items.workedSolution: (a) Convert ruling: d = 10⁻³ / 400 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Grating law gives sin θ = nλ / d = 0.552, so θ = 33.5°. (c) Spot position: y = D tan θ = 2.1 × tan(33.5°) = 1.39 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises large-angle geometry y = D tan θ rather than small-angle D sin θ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the centre-to-centre spacing d between adjacent grating slits in metres.
Calculate the diffraction angle θ_3 (in degrees) of the order n = 3 maximum.
Determine the linear distance along the flat screen from the central maximum (n = 0) to the n = 3 maximum.
workingSteps: At large diffraction angles, use exact trigonometry y = D tan θ (do not assume tan θ ≈ sin θ).

items.stem: Between x₁ = 0.09 m (P) and x₂ = 0.48 m (Q), find the phase difference in degrees for a 25 Hz wave in a water tank (wavelength 0.6 m, amplitude 0.022 m).
items.workedSolution: With Δx = 0.48 m − 0.09 m = 0.39 m and one complete cycle = 0.6 m, fraction is 0.650 cycles; thus Δφ = 360° × 0.650 = 234°.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 360° to get 234° (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in radians without converting to degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (180°) instead of a full cycle (360°) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

items.stem: A narrow gap (0.08 mm wide) spreads a normal-incidence 514 nm beam across a screen 1.8 m behind the slit.
items.workedSolution: (a) Diffraction angle: θ = λ / b = 6.42 × 10⁻³ rad. (b) Screen offset: y₁ = θD = 0.0116 m. (c) Full peak width: w = 2y₁ = 0.0231 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies θ = λ / b in SI units.
Multiplies θ by screen distance D.
Doubles half-width to span both sides of the central peak.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular position θ (in radians) of the first diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Use the small-angle single-slit first-minimum relation θ = λ / b.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear distance on the screen from the centre of the pattern to the first dark minimum.
Calculate the full linear width of the central bright maximum on the screen.
workingSteps: The central maximum spans from −y₁ to +y₁: w = 2y₁.

items.stem: Hertz rotated a dipole loop detector through a full circle facing a vertical spark-gap transmitter. What amplitude pattern was recorded, and what did it prove?
items.workedSolution: Hertz's polarisation test confirmed Maxwell's prediction. The detected signal varies as the magnitude of the cosine of the rotation angle. Maxima occur at zero and one hundred eighty degrees, and zeros occur at ninety and two hundred seventy degrees. This proved that radio waves are transverse.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies cosine-magnitude signal variation: maxima at zero and one hundred eighty degrees, zeros at ninety and two hundred seventy degrees. Proves radio waves are transverse.

options.label: A
options.text: Detected signal stayed constant at every rotation angle proving radio waves are longitudinal compressions.
options.distractorRationale: A longitudinal wave cannot be polarised; Hertz observed clear maxima and zeros every 90 degrees.

options.label: B
options.text: Detected signal peaked at ninety degrees and vanished at zero degrees because magnetic force dominates.
options.distractorRationale: Maximum induced emf occurs when the dipole aligns parallel to the transmitter's electric field (0 and 180 degrees).

options.label: C
options.text: He found that the detected signal varies as magnitude of cosine of rotation angle with maxima at zero and one hundred eighty degrees and zeros at ninety and two hundred seventy degrees proving radio waves are transverse.

options.label: D
options.text: Detected signal vanished only at one hundred eighty degrees proving waves travel along one direction only.
options.distractorRationale: At 180 degrees the dipole is again parallel to the oscillating E-field, producing a second maximum.

items.stem: How does negative feedback alter the voltage-gain versus frequency (Bode) curve of a real operational amplifier?
items.workedSolution: On the log–log Bode plot, the closed-loop gain remains constant up to the cutoff frequency then follows the constant gain-bandwidth product slope.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that closed-loop gain remains constant up to the cutoff frequency then follows the constant gain-bandwidth product slope.

options.label: A
options.text: Negative feedback increases both voltage gain and bandwidth simultaneously above the open-loop curve.
options.distractorRationale: A real op-amp's closed-loop gain can never exceed the open-loop boundary; $\text{gain} \times \text{bandwidth}$ stays fixed.

options.label: B
options.text: Negative feedback makes the bandwidth collapse to 10 Hz regardless of resistor values.
options.distractorRationale: Lowering closed-loop gain WIDENS bandwidth proportionally.

options.label: C
options.text: Negative feedback eliminates power-supply saturation limits so output voltage can exceed the supply rails.
options.distractorRationale: Real op-amp output still saturates near the DC power supply rails.

options.label: D
options.text: The closed-loop gain remains constant up to the cutoff frequency then follows the constant gain-bandwidth product slope, trading reduced voltage gain for a proportionally wider usable bandwidth.

items.stem: In an optics experiment, vertically plane-polarized light (84 W m⁻²) crosses an ideal analyzer turned to θ = 20° from the vertical. Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ for plane-polarized light.
items.workedSolution: (a) Field projection: E / E₀ = cos(20°) = 0.940. (b) Emerging intensity: I = I₀ cos²(20°) = 74.2 W m⁻². (c) Difference absorbed = 84 − 74.2 = 9.83 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Projects electric-field vector via E / E₀ = cos θ.
Subtracts transmitted intensity from incident intensity.

parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio E / E₀ of the transmitted electric-field amplitude to the incident electric-field amplitude.
workingSteps: Only the electric-field component parallel to the analyzer axis is transmitted: E / E₀ = cos θ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity I of the beam emerging from the analyzer.
Determine the intensity removed (absorbed or rejected) from the beam by the analyzer.

items.stem: Light of wavelength $\lambda = 600\text{ nm}$ passes normally through a $3$-slit mask whose slit separation is $d = 150\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ and individual slit width is $b = 25.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$. Using the IB single-slit diffraction relation $\theta = \lambda / b$, at what angle does the first minimum of the modulating single-slit envelope occur?
items.workedSolution: $\theta = \frac{\lambda}{b} = \frac{600 \times 10^{-9}}{25.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 2.40 \times 10^{-2}\text{ rad} = 24.0 mrad$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\theta = \lambda / b$ with $b = 25.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ to obtain $24.0 mrad$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes slit separation d = 150 μm instead of individual slit width b = 25.0 μm.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes full angular width 2λ/b of the central envelope rather than the first minimum angle λ/b.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies an incorrect factor of one-half to θ = λ/b.

items.stem: In a resonance test (assuming ideal end conditions), a cylindrical pipe closed at one end (0.42 m long) sustains odd harmonic n = 5 at 1036 Hz. Determine the sound speed.
items.workedSolution: Closed-one-end harmonic n = 5: λ_n = 4L / n = 4(0.42) / 5 = 0.336 m, giving v = f_n λ_n = 348 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = 4Lf_n / n to obtain 348 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses open-pipe wavelength 2L / n instead of closed-pipe 4L / n, halving the speed of sound.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes an even harmonic index (n − 1) instead of the odd harmonic n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th harmonic frequency as the first-harmonic mode v = 4Lf.

items.stem: A stretched string of length $0.800\text{ m}$ has both ends fitted to frictionless rings that oscillate freely (two free boundaries, displacement antinodes at both ends). If wave speed is $128\text{ m s}^{-1}$, what is the frequency of the second harmonic?
items.workedSolution: With displacement antinodes at both ends, $L = n\frac{\lambda_n}{2}$. For the second harmonic ($n = 2$), $\lambda_2 = L = 0.800\text{ m}$ and $f_2 = \frac{128}{0.800} = 160 Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies antinode–antinode condition $\lambda_2 = L$ to obtain $f_2 = 160 Hz$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the first harmonic frequency v/(2L) instead of the second harmonic 2v/(2L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes the third harmonic frequency instead of the second harmonic.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an extra factor of two when rearranging the wave relation.

items.stem: How does the phase of oscillation vary along a stationary wave vibrating in its third harmonic compared with a progressive wave?
items.workedSolution: Points within one loop have phase difference 0, whereas points separated by an odd number of nodes have phase difference π rad. All points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase. Points in neighbouring loops across a node oscillate in antiphase, with a phase difference of pi radians. Therefore option C is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase, while points across a node oscillate in antiphase (pi radians).

options.label: A
options.text: Phase changes smoothly by 2 pi radians over every wavelength between adjacent nodes along a stationary wave.
options.distractorRationale: Continuous spatial phase progression describes a progressive wave, not a stationary wave.

options.label: B
options.text: All points along the entire string oscillate completely in phase regardless of how many nodes lie between them.
options.distractorRationale: Adjacent loops move in opposite vertical directions, giving a phase difference of π radians across every node.

options.label: C
options.text: In contrast to a progressive wave's continuous phase lag, all points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase with each other, while points in neighbouring loops across a node oscillate in antiphase with a phase difference of pi radians.

options.label: D
options.text: Points in the same loop between two nodes differ in phase by pi/2 radians.
options.distractorRationale: All points within one loop reach maximum displacement and zero at the same time (phase difference 0).

items.stem: With a stainless steel wire kept under constant tension by a 0.75 kg hanging mass ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²), a student runs Required Practical 1. Changing vibrating length $L$ produces a linear $f_1$ against $1/L$ plot through the origin with gradient 31.1 m s⁻¹. Uncertainties are 0.9% in mass, 0.6% in frequency, and 0.5% in length.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v = 2 \times 31.1 = 62.2 m s⁻¹$. (b) $T = 7.36 N$, $\mu = T/v^2 = 1.90 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$. (c) $\%\Delta \mu = 0.9 + 2(0.6) + 2(0.5) = 3.10\%$. (d) measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $T = mg = 7.36 N$ and substitutes into $\mu = T/v^2$.
Mass per unit length $\mu = 1.90 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$.
Doubles percentage uncertainties in both $f_1$ and $L$ before adding $\%\Delta m$.
Measures vibrating length between wooden bridge and top of pulley (fixed nodes).
Links fixed-node span to first-harmonic condition $f_1 = v/(2L)$.

parts.prompt: Use the gradient of the $f_1$ against $1/L$ graph to determine the wave speed $v$ on the string.
Calculate the mass per unit length $\mu$ of the string.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $\mu$ from the stated measurement uncertainties.
Explain clearly between which two points $L$ must be measured to avoid a systematic error.
parts.expectedAnswer: measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length
workingSteps: Measure directly between the fixed nodes at the bridge apex and pulley top.
First harmonic has λ = 2L between those fixed nodes.

items.stem: A space-based optical reflector of diameter 2.40 m observes an asteroid pair at a distance of 1.20 × 10¹¹ m using light of wavelength 600 nm.
items.workedSolution: (a) central maximum of one diffraction pattern coincides with the first minimum of the other. (b) $\theta \approx 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ rad$. (c) $s = r\theta = 30.0 km$.

markScheme.criterion: Refers to the Airy / central diffraction maxima of the two images.
States central maximum of one coincides with the first minimum of the other.
Multiplies distance by $\theta$ and converts to km.

parts.prompt: State the Rayleigh criterion for the resolution of two point sources.
parts.expectedAnswer: Two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one diffraction pattern coincides with the first minimum of the other.
workingSteps: Describe the diffraction Airy patterns of both sources.
Specify coincidence of central maximum and first minimum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum resolvable angular separation of the telescope.
Determine the minimum linear separation in kilometres between the two asteroids if they are to be resolved.

items.stem: Sound of frequency 620 Hz comes from a loudspeaker on a car receding from a fixed observer at 56 m s⁻¹. Take sound speed in still air as 332 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero-speed wavelength: λ₀ = v / f = 0.535 m. (b) Apparent wavelength at receiver: λ′ = (v + v_s) / f = 0.626 m. (c) Hence f′ = v / λ′ = 531 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f′ = v / λ′ or exact moving-source Doppler formula.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength that the sound waves would have in still air if the source were stationary.
Calculate the wavelength λ′ of the sound waves in the air between the moving source and the stationary observer.
Determine the frequency detected by the stationary observer.

items.stem: Adjacent bright fringes lie 4.08 mm apart on a flat screen 2.4 m from two narrow parallel slits. If the slit spacing is 0.36 mm, determine the wavelength used.
items.workedSolution: From Δy = λD / d, solve for wavelength: λ = Δy × d / D = (4.08 × 10⁻³ × 3.60 × 10⁻⁴) / 2.4 = 6.12 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges double-slit relation to obtain λ = 6.12 × 10⁻⁷ m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes an extra factor of ½ from single-slit central-width formulas.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats bright-to-bright fringe spacing as half-wavelength path difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies fringe spacing by screen distance D and divides by slit separation instead of multiplying by slit separation / D.

items.stem: A digital acoustic recorder digitises 8 independent microphone channels over a 4.10 V input span using an ADC with 10 bits per sample. Each microphone signal has maximum frequency 5.00 kHz and is actually sampled at 12.0 kHz before TDM interleaving.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n = 4.00 mV$. (b) Minimum Nyquist rate $2 f_{\max} = 10.0 kHz$. (c) TDM total bit rate $= 960 kbit s⁻¹$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the voltage resolution of the ADC in mV.
State the minimum theoretical Nyquist sampling frequency required to avoid aliasing (in kHz).
Calculate the aggregate bit rate transmitted across the TDM link in $\text{kbit s}^{-1}$.
workingSteps: Total bit rate $= N \times f_{\mathrm{s}} \times n = 8 \times 12.0 \times 10 = 960 kbit s⁻¹$.

items.stem: An elderly patient's threshold curve (patient curve P) matches the normal curve at low frequencies but rises steadily across all higher frequencies. Which defect does this illustrate?
items.workedSolution: On equal-loudness charts, age-related hearing loss raises threshold steeply at high frequencies, whereas low-frequency thresholds remain closer to normal.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that age-related hearing loss raises threshold steeply at high frequencies.

options.label: A
options.text: It demonstrates that age-related hearing loss raises threshold steeply at high frequencies, reducing the upper audible frequency limit.

options.label: B
options.text: Noise-induced loss confined strictly to a narrow band near 200 Hz.
options.distractorRationale: Noise-induced loss typically forms a distinct notch near 4 kHz.

options.label: C
options.text: Improved sensitivity to treble frequencies as the ossicles stiffen with age.
options.distractorRationale: A higher threshold curve means greater intensity is needed to hear—worse sensitivity, not improved.

options.label: D
options.text: Complete loss of sound detection at 1 kHz while ultrasonic frequencies remain audible.
options.distractorRationale: High-frequency hearing deteriorates first with age.

items.stem: An unpolarized light beam of unknown intensity I₀ passes through an ideal polarizer P₁ and then through an ideal analyzer A. The transmission axis of A is tilted at θ = 35° relative to P₁, and the emerging intensity is 21.5 W m⁻². Given I = I₁ cos²θ for plane-polarized light, calculate I₀.
items.workedSolution: Since I = ½ I₀ cos²θ, rearranging gives I₀ = 2I / cos²(35°) = (2 × 21.5) / 0.671 = 64.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Solves I = ½ I₀ cos²θ to obtain I₀ = 64.0 W m⁻² (D).

items.stem: In a standing-wave experiment, a taut string clamped at both ends has vibrating length 0.64 m and linear mass density 0.006 kg m⁻¹. The string is under a tension of 153.6 N and resonates in harmonic n = 5. Transverse waves travel along a string of tension T and mass per unit length μ at speed v = √(T / μ).

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T and μ into v = √(T / μ).
Divides wave speed from (a) by wavelength from (b).

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of transverse waves along the string.
Determine the wavelength of the n = 5 harmonic mode.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this standing wave.

items.stem: The stationary wave shown forms $3$ loops (third harmonic) along a stretched string of length $1.35\text{ m}$ when driven at $180\text{ Hz}$. Calculate the speed of progressive waves travelling along the string.
items.workedSolution: Three loops span $\frac{3}{2}\lambda = 1.35\text{ m}$, so $\lambda = 0.900\text{ m}$ and $c = f\lambda = 180 \times 0.900 = 162 m s⁻¹$. Option A (162 m s⁻¹) matches.

items.stem: A vascular clinic uses a 5.00 MHz Doppler ultrasound probe angled at 45.0° to a patient's brachial artery. Blood flows towards the probe at 0.600 m s⁻¹, and the speed of ultrasound is $c = 1540\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δf = 2.75 × 10³ Hz. (b) 2.75 kHz. (c) Ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift because moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect the wave. (d) Acoustic coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound transmits into tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes f in Hz, v, cos θ, c, and factor of 2 into Δf = (2fv cos θ)/c.
Converts to 2.75 kHz and states received frequency is higher.
States moving red blood cells receive a Doppler-shifted frequency.
States the reflected wave experiences a second Doppler shift back to the probe as moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect it.
States gel displaces air from the gap between the probe and skin.
Explains acoustic impedance matching enables transmission into tissue rather than reflection at the skin.

parts.prompt: Using $\Delta f / f = (2v\cos\theta)/c$, calculate the Doppler frequency shift $\Delta f$ in hertz.
Express this frequency shift in kilohertz and state whether the received frequency is higher or lower than the emitted frequency.
workingSteps: Blood flows towards probe, so received frequency is higher.

parts.prompt: Explain why the factor of 2 appears in the Doppler ultrasound equation.
parts.expectedAnswer: The factor of 2 arises because ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift: moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect the wave.
workingSteps: Red blood cells act first as moving receivers of shifted wavefronts.
They then reflect the wave back as moving emitters, so the ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift.

parts.prompt: Explain why acoustic coupling gel must be applied between the probe and the patient's skin.
parts.expectedAnswer: Acoustic coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound enters tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.
workingSteps: Air has much lower acoustic impedance than skin and soft tissue, causing nearly total reflection.
Acoustic coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound transmits into tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.

items.stem: An ultrasound pulse passes at normal incidence from muscle (density 1050 kg m⁻³, speed 1540 m s⁻¹) into adipose fat tissue (density 950 kg m⁻³, speed 1450 m s⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) Reflected $= 0.640\%$. (b) Transmitted $= 99.4\%$. (c) Backing block damps crystal vibrations rapidly to produce short pulses improving axial resolution.

markScheme.criterion: States backing block rapidly damps crystal vibrations to create short pulses.
Links short pulse duration to improved axial resolution.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of incident ultrasound intensity reflected at the muscle–fat boundary.
Hence determine the percentage of incident intensity transmitted into the fat layer.
Explain why a damping backing block is needed in the ultrasound probe when imaging thin soft-tissue layers.
parts.expectedAnswer: The backing block damps crystal vibrations rapidly to produce short pulses improving axial resolution so successive echoes remain distinct.
workingSteps: Absorbs backward vibrations so the pulse ends quickly.
Shorter pulse length allows closer boundaries to be resolved without echo overlap.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 575 nm strikes a diffraction grating with 450 lines mm⁻¹ at normal incidence. What total number of bright principal maxima can be observed across the forward semicircle?
items.workedSolution: d = 10⁻³ / 450 = 2.22 × 10⁻⁶ m, so d / λ = 3.86 and n_max = 3. Including ±1..±3 and n = 0 gives 2(3) + 1 = 7 principal maxima.

items.stem: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has a wavelength of $1.5 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$. Using the electromagnetic spectrum orders of magnitude shown, to which spectral region does this radiation belong?
items.workedSolution: In the IB Physics Data Booklet EM spectrum, wavelengths of order 10⁻¹⁰ m (0.1 nm, atomic scale) belong to X-rays. Therefore the correct statement is: X-rays with approximate wavelength order around ten to the minus ten metres.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: X-rays with approximate wavelength order around ten to the minus ten metres.

items.stem: An acoustic technician walks radially away from a point siren, moving from 3.00 m to 30.0 m in an open field. By how many decibels does the sound intensity level decrease?
items.workedSolution: Increasing distance by a factor of 10 reduces intensity by $10^2 = 100$. Thus $\Delta L = 10\lg(100) = 20.0 dB$.

items.stem: A helium–neon laser ($\lambda = 633\text{ nm}$) illuminates a single vertical slit of width $a = 0.20\text{ mm}$ placed $1.80\text{ m}$ in front of a screen.
items.workedSolution: (a) $W = 2\lambda D / a = 11.4 mm$. (b) central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitute SI values into $W = 2\lambda D / a$.
Central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
Narrowing the slit widens the diffraction pattern (and reduces brightness).

parts.prompt: Calculate the width of the central diffraction maximum (between the two first-order minima) in millimetres using $W \approx 2\lambda D / a$.
Compare the width of the central maximum with a secondary maximum, and state what happens to the pattern if the slit is made narrower.
parts.expectedAnswer: The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum. Narrowing the slit widens the pattern and reduces peak intensity because less light passes through.
workingSteps: State 2:1 width ratio and inverse scaling with slit width a.

items.stem: Two coherent loudspeakers emit 1360 Hz sound waves (speed 340 m s⁻¹). At detector position P, the path difference |S₂P − S₁P| is 0.625 m. Express this path difference in wavelengths λ (identifying a destructive minimum).
items.workedSolution: λ = c / f = 340 / 1360 = 0.250 m; Δl / λ = 0.625 / 0.250 = 2.50 λ (half-integer → destructive minimum).

items.stem: Placed perpendicular to a green laser beam at $D = 1.60$ m from a wall, a 600 lines mm⁻¹ grating forms two $n = \pm 1$ maxima separated by $2h = 1.076$ m. Find the highest observable order on either side of the central beam.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing $d = 10^{-3}/600 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m$. Half-span $h = 0.538$ m gives $\theta = \arctan(0.538/1.6) = 18.6^\circ$. Thus $\lambda = d\sin\theta / 1 = 531 nm$ and $n_{\max} = \lfloor d/\lambda \rfloor = 3$.

items.stem: A student plans to determine the wavelength of light from a Class 2 diode laser using Young's double slits and a darkened laboratory bench.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Secure a Class 2 laser horizontally below eye level, post a warning sign, remove reflective surfaces, and never look into the beam. Align the double slit perpendicular to the beam with a set square, and place a matte white screen at least 1.5 m away. Measure slit-to-screen distance D with a metre ruler. In a dimly lit room, mark the centres of 11 consecutive bright fringes on graph paper. Measure the 10-space span with Vernier callipers to find w = span / 10, and repeat for at least five different distances D. Plot w against D, draw a best-fit line through the origin, find the gradient using a triangle spanning > 50% of the line, and calculate λ = gradient × s.

parts.prompt: Describe a safe, precise graphical procedure to determine the laser wavelength. Include apparatus alignment, measurements, safety controls, and data analysis. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Mount the laser, double slit, and matte screen firmly on a bench with the slit parallel to the screen. Avoid looking directly into the laser beam and remove reflective surfaces. Vary D across several distances and measure across ten fringe spaces (eleven bright fringes) to find w with low percentage uncertainty. Plot w against D so wavelength equals the gradient multiplied by slit separation s.
workingSteps: Level 1: Set up Class 2 laser, double slit, and screen at large D (> 1.5 m) with beam safety controls.
Level 2: Measure distance D with a metre ruler and centre-to-centre span across many fringe spaces (n+1 fringes = n spaces) using Vernier callipers/ruler in darkened room.
Level 3: Repeat for >= 5 values of D, plot w against D (straight line through origin), extract λ = s × gradient, and evaluate precision/alignment with a set square.

items.stem: A physics student is given a Class 2 laser and a diffraction grating of known ruling N (lines mm⁻¹). The student also has a metre ruler, a set square, and a wide flat screen.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Mount the Class 2 laser horizontally below eye height, clear reflective items, post warning signs, and never look into any beam. Use a set square to check that the grating is perpendicular to the beam and parallel to the screen. Measure grating-to-screen distance D with a metre ruler (at least 1.0 m). Mark the zero-order spot and symmetric ±1, ±2, ... maxima on the screen. For each order n, measure the full span 2h between +n and −n spots; halving to h cuts percentage uncertainty and checks alignment. Compute θ = arctan(h/D) and sin θ for every order without small-angle approximations. Convert ruling N to grating spacing d = 1/N in metres, plot sin θ against n, draw a best-fit line through the origin, and find λ = d × gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States authentic Class 2 laser safety precautions (no direct viewing of primary/diffracted beams, remove reflective surfaces, warning notice).
Checks normal incidence of the grating and parallel screen using a set square (and equal left/right spot distances).
Measures grating-to-screen distance D and symmetric full distance 2h between +n and −n spots across multiple orders.
Calculates exact diffraction angle θ = arctan(h/D) using half-span h (explicitly avoiding small-angle sin θ ≈ tan θ).
Converts lines per mm to grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / N in metres.
Plots sin θ against order n (or averages d sin θ / n across orders) and obtains λ = d × gradient.

parts.prompt: Design an experiment to determine the laser wavelength accurately from multiple diffraction orders. Explain the safety steps, alignment, measurements, and graphical analysis. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Clamp the laser horizontally below eye level with warning signs and no reflective objects, and never look directly into the laser. Align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square and measure the symmetric span between matching orders. Calculate d = 1/N and find sin θ from tan θ = h/D for each visible order n. Plot sin θ against n so the wavelength equals d multiplied by the gradient.
workingSteps: Level 1: Laser safety controls and normal alignment of grating with a set square.
Level 2: Measure D to screen and symmetric span 2h between +n and −n maxima for every observable order.
Level 3: Compute θ = arctan(h/D), plot sin θ vs n, extract λ = d × gradient using d = 1/N.

items.stem: The diagram shows monochromatic plane wavefronts striking a transmission diffraction grating of slit spacing d at normal incidence.
items.workedSolution: Adjacent slits separated by d give path difference d sin theta = n lambda. Consider parallel rays emerging at angle θ from two adjacent slits separated by distance d. Dropping a perpendicular wavefront onto the neighbouring ray forms a right-angled triangle of hypotenuse d and angle θ, so Δl = d sin θ. Constructive interference occurs when Δl = nλ (integer order n), giving d sin θ = nλ. With white light, all three setups give a central white maximum (Δl = 0). Outer spectra have violet inner and red outer edges because longer wavelength λ diffracts through a larger angle. A single slit has a broad central maximum twice as wide as dim outer fringes; double slits give equally spaced dim overlapping spectra. A grating gives bright, razor-sharp, widely dispersed spectra suited to measuring stellar atomic wavelengths.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Identifies adjacent slit separation d and parallel rays diffracted at angle θ to the normal.
L1: Uses the right-angled wavefront triangle to establish path difference Δl = d sin θ.
L2: Applies the constructive interference condition Δl = nλ (integer n) to conclude d sin θ = nλ.
L2: Explains why the central fringe is white (zero path difference for all λ) and why violet appears closer to the centre than red.
L3: Contrasts single-slit diffraction (central max twice as wide as outer fringes, rapid intensity drop) against double-slit fringes.
L3: Explains why gratings produce sharper, brighter, more widely separated orders suited to measuring atomic and stellar spectra.

parts.prompt: Derive the diffraction-grating equation d sin θ = nλ from the path difference between rays from adjacent slits. Compare the white-light patterns of a single slit, Young's double slit, and a diffraction grating, and explain why gratings are used in stellar spectroscopy. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Adjacent slits separated by d give path difference d sin theta = n lambda. Consider parallel rays emerging at angle θ from two adjacent slits separated by distance d. Dropping a perpendicular wavefront onto the neighbouring ray forms a right-angled triangle of hypotenuse d and angle θ, so Δl = d sin θ. Constructive interference occurs when Δl = nλ (integer order n), giving d sin θ = nλ. With white light, all three setups give a central white maximum (Δl = 0). Outer spectra have violet inner and red outer edges because longer wavelength λ diffracts through a larger angle. A single slit has a broad central maximum twice as wide as dim outer fringes; double slits give equally spaced dim overlapping spectra. A grating gives bright, razor-sharp, widely dispersed spectra suited to measuring stellar atomic wavelengths.
workingSteps: Draw perpendicular wavefront between adjacent rays at angle θ with slit separation d as hypotenuse.
Identify path difference Δl = d sin θ and set Δl = nλ for constructive interference.
Explain central white fringe (Δl = 0) and violet-inner / red-outer ordering from larger λ → larger θ.
Contrast single-slit (2× central width), double-slit (broad/dim), and grating (sharp/bright/high dispersion for spectroscopy).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 650 nm is incident normally on two narrow parallel slits. Each slit has a width of 0.06 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.18 mm. The diffraction-modulated interference pattern is observed on a screen 1.4 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Interference fringe spacing Δy = λD / d = 5.06 × 10⁻³ m. (b) Central envelope full width w_env = 2λD / b = 0.0303 m. (c) First missing order n = d / b = 3.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λD / d with slit separation d.
Uses 2λD / b with individual slit width b.
Equates interference maximum angle to first diffraction minimum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent double-slit interference maxima near the centre of the pattern.
Calculate the full width of the central single-slit diffraction envelope on the screen.
Determine the lowest positive interference order n that is missing due to coincidence with a single-slit diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Equate nλ / d = λ / b => n = d / b.

items.stem: In a laboratory spectrum, a sodium absorption line lies at $\lambda = 589.0\text{ nm}$. In the spectrum of a nearby star, the same line is observed at $588.1\text{ nm}$, giving a shift magnitude of $\Delta\lambda = 0.900\text{ nm}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Since $588.1\text{ nm} < 589.0\text{ nm}$, this is a blueshift toward shorter wavelength indicating the star is approaching. (b) $v = c\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = 3.00 \times 10^8 \times \frac{0.900}{589.0} = 458 km s⁻¹$. (c) The equation is valid because $v \ll c$. In practice, the Doppler effect is used for measuring blood flow velocity in arteries and vehicle speed from the frequency shift of reflected waves.

markScheme.criterion: Notes observed wavelength decreases (shifts toward shorter/blue end).
States blueshift toward shorter wavelength indicating the star is approaching.
Applies $v = c\Delta\lambda / \lambda$ with $\Delta\lambda = 0.900\text{ nm}$ and $\lambda = 589.0\text{ nm}$.
Correct radial speed 458 km s⁻¹ (or $4.58 \times 10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}$).
States $v \ll c$ justifies the linear approximation.
Outlines measuring blood flow velocity in arteries and vehicle speed from the frequency shift of reflected waves.

parts.prompt: Deduce whether the star is approaching or receding from Earth, justifying your answer from the spectral shift.
parts.expectedAnswer: The observed wavelength is shorter than the laboratory value, which is a blueshift toward shorter wavelength indicating the star is approaching.
workingSteps: Compare observed wavelength $588.1\text{ nm}$ with rest wavelength $589.0\text{ nm}$.
Conclude this represents a blueshift toward shorter wavelength indicating the star is approaching.

parts.prompt: Calculate the radial speed of the star relative to Earth in $\text{km s}^{-1}$.
State why the relation $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}$ is valid here, and outline one practical use of the Doppler effect in medical physics or radar.
parts.expectedAnswer: The approximation holds because $v \ll c$ ($v/c \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-3}$). Practical applications include measuring blood flow velocity in arteries and vehicle speed from the frequency shift of reflected waves.
workingSteps: Note that the star's radial speed is much smaller than the speed of light ($v \ll c$).
Outline Doppler sensing: measuring blood flow velocity in arteries and vehicle speed from the frequency shift of reflected waves.

items.stem: Fixed at both ends, a stretched string (0.72 m long) vibrates in harmonic mode n = 5. Transverse waves travel along it at 252 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Standing wavelength: λ_5 = 2L / n = 2(0.72) / 5 = 0.288 m. (b) Pitch: f_5 = v / λ_5 = 252 / 0.288 = 875 Hz. (c) First harmonic: f₁ = f_5 / 5 = 175 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of this n = 5 harmonic standing wave.
workingSteps: For a string fixed at both ends, λ_n = 2L / n.

parts.prompt: Determine the oscillation frequency of this standing wave.
Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string when kept at the same tension.

items.stem: When a mobile sound receiver travels towards a stationary alarm of frequency 700 Hz, a frequency meter reads 853 Hz. With sound moving at 330 m s⁻¹, determine how fast the observer travels.
items.workedSolution: Doppler shift obeys f′ = f(v + v_o) / v; hence v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 330 × |853 / 700 − 1| = 72.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 72.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Measurements are taken at the n = 5 bright fringe on a viewing card 3.4 m from two narrow parallel slits. Monochromatic 420 nm light enters the 0.55 mm slit pair normally.
items.workedSolution: (a) Constructive shift: Δℓ = nλ = 5 × 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.10 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Direction: θ_5 = arcsin(nλ / d) = 0.219°. (c) Position: y_5 = nλD / d = 0.0130 m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the path difference between waves from S₁ and S₂ arriving at the n = 5 bright fringe.
workingSteps: For constructive interference at order n, Δℓ = nλ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deflection θ_5 (in degrees) of the n = 5 bright fringe from the central axis.
Determine the linear distance from the central bright fringe to the n = 5 bright fringe on the screen.

items.stem: A progressive sinusoidal wave travels to the right on a stretched string, as shown by the instantaneous displacement–position graph. The wave has amplitude 0.015 m, wavelength 0.6 m, and frequency 15 Hz.
items.workedSolution: (a) Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 15 = 0.0667 s. (b) Wave speed v = fλ = 15 × 0.6 = 9.00 m s⁻¹. (c) Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 94.2 rad s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = 1 / f with given frequency.
Substitutes into v = fλ or v = λ / T.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period of oscillation of a point in the medium.
Determine the propagation speed of the progressive wave.
workingSteps: Apply v = fλ (or v = λ / T).

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular frequency ω of the wave oscillations.

items.stem: The speed of sound equals 340 m s⁻¹ inside an open air pipe (0.32 m long) sustaining mode n = 3. Antinodes sit 0.02 m beyond each open end.
items.workedSolution: (a) Effective length: L_eff = L + 2e = 0.32 + 2(0.02) = 0.360 m. (b) Mode wavelength: λ_3 = 2L_eff / 3 = 0.240 m. (c) Frequency: f_3 = 340 / 0.240 = 1.42 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Adds twice the end correction: L_eff = L + 2e.

parts.prompt: Calculate the effective acoustic length L_eff between the two outer antinodes.
workingSteps: An open-both-ends pipe has two open ends, so L_eff = L + 2e.

parts.prompt: Determine the wavelength of the n = 3 harmonic mode.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this standing wave.

items.stem: Along a long stretched rope, a sinusoidal wave carries a 4 Hz oscillation (wavelength 0.6 m, amplitude 0.022 m). Two markers sit at x₁ = 0.15 m (P) and x₂ = 0.375 m (Q).
items.workedSolution: (a) Speed: v = fλ = 4 × 0.6 = 2.40 m s⁻¹. (b) One cycle takes T = 1 / 4 = 0.250 s. (c) Distance Δx = 0.225 m gives Δφ = 2π Δx / λ = 2.36 rad.

parts.prompt: Calculate the propagation speed of the wave.
Determine the oscillation period of particle P.
Calculate the phase difference, in radians, between the oscillations at P and Q.

items.stem: With a screen 1.8 m behind a single slit, 514 nm light produces a central maximum 7.40 mm wide. Determine the slit width b.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges w = 2λD / b to obtain b = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m (C).

options.label: B

items.stem: A real operational amplifier has a constant gain–bandwidth product of $2.40\text{ MHz}$ on its Bode frequency-response curve. An engineer wires it with negative feedback to provide a closed-loop voltage gain of $60.0$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\text{BW} = 2.40 \times 10^3 / 60.0 = 40.0 kHz$. (b) closed-loop gain remains constant up to the cutoff frequency then follows the constant gain-bandwidth product slope, so halving gain doubles bandwidth. (c) Real op-amps saturate near the supply rails and have finite $A_{\text{OL}}$, finite $R_{\text{in}}$, and non-zero $R_{\text{out}}$.

markScheme.criterion: Explains closed-loop gain remains constant up to the cutoff frequency then follows the constant gain-bandwidth product slope.
Concludes bandwidth doubles when gain halves.
Mentions output saturation at supply rails.

Explain how the Bode plot curve changes when the closed-loop gain is halved using feedback resistors.
parts.expectedAnswer: The closed-loop gain stays constant up to the cutoff frequency, then falls along the constant gain-bandwidth product slope. Halving the closed-loop gain lowers the flat plateau and doubles the usable bandwidth.

Conclude halving gain doubles cutoff bandwidth (to 80.0 kHz).

parts.prompt: State two limitations of a real operational amplifier besides its finite gain–bandwidth product.
parts.expectedAnswer: Output voltage saturates near the DC power supply rails, causing clipping. Real op-amps also have finite open-loop gain, finite input resistance, non-zero output resistance, and finite slew rate.
workingSteps: Limitation 1: output saturation/clipping at the power supply rails.
Limitation 2: finite open-loop gain $A_{\text{OL}}$, finite input resistance, or non-zero output resistance.

items.stem: Plane-polarized light enters an ideal analyzer at 32 W m⁻² and leaves at 13.2 W m⁻². The transmitted intensity obeys I = I₀ cos²θ. What acute angle θ does the axis make?
items.workedSolution: By I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(13.2 / 32) = 0.643 and θ = arccos(0.643) = 50.0°.

items.stem: Two triangular pulses of peak displacements $+7.00\text{ cm}$ and $-3.00\text{ cm}$ travel towards each other along a stretched slinky at equal speeds of $5.00\text{ cm s}^{-1}$. At $t = 0$, their peaks are $25.0\text{ cm}$ apart.
items.workedSolution: (a) $t = 2.50 s$. (b) $y = +4.00 cm$. (c) When two pulses overlap, the resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. Afterwards, both pulses pass through each other unchanged. (d) Diffraction spreading is strongest when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: Uses relative approach speed 2v = 10.0 cm s⁻¹.
States resultant displacement equals algebraic/vector sum of individual displacements.
States the two pulses pass through each other unchanged after their displacements add during overlap.
States little spreading when b ≫ λ and strong spreading when b ≈ λ.
States diffraction spreading is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time elapsed before the peaks of the two pulses completely coincide.
Determine the resultant displacement at the midpoint at the instant of complete overlap.
State the principle of superposition and describe what happens to the two pulses after they pass through each other.
parts.expectedAnswer: By superposition, the resultant displacement during overlap equals the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. After overlapping, the pulses pass through each other unchanged.
workingSteps: During overlap, the resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of individual displacements. Both pulses then pass through each other unchanged.

parts.prompt: Explain how the ratio of aperture width $b$ to wavelength $\lambda$ affects the diffraction of plane waves passing through a gap.
parts.expectedAnswer: Diffraction spreading through an aperture or around an obstacle is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.
workingSteps: diffraction spreading through an aperture or around an obstacle is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.

items.stem: One end is sealed on a cylindrical pipe of length 0.28 m, ignoring end effects. It vibrates in odd harmonic n = 3 with sound speed 340 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Effective length L_eff = 0.280 m gives first harmonic f₁ = v / (4L_eff) = 304 Hz. (b) Wavelength: λ_3 = 4L_eff / 3 = 0.373 m. (c) Mode frequency: f_3 = 3f₁ = 911 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies quarter-wave first-harmonic relation f₁ = v / (4L_eff).
Multiplies first-harmonic frequency by odd harmonic index 3 (or uses v / λ).

parts.prompt: Calculate the first-harmonic (n = 1) frequency of this closed-end air column.
workingSteps: For a pipe closed at one end, λ₁ = 4L so f₁ = v / (4L).

parts.prompt: Determine the wavelength of the n = 3 harmonic standing wave.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this n = 3 harmonic mode.

items.stem: A concert flute modelled as a cylindrical air pipe open at both ends has length $L = 0.850\text{ m}$ (speed of sound $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$, neglecting end effects).
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_1 = 200 Hz$. (b) $f_2 = 400 Hz$. (c) A pipe with two open ends forms a displacement antinode at each open end and supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n. (d) Useful resonance maximizes energy transfer when driving frequency matches natural frequency, as in wind instruments, radio receivers, and microwave heating.

markScheme.criterion: States displacement antinodes form at both open ends.
Links displacement antinodes at both open ends to all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.
Defines maximum energy transfer when driving frequency matches natural frequency.
Gives valid examples of useful resonance where driving frequency matches natural frequency (wind instruments, radio receivers, or microwave heating).

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the first harmonic in this open–open pipe.
Calculate the frequency of the second harmonic.
Describe the displacement boundary condition at both ends of an open–open pipe.
parts.expectedAnswer: A pipe with two open ends forms a displacement antinode at each open end. It supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.
workingSteps: a pipe with two open ends forms a displacement antinode at each open end and supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.

parts.prompt: Explain what is meant by useful resonance, giving two practical examples.
parts.expectedAnswer: Useful resonance maximizes energy transfer when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency. Examples include wind instruments, radio receivers, and microwave heating.
workingSteps: useful resonance maximizes energy transfer when driving frequency matches natural frequency such as in wind instruments radio receivers and microwave heating.

items.stem: A microwave transmitter directs microwaves onto a vertical metal plate. Moving a probe detector along a metre rule records a span of 7.5 cm across 5 consecutive node-to-node intervals (between the 1st and 6th minima). Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) 3.00 cm. (b) 10.0 GHz. (c) Microwaves reflect from the metal sheet and superpose with the incident beam. A probe moved along the axis detects adjacent minima separated by half a wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f = c / λ in SI units.
Explains incident and reflected microwaves superpose to form stationary nodes spaced by λ/2.
Explains larger measured span lowers percentage uncertainty.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength λ of the microwaves in cm.
Calculate the frequency of the microwaves in GHz.
Explain why alternating maxima and minima appear and why measuring across 5 intervals reduces percentage uncertainty.
parts.expectedAnswer: Microwaves reflect from the metal sheet and superpose with the incident beam, creating adjacent minima separated by half a wavelength. Measuring across 5 intervals makes the distance five times larger for the same ruler uncertainty, cutting percentage uncertainty by a factor of five.
workingSteps: Microwaves reflect from the metal sheet and superpose with the incident beam. Adjacent minima along the axis are separated by half a wavelength.

items.stem: A student keeps the vibrating length $L$ fixed in Required Practical 1 and varies the hanging mass $m$ to obtain the first harmonic each time. Which graph gives a straight line through the origin and why?
items.workedSolution: Plot f₁² against m (or f₁ against √T) to obtain a straight line through the origin. Measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes, since first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Plots f₁² against m (or f₁ against √T), measuring length between the bridge and pulley nodes.

options.label: A
options.text: Plot f₁² against m (or f₁ against √T), and measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

options.label: B
options.text: Plot f₁ directly against m because wave speed is directly proportional to tension.
options.distractorRationale: Wave speed scales with √T, so f₁ ∝ √m rather than f₁ ∝ m.

options.label: C
options.text: Plot f₁ against 1/m because heavier masses slow down transverse oscillations.
options.distractorRationale: Greater tension increases wave speed and raises the resonant frequency.

options.label: D
options.text: Plot 1/f₁ against √m because frequency decreases as tension increases.
options.distractorRationale: Frequency increases linearly with √m.

items.stem: A lunar-mapping reflector of diameter 1.60 m observes craters on the Moon at a distance of 3.84 × 10⁸ m using green light of wavelength 500 nm. Neglecting atmospheric distortion, what is the smallest surface feature separation just resolved?
items.workedSolution: $\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D} = \frac{5.00 \times 10^{-7}}{1.60} = 3.13 × 10⁻⁷ rad$. The linear separation is $s = r\theta = 3.84 \times 10^{8} \times 3.13 × 10⁻⁷ = 120 m$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes mirror radius instead of diameter into the Rayleigh criterion.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides the resolved linear separation by two erroneously.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Makes a factor-of-ten power error converting nanometres to metres.

items.stem: Sound waves leave an ambulance siren at 820 Hz and travel at 336 m s⁻¹ in still air. Moving directly towards a stationary listener at 60 m s⁻¹, what frequency is detected?
items.workedSolution: Substitute into the moving-source formula (towards): f' = fv / (v − v_s) = (820 × 336) / (336 − 60) = 998 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 998 Hz (D).

options.distractorRationale: Uses the moving-observer formula AND reverses the sign of the Doppler frequency shift.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the wrong sign in the denominator, using v + v_s for an approaching source (or v − v_s for a receding source).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the moving-observer equation f(v ± v_s) / v instead of the moving-source equation fv / (v ∓ v_s).

items.stem: Set 1.5 m behind a pair of narrow slits (spacing 0.45 mm), a matte screen catches the pattern from a 488 nm laser beam striking at normal incidence.
items.workedSolution: (a) Spacing = λD / d = (4.88 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.5) / 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.63 × 10⁻³ m. (b) First minimum distance = ½ × 1.63 × 10⁻³ = 8.13 × 10⁻⁴ m. (c) Constructive shift at n = 2: nλ = 2 × 4.88 × 10⁻⁷ = 9.76 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units and substitutes into λD / (slit separation).
Takes half of the bright-fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
Determine the distance on the screen from the central bright maximum to the centre of the first dark fringe.
workingSteps: First destructive minimum occurs halfway between the central and first-order bright maxima: y_dark,1 = 0.5 × fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the geometric path difference between waves arriving from the two slits at the order n = 2 bright fringe.
workingSteps: Constructive interference at order n requires path difference Δℓ = nλ.

items.stem: Which statement accurately summarises the principal advantages and trade-offs of VHF FM radio broadcasting compared with medium-wave AM broadcasting?
items.workedSolution: Electrical interference mainly adds amplitude spikes, which FM receivers clip away. Therefore, FM gives better noise immunity and audio quality than AM, at the cost of wider channel bandwidth and shorter line-of-sight range.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that FM provides superior noise immunity and audio fidelity than AM at the cost of wider channel bandwidth and shorter line-of-sight range.

options.label: A
options.text: AM provides superior noise immunity and wider audio bandwidth while occupying much wider channels than FM.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses both noise immunity and bandwidth characteristics of AM versus FM.

options.label: B
options.text: FM requires far narrower bandwidth than AM and diffracts easily around hills via ground waves.
options.distractorRationale: FM needs ~180–200 kHz vs AM ~9 kHz, and VHF FM travels mostly line-of-sight.

options.label: C
options.text: Both AM and FM have identical noise immunity because lightning interference alters carrier frequency equally.
options.distractorRationale: Electrical interference mainly changes amplitude, which FM limiters remove.

options.label: D
options.text: FM provides superior noise immunity and audio fidelity than AM at the cost of wider channel bandwidth and shorter line-of-sight range.

items.stem: Sound waves enter the outer auditory canal and vibrate an eardrum of area $66.0\text{ mm}^2$ with a pressure amplitude of $0.0600\text{ Pa}$. The middle-ear ossicles provide a lever force ratio of $1.35$ and drive an oval window of area $3.30\text{ mm}^2$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Pressure gain $= 1.35 \times (66.0 / 3.30) = 27.0$. (b) $P_{\text{oval}} = 27.0 \times 0.0600 = 1.62 Pa$. (c) The ossicles lever increases force and smaller oval window amplifies pressure into cochlea fluid to match air to fluid impedance.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies lever ratio $1.35$ by area ratio $66.0 / 3.30$.
Explains ossicles lever increases force and smaller oval window amplifies pressure into cochlea fluid.
Notes impedance matching prevents excessive reflection at the air–fluid boundary.

parts.prompt: Calculate the overall pressure amplification factor between the eardrum and oval window.
Calculate the resulting pressure amplitude acting on the cochlear fluid.
workingSteps: Multiply 27.0 by $0.0600\text{ Pa}$ to get 1.62 Pa.

parts.prompt: Explain why this mechanical amplification is necessary when transferring sound from air into the inner ear.
parts.expectedAnswer: The ossicles lever increases force and the smaller oval window amplifies pressure into the cochlear fluid. This overcomes the acoustic impedance mismatch between air and fluid so waves are transmitted rather than reflected.
workingSteps: State ossicles lever increases force and smaller oval window amplifies pressure into cochlea fluid.
Explain this matches the acoustic impedance of air to dense cochlear fluid.

items.stem: The diagram shows unpolarized light of intensity 260 W m⁻² incident on two ideal polarizing filters. The beam passes first through polarizer P₁ and then through analyzer A tilted at θ = 70° to P₁. For plane-polarized light, transmitted intensity obeys I = I₁ cos²θ.
items.workedSolution: (a) After P₁, I₁ = ½ I₀ = 130 W m⁻². (b) After analyzer A, I = I₁ cos²(70°) = 15.2 W m⁻². (c) Overall fraction I / I₀ = ½ cos²(70°) = 0.0585.

markScheme.criterion: Halves unpolarized incident intensity at ideal polarizer P₁.
Applies I = I₁ cos²θ to the polarized beam.
Divides final transmitted intensity by incident unpolarized intensity I₀.

parts.prompt: State and calculate the intensity I₁ of the plane-polarized beam between polarizer P₁ and analyzer A.
workingSteps: Averaging cos²φ = ½ over all random polarization orientations reduces unpolarized intensity by half: I₁ = ½ I₀.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity I emerging from analyzer A.
workingSteps: Apply Malus's law I = I₁ cos²θ.

parts.prompt: Determine the overall fraction I / I₀ of the original unpolarized intensity transmitted by the two-filter combination.
workingSteps: Overall transmission fraction = I / I₀ = ½ cos²θ.

items.stem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.64 m and mass per unit length 0.0015 kg m⁻¹. Its n = 1 harmonic resonates at 164.1 Hz. The transverse wave speed on a taut string is v = √(T / μ). Calculate the tension T in the string.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.64) / 1 = 1.28 m, so required wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 210 m s⁻¹. Rearranging v = √(T / μ) gives T = μv² = 0.0015 × (210)² = 66.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 2Lf_n / n and computes T = μv² = 66.2 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to square the wave speed when rearranging v = √(T / μ) to T = μv².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, halving v and underestimating T = μv² by a factor of 4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides v² by linear mass density μ instead of multiplying T = μv².

items.stem: A stretched wire of length $1.60\text{ m}$ vibrates in its fourth harmonic ($4$ loops) at $200\text{ Hz}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) superposition of two progressive waves with equal frequency wavelength and amplitude travelling in opposite directions. (b) Adjacent nodes are $0.400\text{ m}$ apart ($\lambda = 0.800\text{ m}$), giving $c = 160\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

markScheme.criterion: Two progressive waves of same frequency, wavelength, and amplitude travelling in opposite directions.
Superpose (vector sum of displacements — reject bare 'interfere' when defining superpose).

parts.prompt: Explain how a stationary wave is formed on the wire.
parts.expectedAnswer: Two progressive waves of equal frequency, wavelength, and amplitude travel in opposite directions. Their displacements add by vector superposition to form a stationary wave.
workingSteps: State equal f, λ, amplitude progressive waves travelling in opposite directions superposing (vector sum of displacements).

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance between two adjacent nodes and the progressive wave speed along the wire.
parts.expectedAnswer: Node spacing $= 0.400 m$; wave speed $= 160 m s⁻¹$
workingSteps: Node spacing $= L/4 = 0.400\text{ m}$, so $\lambda = 0.800\text{ m}$.

items.stem: A Doppler ultrasound probe emits waves of frequency 5.00 MHz at 60.0° to a femoral artery. Blood flows towards the probe at 0.450 m s⁻¹, and the speed of ultrasound in blood is 1540 m s⁻¹. Using $\Delta f / f = (2v\cos\theta)/c$, calculate the magnitude of the frequency shift $\Delta f$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Δf = (2 f v cos θ) / c to obtain 1.46 × 10³ Hz.

items.stem: In the single-slit diffraction experiment shown, the red laser is replaced by a blue laser of shorter wavelength. The slit width and screen distance stay fixed. Which statement remains true about the new diffraction pattern?
items.workedSolution: A shorter wavelength narrows the entire pattern proportionally. However, the central maximum stays twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases. Therefore option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases.

options.label: A
options.text: The pattern becomes wider overall because shorter blue wavelengths diffract through larger angles
options.distractorRationale: Shorter wavelength reduces diffraction spreading (width ∝ λ/a).

options.label: B
options.text: The pattern becomes narrower overall, while the central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases

options.label: C
options.text: The pattern changes so every fringe has identical width and equal peak brightness
options.distractorRationale: Single-slit diffraction always retains a 2:1 central width ratio and steeply decaying side peaks.

options.label: D
options.text: The pattern shifts sideways away from the optical axis towards the violet side
options.distractorRationale: The pattern stays symmetric about the central maximum.

items.workedSolution: (a) 2.00 μm. (b) 19.3°. (c) n = 3. (d) adjacent grating slits separated by d create a path difference d sin theta between parallel rays, yielding constructive interference when d sin theta equals n lambda.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ ≤ 1 to evaluate d / λ = 3.03.
Rounds down to integer maximum order n = 3.
Identifies path difference d sin θ from right-angled triangle between adjacent slits.
Sets path difference equal to integer multiple nλ for constructive superposition.

items.stem: A flat screen sits $D = 1.40$ m behind a 300 lines mm⁻¹ diffraction grating illuminated by a monochromatic red laser. Between the $n = +2$ and $n = -2$ bright spots, the symmetric distance is $2h = 1.152$ m.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\theta = \arctan(0.576/1.4) = 22.4^\circ$. (b) $\lambda = d\sin\theta/2 = 634 nm$. (c) $n_{\max} = \lfloor d/\lambda \rfloor = 5$. (d) Align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square. Measure the symmetric span between matching orders, and never look directly into the laser.

markScheme.criterion: Halves 2h to obtain h and applies $\tan\theta = h/D$.
Sets $\sin\theta \le 1$ to evaluate $d/\lambda$ and rounds down.
Aligns grating perpendicular to incident beam using a set square.
Measuring symmetric span 2h reduces % uncertainty and checks symmetry.

parts.prompt: Calculate the diffraction angle $\theta$ for the $n = 2$ order maximum.
Determine the wavelength $\lambda$ of the laser in nm.
Calculate the maximum diffraction order $n_{\max}$ observable on either side of the central maximum.
Explain how the student verifies normal incidence of the grating and why measuring $2h$ is superior to measuring $h$ alone.
parts.expectedAnswer: Align the grating perpendicular to the beam using a set square. Measure the symmetric span between matching orders, and never look directly into the laser.
workingSteps: Check 90° alignment with a set square against bench/screen and verify equal +n and −n distances.
Measuring 2h halves percentage uncertainty and averages out small zero-order alignment offsets.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 650 nm illuminates two narrow parallel slits placed 2.6 m from a screen. Each slit has width 0.08 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.32 mm. Which positive interference order n is the first missing order due to single-slit diffraction?
items.workedSolution: Interference maxima satisfy sin θ = nλ / d and the first single-slit minimum satisfies sin θ = λ / b. Dividing gives n = d / b = 3.20 × 10⁻⁴ / 8.00 × 10⁻⁵ = 4.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Selects the last bright interference order visible inside one side of the central envelope (d/b − 1) instead of the missing order d/b.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Counts the total number of bright fringes inside the central diffraction envelope (2d/b − 1) instead of the missing order index.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles d / b by using full angular width 2λ / b instead of first-minimum angle λ / b.

items.stem: The wavefront diagram shows a sound source S moving steadily toward stationary Observer A while moving away from stationary Observer B. Why does Observer A detect a higher frequency than the emitted frequency?
items.workedSolution: The source moves forward between consecutive wave emissions while each wavefront travels outward at fixed speed $v$ in air. This creates compressed wavefronts with a shorter wavelength ahead of the moving source, increasing the observed frequency $f' = v/\lambda'$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that compressed wavefronts with shorter wavelength ahead of the moving source.

options.label: A
options.text: Motion of the source creates compressed wavefronts with shorter wavelength ahead of the moving source, so more wavefronts reach Observer A each second at unchanged wave speed in air.

options.label: B
options.text: The speed of sound in air increases ahead of the source while the wavelength stays constant.
options.distractorRationale: Wave speed in air depends only on the medium, not the speed of the source.

options.label: C
options.text: The source oscillates at a higher intrinsic frequency in the forward direction than in the backward direction.
options.distractorRationale: The source emits wavefronts at one constant intrinsic frequency in all directions.

options.label: D
options.text: Wavefronts stretch further apart ahead of the source so each crest carries greater energy.
options.distractorRationale: Wavefronts are stretched behind the source (toward B), not ahead of it.

items.stem: In harmonic mode n = 5, a 0.96 m taut string clamped at both ends carries transverse waves at 168 m s⁻¹. Determine its frequency of oscillation.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f_n = nv / (2L) to obtain 438 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic frequency v / (2L) instead of multiplying by harmonic number n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the closed-one-end pipe formula nv / (4L) instead of fixed-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n, computing f = nv / L.

items.stem: Still air carries sound at 340 m s⁻¹. A listener receding from a stationary loudspeaker at 78 m s⁻¹ intercepts its 580 Hz waves. Calculate the apparent frequency.
items.workedSolution: Heard frequency equals f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 580 × (340 − 78) / 340 = 447 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 447 Hz (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Places observer speed in the denominator fv / (v ∓ v_o) as if the source were moving rather than the observer.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the observer Doppler sign in f(v ± v_o) / v.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the moving-source denominator formula AND reverses the Doppler sign.

items.stem: Spaced 0.22 mm apart, two narrow parallel slits cast Young's fringes from 532 nm rays onto a wall 3.4 m away. Determine the position of the n = 4 bright fringe from the central maximum.
items.workedSolution: Band separation = λD / d = 8.22 × 10⁻³ m. Order n = 4 lies from n = 0 at y_4 = 4 × λD / d = 0.0329 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates single adjacent fringe spacing λD / d instead of multiplying by order n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies destructive half-integer factor (n − ½) instead of constructive integer order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Counts one extra interval, multiplying fringe spacing by (n + 1) fringes instead of n intervals from n = 0.

items.stem: A sinusoidal wave travelling on a long stretched rope has amplitude 0.036 m and wavelength 1.5 m, as shown in the displacement–position graph y(x). The wave source vibrates at 85 Hz. What is the speed of the wave?
items.workedSolution: From the displacement–position profile, wavelength λ = 1.5 m and frequency f = 85 Hz. Using the wave equation v = fλ = 85 Hz × 1.5 m = 128 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = fλ to obtain 128 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides wavelength by frequency (λ / f), confusing frequency f with period T.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides frequency by wavelength (f / λ) instead of applying v = fλ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the wavelength by misreading a two-cycle span as a single wavelength.

items.stem: Sound moves at 334 m s⁻¹ inside a resonance tube open at both ends (with ideal open-end conditions). If its n = 4 harmonic resonates at 530.2 Hz, determine the pipe's length.
items.workedSolution: Solve for pipe length: L = nv / (2f_n) = (4 × 334) / (2 × 530) = 1.26 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = nv / (2f_n) to obtain 1.26 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits harmonic number n, computing first-harmonic half-wavelength v / (2f_n).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies the closed-one-end pipe relation L = nv / (4f_n) instead of open-both-ends L = nv / (2f_n).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in L = nλ / 2.

items.stem: With 200 lines mm⁻¹, a grating diffracts 430 nm light at normal incidence onto a screen 1.6 m away. Analyse the bright spot at order n = 3.
items.workedSolution: (a) Slit separation: d = 10⁻³ / 200 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) From sin θ = nλ / d = 0.258 we obtain θ = 15.0°. (c) On screen: y = D tan θ = 1.6 × tan(15.0°) = 0.427 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises large-angle geometry y = D tan θ rather than small-angle D sin θ.

items.stem: On a time trace for a slinky spring, an 8 Hz wave has amplitude 0.022 m and wavelength 1.2 m. What is the phase difference in radians between t = 0.01875 s (point P) and t = 0.1125 s (point Q)?
items.workedSolution: First find Δt = 0.1125 s − 0.01875 s = 0.09375 s. Comparing against one cycle (1 / f = 0.125 s) gives 0.750 cycles, so Δφ = 2π × 0.750 = 4.71 rad.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 2π rad to get 4.71 rad (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (π rad) instead of a full cycle (2π rad) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in degrees instead of radians.

items.stem: Behind a single narrow vertical slit (0.18 mm wide) stands a flat screen at 1.8 m. A 405 nm laser beam enters normally.
items.workedSolution: (a) Minimum angle: θ = λ / b = 2.25 × 10⁻³ rad. (b) Half-width: y₁ = θD = 4.05 × 10⁻³ m. (c) Total central width: w = 2y₁ = 8.10 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies θ = λ / b in SI units.
Multiplies θ by screen distance D.
Doubles half-width to span both sides of the central peak.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular position θ (in radians) of the first diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Use the small-angle single-slit first-minimum relation θ = λ / b.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear distance on the screen from the centre of the pattern to the first dark minimum.
Calculate the full linear width of the central bright maximum on the screen.
workingSteps: The central maximum spans from −y₁ to +y₁: w = 2y₁.

items.stem: Why was James Clerk Maxwell's derivation of $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$ regarded as a milestone unifying electricity, magnetism, and optics?
items.workedSolution: Evaluating $1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$ gave $3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$—calculating electromagnetic wave speed from permittivity and permeability matched the measured speed of light showing light is an electromagnetic wave.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that calculating electromagnetic wave speed from permittivity and permeability matched the measured speed of light showing light is an electromagnetic wave.

items.stem: A geostationary communications satellite receives an up-link signal around $6\text{ GHz}$ and re-transmits the down-link around $4\text{ GHz}$. Why must satellite up-links and down-links use different carrier frequencies?
items.workedSolution: The signal arriving from Earth is very weak compared with the satellite's amplified broadcast. Using different up-link and down-link frequencies prevents the powerful transmitter from de-sensing the sensitive receiver.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that different up-link and down-link frequencies prevent the powerful transmitter de-sensing the sensitive receiver.
