items.stem: Exciting odd harmonic n = 3 in an air column closed at one end (0.76 m long, with zero end effect), a student takes sound speed as 330 m s⁻¹. Work out its frequency.
items.workedSolution: Effective length for one open end: L_eff = L + e = 0.760 m. At n = 3, f_n = nv / (4L_eff) = (3 × 330) / (4 × 0.760) = 326 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the n = 1 first-harmonic frequency v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the prohibited even harmonic (n − 1) into nv / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies open-both-ends formula nv / (2L) instead of closed-one-end nv / (4L).

items.stem: Civil engineers install tuned mass dampers inside tall suspension bridges and skyscrapers located in windy or seismic zones. Why is damping necessary to prevent destructive resonance?
items.workedSolution: When the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, energy builds up each cycle and amplitudes grow dangerously large. Dampers dissipate this vibrational energy so amplitudes stay safe. Therefore option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: destructive resonance causes dangerously large amplitudes when forcing matches natural frequency, so damping dissipates energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Because resonance stops structures from vibrating altogether unless damping forces them to oscillate.
options.distractorRationale: Resonance causes excessive oscillation amplitude; damping dissipates mechanical energy to limit amplitude.

options.label: B
options.text: Because periodic wind or seismic driving transfers zero energy whenever its frequency matches the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Maximum energy transfer occurs precisely when the driving frequency matches the structure's natural frequency.

options.label: C
options.text: Because adding damping eliminates the structure's mass so its natural frequency becomes infinite.
options.distractorRationale: Damping dissipates vibrational energy as thermal energy rather than eliminating mass.

options.label: D
options.text: Destructive resonance drives dangerously large oscillation amplitudes when periodic forcing matches structural natural frequency so damping is introduced to dissipate energy.

items.stem: The three snapshots show two progressive waves combining along a stretched string. Which exact condition is required to form a stationary wave with permanent zero-displacement nodes?
items.workedSolution: Opposite travel directions with matching frequency, wavelength, and amplitude keep nodes fixed in place. Two identical progressive waves travelling in opposite directions superpose to produce fixed nodes and antinodes. Therefore option A is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: two progressive waves of identical frequency, wavelength, and amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose to produce fixed nodes and antinodes.

options.label: A
options.text: To establish a stationary wave pattern, two progressive waves of identical frequency, wavelength, and amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose to produce fixed nodes and antinodes.

options.label: B
options.text: Two progressive waves of different frequencies travel in the same direction with unequal amplitudes.
options.distractorRationale: Waves travelling in the same direction with different frequencies produce moving beats, not fixed nodes.

options.label: C
options.text: A single progressive wave slows down continuously until its speed reaches zero at fixed positions.
options.distractorRationale: The wave speed v on the string stays constant; nodes arise from continuous destructive superposition of two opposite waves.

options.label: D
options.text: Two progressive waves of identical speed travel in the same direction with a fixed phase difference of pi/2 radians.
options.distractorRationale: Superposing two same-direction waves simply produces another progressive wave.

items.stem: Plotting first-harmonic frequency $f_1$ against $1/L$ for an enamelled copper string in Required Practical 1 gives gradient 36.1 m s⁻¹ through the origin. Tension comes from a 0.85 kg hanging mass ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²) as length $L$ varies. Mass, frequency, and length have percentage uncertainties of 1.1%, 0.5%, and 0.3% respectively.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v = 2 \times 36.1 = 72.2 m s⁻¹$. (b) $T = 8.34 N$, $\mu = T/v^2 = 1.60 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$. (c) $\%\Delta \mu = 1.1 + 2(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 2.70\%$. (d) measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $T = mg = 8.34 N$ and substitutes into $\mu = T/v^2$.
Mass per unit length $\mu = 1.60 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$.
Doubles percentage uncertainties in both $f_1$ and $L$ before adding $\%\Delta m$.
Measures vibrating length between wooden bridge and top of pulley (fixed nodes).
Links fixed-node span to first-harmonic condition $f_1 = v/(2L)$.

items.stem: Monochromatic light (405 nm) travels normally through a double slit of spacing 0.5 mm. Determine the distance between adjacent bright maxima 3.6 m away.
items.workedSolution: Using λ = 4.05 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m, adjacent bright-fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) = (4.05 × 10⁻⁷ × 3.6) / 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.92 × 10⁻³ m.

items.stem: A telecommunications network sends dozens of voice channels along one long-distance cable. It uses pulse-code modulation (PCM), time-division multiplexing (TDM), and periodic regenerators.
items.workedSolution: An analogue signal is sampled above twice its maximum frequency, quantised into binary words, interleaved by TDM, and cleaned by regenerators. Nyquist sampling prevents aliasing, and higher bit depth reduces $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n$ at the cost of a higher bit rate. TDM fills gaps between samples on one link, regenerators remove noise, and demultiplexing with a DAC and filter recovers speech.

markScheme.criterion: Explains periodic sampling at or above the Nyquist rate ($f_{\mathrm{s}} \ge 2 f_{\max}$) to prevent aliasing distortion.
Explains ADC quantisation into $n$-bit binary PCM words with resolution $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n$.
Notes the trade-off between finer resolution (higher $n$, lower quantisation noise) and higher required bit rate ($f_{\mathrm{s}} n$) / bandwidth.
Explains time-division multiplexing interleaving binary words from multiple channels into time slots between consecutive samples.
Explains how regenerators restore crisp logic levels and remove accumulated noise, unlike analogue amplifiers.
Explains synchronised demultiplexing, DAC conversion, and low-pass smoothing to recover the original analogue signals.

parts.prompt: Explain how multiple analogue voice signals are converted into a shared digital PCM/TDM stream and sent cleanly over long distances with regenerators. Explain how the signals are reconstructed without aliasing or excessive quantisation noise.
parts.expectedAnswer: Each analogue voice channel is band-limited and sampled above twice its maximum frequency (Nyquist criterion) to avoid aliasing distortion. An ADC quantises each sample into an $n$-bit binary PCM word. Increasing bit depth $n$ reduces step size $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n$ and quantisation noise, but raises bit rate $f_{\mathrm{s}} \times n$. Because each binary word takes only a short fraction of the sample period $T_{\mathrm{s}}$, a synchronised TDM multiplexer interleaves words from many channels onto one link. Along the cable, periodic regenerators compare attenuated noisy pulses against a threshold and rebuild clean binary pulses, removing noise before bit errors occur. At the receiver, a synchronised demultiplexer separates the channels, and DACs with low-pass filters recover smooth analogue speech.
workingSteps: L1: State that the analogue signal is sampled periodically at $f_{\mathrm{s}} \ge 2 f_{\max}$ to avoid aliasing.
L1: State that each sample is quantised by an ADC into an $n$-bit binary word (PCM).
L2: Link bit depth $n$ to quantisation resolution $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n$ and bit rate $f_{\mathrm{s}} n$ trade-off.
L2: Explain TDM: short binary pulses occupy tiny time slots, allowing words from multiple channels to interleave on one cable with receiver synchronisation.
L3: Explain periodic regenerators restoring clean binary logic levels and eliminating noise (unlike analogue amplifiers that amplify noise too).
L3: Describe receiver demultiplexing, DAC conversion, and low-pass filtering to reconstruct smooth audio.

items.stem: Why is sound intensity level measured on the logarithmic decibel scale rather than on a simple linear scale of $\text{W m}^{-2}$?
items.workedSolution: The ear detects intensities spanning roughly twelve orders of magnitude ($10^{-12}$ to $1\text{ W m}^{-2}$) and human loudness perception is logarithmic across a vast intensity range.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that human loudness perception is logarithmic across a vast intensity range.

options.label: A
options.text: Because sound waves cannot propagate linearly above 1 W m⁻² without becoming transverse waves.
options.distractorRationale: Sound remains longitudinal; the decibel scale reflects human sensory perception and dynamic range.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the threshold of hearing is zero watts per square metre, making linear ratios impossible.
options.distractorRationale: The threshold of hearing is finite ($I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$).

options.label: C
options.text: Because human loudness perception is logarithmic across a vast intensity range, so equal increments in dB match roughly equal perceived loudness steps.

options.label: D
options.text: Because perceived loudness is directly proportional to the square of sound intensity.
options.distractorRationale: Perceived loudness follows a logarithmic, not quadratic, dependence on intensity.

items.stem: An unpolarized light beam of unknown intensity I₀ passes through an ideal polarizer P₁ and then through an ideal analyzer A. The transmission axis of A is tilted at θ = 70° relative to P₁, and the emerging intensity is 3.74 W m⁻². Given I = I₁ cos²θ for plane-polarized light, calculate I₀.
items.workedSolution: Since I = ½ I₀ cos²θ, rearranging gives I₀ = 2I / cos²(70°) = (2 × 3.74) / 0.117 = 64.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Solves I = ½ I₀ cos²θ to obtain I₀ = 64.0 W m⁻² (D).

items.stem: A trainee sonographer holds a Doppler ultrasound probe almost perpendicular to a deep artery (θ ≈ 80°). Too little coupling gel is applied, and the blood speed reading is noisy and inaccurate.
items.workedSolution: Doppler ultrasound measures arterial blood speed non-invasively in real time without ionising radiation or surgical catheterisation. Too little gel leaves air gaps with a large acoustic impedance mismatch, reflecting most energy at the skin. Near 80°, cos θ is very small and changes rapidly with small angle errors. This gives a weak Δf and a large percentage uncertainty in v = cΔf/(2f cos θ). Applying enough gel, reducing θ to roughly 30°–60°, and measuring θ accurately using B-scan imaging restores reliable non-invasive flow speeds.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Notes that missing gel traps air with much lower acoustic impedance than soft tissue.
L1: Explains large acoustic impedance mismatch reflects nearly all ultrasound at the skin boundary.
L2: Uses Δf/f = (2v cos θ)/c to show cos θ approaches zero near 90°, giving a tiny Doppler shift.
L2: Explains that small errors in estimating θ near 80° cause large fractional errors in cos θ and calculated v.
L3: Recommends generous coupling gel and positioning beam at moderate known angle (30°–60°).
L3: Highlights safe, real-time, non-invasive vascular diagnosis without ionising radiation.

parts.prompt: Evaluate the physical errors in this scan technique. Explain how a clinician modifies the setup to obtain accurate arterial flow speeds while keeping the benefits of Doppler ultrasound. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Doppler ultrasound measures arterial blood speed non-invasively in real time without ionising radiation or surgical catheterisation. Too little gel leaves air gaps with a large acoustic impedance mismatch, reflecting most energy at the skin. Near 80°, cos θ is very small and changes rapidly with small angle errors. This gives a weak Δf and a large percentage uncertainty in v = cΔf/(2f cos θ). Applying enough gel, reducing θ to roughly 30°–60°, and measuring θ accurately using B-scan imaging restores reliable non-invasive flow speeds.
workingSteps: Explain acoustic impedance reflection loss from air gaps when coupling gel is inadequate.
Analyse why large θ near 90° shrinks Δf ∝ cos θ and amplifies angle uncertainty.
Recommend practical improvements (gel, smaller known θ via B-mode, steady probe) and summarise non-invasive advantages.

items.stem: An obstetric 3.50 MHz ultrasound probe (crystal wave speed 4200 m s⁻¹) performs an A-scan across a fetal skull ($c = 1540\text{ m s}^{-1}$), producing echoes at $60\,\mu\text{s}$ and $130\,\mu\text{s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Crystal thickness $= 0.600 mm$. (b) Diameter $= 53.9 mm$. (c) A-scan plots echo amplitude against time for one dimensional depth measurement whereas B-scan modulates spot brightness to form a two dimensional cross section.

markScheme.criterion: Describes A-scan as 1D amplitude vs time for depth/diameter.

parts.expectedAnswer: Clinically, A-scan plots echo amplitude against time for one dimensional depth measurement whereas B-scan modulates spot brightness to form a two dimensional cross section.
workingSteps: A-scan plots echo voltage spikes against time for precise 1D diameter measurement.
B-scan converts echo amplitude into dot brightness across probe angles to form a 2D anatomical image.

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 532 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 500 lines mm⁻¹. Including the central zero-order maximum, how many total principal maxima emerge across the forward semicircle (−90° ≤ θ ≤ +90°)?
items.workedSolution: d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m, so d / λ = 3.76 and n_max = 3. Including ±1..±3 and n = 0 gives 2(3) + 1 = 7 principal maxima.

options.distractorRationale: Gives the highest single-side order n_max instead of total maxima 2n_max + 1.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Counts ±1.. ±n_max side orders (2n_max) while forgetting the central n = 0 maximum.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Rounds d / λ = 3.76 up to 4 before applying 2n_max + 1.

items.stem: A wave propagates horizontally from left to right along a medium. Which statement correctly distinguishes a transverse travelling wave from a longitudinal travelling wave?
items.workedSolution: Transverse displacement is perpendicular to propagation direction, as in string or EM waves. Longitudinal displacement is parallel to energy transfer, as in sound. Therefore option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: transverse oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer, whereas longitudinal oscillations are parallel.

options.label: A
options.text: Transverse waves carry matter permanently forward along the wave whereas longitudinal waves transfer only energy.
options.distractorRationale: Neither travelling wave type produces net transport of medium particles over complete cycles.

options.label: B
options.text: In a transverse wave particles oscillate perpendicular to energy transfer whereas in a longitudinal wave particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer.

options.label: C
options.text: In a transverse wave particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer whereas in a longitudinal wave they oscillate perpendicular to energy transfer.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the geometric definitions of transverse and longitudinal particle oscillations.

options.label: D
options.text: Transverse waves travel only through gases whereas longitudinal waves can travel only through vacuum.
options.distractorRationale: Sound (longitudinal) cannot travel through vacuum, while electromagnetic waves (transverse) do travel through vacuum.

items.stem: A small laboratory buzzer radiates acoustic power of 0.050 W uniformly in all directions. Taking the threshold of hearing as $I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$, calculate the sound intensity level at a distance of 5.00 m from the buzzer.
items.workedSolution: $I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2} = \frac{0.050}{4\pi(5.00)^2} = 1.59 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻²$. Intensity level $= 10\lg\left(\frac{I}{1.0 \times 10^{-12}}\right) = 82.0 dB$.

items.stem: Two identical loudspeakers S₁ and S₂ are connected in parallel to a single signal generator in an open hall. Why does a listener walking parallel to the line S₁S₂ hear alternating loud and quiet positions?
items.workedSolution: Driving both loudspeakers from one oscillator guarantees coherence, so path difference Δl = |S₂P − S₁P| sets maxima (nλ) and minima ((n + 0.5)λ). Therefore option C is correct: coherent sources produce maxima at path difference n lambda and minima at (n + 0.5) lambda.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: two speakers fed by one oscillator are coherent, giving maxima at path difference n lambda and minima at (n + 0.5) lambda.

options.label: A
options.text: Sound waves are longitudinal, so they only interfere constructively when the two speakers emit different frequencies.
options.distractorRationale: Stable interference fringes require identical frequency and constant phase relationship (coherence).

options.label: B
options.text: Quiet positions occur wherever the path difference equals an integer multiple of the wavelength n lambda.
options.distractorRationale: Path difference nλ gives constructive interference (loud maximum); (n + 0.5)λ gives destructive interference (quiet minimum).

options.label: C
options.text: Because of superposition from a shared source, two loudspeakers or microwave transmitters fed by one oscillator are coherent sources producing maxima where path difference equals n lambda and minima where it equals (n + 0.5) lambda.

options.label: D
options.text: Two separate battery-powered oscillators set to slightly different frequencies produce sharper stationary maxima.
options.distractorRationale: Independent oscillators drift in phase and are incoherent, washing out a stationary interference pattern.

items.stem: On a flat screen placed $D = (2.10 \pm 0.01)$ m behind a double slit, a red diode laser produces fringes for Required Practical 2. The slit separation is $s = (0.38 \pm 0.01)$ mm, and 9 consecutive bright fringes cover $(28.4 \pm 0.5)$ mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $w = 28.4/8 = 3.55 mm$. (b) $\lambda = ws/D = 642 nm$. (c) $\%\Delta\lambda = 4.87\%$. (d) avoid looking directly into the laser beam remove reflective surfaces and measure across many fringe spaces to reduce percentage uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Converts mm to m and substitutes into $\lambda = ws/D$.
Sums percentage uncertainties of span, $D$, and $s$.
Avoid eye exposure / remove reflective objects / display warning sign (reject sunglasses).
Measuring across many fringe spaces lowers fractional/percentage uncertainty.

items.stem: In Required Practical 2, a 300 lines mm⁻¹ grating sits $D = 1.40$ m from a screen under a monochromatic red laser. The distance across the $n = +2$ and $n = -2$ maxima is $2h = 1.152$ m. Calculate the wavelength of the laser.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing $d = 10^{-3}/300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m$. Half-span $h = 0.576$ m gives $\theta = \arctan(0.576/1.4) = 22.4^\circ$. Thus $\lambda = d\sin\theta / 2 = 634 nm$ and $n_{\max} = \lfloor d/\lambda \rfloor = 5$.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 514 nm is incident normally on two narrow parallel slits. Each slit has a width of 0.06 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.36 mm. The diffraction-modulated interference pattern is observed on a screen 2.2 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Interference fringe spacing Δy = λD / d = 3.14 × 10⁻³ m. (b) Central envelope full width w_env = 2λD / b = 0.0377 m. (c) First missing order n = d / b = 6.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λD / d with slit separation d.
Uses 2λD / b with individual slit width b.
Equates interference maximum angle to first diffraction minimum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent double-slit interference maxima near the centre of the pattern.
Calculate the full width of the central single-slit diffraction envelope on the screen.
Determine the lowest positive interference order n that is missing due to coincidence with a single-slit diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Equate nλ / d = λ / b => n = d / b.

items.stem: A test vehicle carrying a $600\text{ Hz}$ acoustic beacon drives directly toward a stationary roadside microphone. The microphone records a frequency of $660\text{ Hz}$ when the speed of sound in still air is $330\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $330 - u_{\text{s}} = 330 \times \frac{600}{660} = 300\text{ m s}^{-1} \Rightarrow u_{\text{s}} = 30.0 m s⁻¹$. (b) $f' = 600 \times \frac{330 + 30.0}{330} = 655 Hz$. (c) Sound propagates through air, so moving relative to the air compresses wavefronts when the source moves but keeps $\lambda$ constant when the observer moves. In vacuum, electromagnetic Doppler shift depends only on relative velocity whereas acoustic Doppler depends on whether source or observer moves relative to the medium.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly rearranges to $330 - u_{\text{s}} = 300\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
States sound requires a material medium providing a rest reference frame.
Contrasts compressed wavelength for moving source with unchanged wavelength for moving observer.
States electromagnetic waves require no medium and travel at invariant speed $c$ in vacuum.
Concludes electromagnetic Doppler shift depends only on relative velocity whereas acoustic Doppler depends on whether source or observer moves relative to the medium.

parts.prompt: Determine the speed $u_{\text{s}}$ of the test vehicle.
workingSteps: Rearrange to $v - u_{\text{s}} = v\frac{f}{f'} = 330 \times \frac{600}{660} = 300\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

parts.prompt: In a separate trial, the $600\text{ Hz}$ beacon is kept stationary while the microphone is carried directly toward it at the same speed found in (a). Calculate the frequency recorded by the moving microphone.
workingSteps: Apply the single-mover moving-observer equation $f' = f\frac{v + u_{\text{o}}}{v}$.
Substitute $u_{\text{o}} = 30.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to obtain $f' = 600 \times \frac{360}{330} = 655 Hz$.

parts.prompt: Explain why the two acoustic frequencies in (a) and (b) are not identical despite the same relative approach speed. Explain why no such difference exists for light waves travelling through a vacuum.
parts.expectedAnswer: In air, the medium defines a rest reference frame: a moving source compresses $\lambda$, whereas a moving observer changes relative wave speed. Light needs no medium and always travels at $c$ in vacuum for all observers. Therefore, the electromagnetic Doppler shift depends only on relative velocity.
workingSteps: Identify air as the material medium that sets a rest frame for sound waves.
Contrast moving-source wavelength compression ($\lambda' = (v - u_{\text{s}})/f$) with moving-observer relative speed ($v + u_{\text{o}}$).
Explain that electromagnetic waves require no medium and travel at invariant speed $c$ in vacuum.
Conclude that electromagnetic Doppler shift depends only on relative velocity whereas acoustic Doppler depends on whether source or observer moves relative to the medium.

items.stem: A standing wave in the 6th harmonic runs across a 0.6 m taut string clamped at both ends. Pulses travel at 72 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Mode wavelength: λ_6 = 2L / n = 2(0.6) / 6 = 0.200 m. (b) Frequency: f_6 = v / λ_6 = 72 / 0.200 = 360 Hz. (c) Dividing by harmonic number gives f₁ = f_6 / 6 = 60.0 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of this n = 6 harmonic standing wave.
workingSteps: For a string fixed at both ends, λ_n = 2L / n.

parts.prompt: Determine the oscillation frequency of this standing wave.
Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string when kept at the same tension.

items.stem: An emitted 920 Hz tone from a stationary siren is heard as 1.11 × 10³ Hz by a car carrying a microphone moving towards it. Given sound speed 343 m s⁻¹, what is the observer's speed?
items.workedSolution: With a fixed emitter, f′ = f(v + v_o) / v, so v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 343 × |1.11 × 10³ / 920 − 1| = 72.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 72.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The displacement–position graph shows a progressive wave travelling along a long stretched rope at a single instant. The wave has an amplitude of 0.042 m and a wavelength of 0.48 m. The source oscillates at a steady frequency of 55 Hz.

items.stem: From the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries, physicists debated whether light consisted of particles or waves. This debate led to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory and Hertz's radio experiments.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: Young's double-slit interference and Foucault's speed measurement disproved Newton's corpuscular theory. Maxwell's equations ($c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$) and Hertz's standing radio waves and polarisation tests established light as transverse electromagnetic radiation.

markScheme.criterion: Explains Newton's corpuscular model predicted greater speed in water/glass due to normal attractive forces.
Explains Huygens' wave model predicted slower speed in denser media bending wavefronts toward the normal.
Explains Young's double-slit interference demonstrated wave superposition (and notes Newton's early prestige).
Explains Foucault's measurement showing $v_{\text{water}} < v_{\text{air}}$ decisively disproved Newton's corpuscular refraction.
Explains Maxwell predicted coupled perpendicular $E$ and $B$ waves with $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$ matching the speed of light.
Explains Hertz confirmed Maxwell using standing radio waves (node spacing $\lambda/2$ to find $c$) and dipole polarisation nulls at $90°$.

parts.prompt: Explain how Newton's corpuscular theory and Huygens' wave theory accounted for refraction. Explain why Newton's view prevailed at first before being overturned by Young and Foucault. Describe how Maxwell and Hertz established the electromagnetic nature of light.
parts.expectedAnswer: Young's double-slit interference and Foucault's speed measurement disproved Newton's corpuscular theory, while Maxwell and Hertz showed light is transverse electromagnetic radiation. Newton modelled light as tiny elastic corpuscles pulled faster into water or glass, predicting $v_{\text{water}} > v_{\text{air}}$. Huygens modelled light as wavefronts that slow down in denser media ($v_{\text{water}} < v_{\text{air}}$), bending toward the normal. Newton's reputation and the lack of clear diffraction or speed data kept corpuscular theory dominant for over a century. In 1801, Thomas Young's double-slit fringes showed wave superposition. In 1850, Léon Foucault measured light travelling slower in water than air, disproving Newton's refraction model. James Clerk Maxwell then derived equations for perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling at $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0} \approx 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, matching the speed of light. Finally, Heinrich Hertz produced spark-gap radio waves, found their speed from standing-wave node spacing $\lambda/2$ ($c = f\lambda$), and showed transverse polarisation via $90°$ detector nulls.
workingSteps: Explain Newton's corpuscular refraction (perpendicular pull speeds corpuscles up in denser media, $v_{\text{water}} > v_{\text{air}}$).
Explain Huygens' wave refraction (wavefronts slow in denser media, $v_{\text{water}} < v_{\text{air}}$).
Explain why Newton prevailed initially (reputation, no observed interference or speed measurement).
Describe Young's double-slit interference and Foucault's 1850 water-speed proof overturning corpuscles.
Describe Maxwell's transverse coupled $E/B$ waves and $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$ matching light speed.
Describe Hertz's radio standing waves ($\lambda/2$ node spacing giving $c$) and dipole rotation polarisation proving transverse nature.

items.stem: Modern global data networks combine real-time communication chains, geostationary microwave satellites, optical fibres, and modulated radio links.
items.workedSolution: A real-time communication link connects: input transducer $\to$ encoder/modulator $\to$ transmitter $\to$ medium $\to$ receiver $\to$ demodulator/decoder $\to$ output transducer. Satellites separate up-link and down-link frequency bands so the powerful transmitter does not de-sense the sensitive receiver. Optical fibre gives the highest bandwidth, data rate, and security. Radio and satellite links offer wide remote and mobile coverage, but share limited spectrum and are easier to intercept.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Identifies transmitter stages: input transducer converts information to an electrical signal; encoder/modulator puts it on a carrier; transmitter boosts and launches it.
L1: Identifies the medium and receiver stages: the medium carries the signal to the receiver, decoder/demodulator extracts information, and output transducer reproduces it.
L2: Explains satellite anti-desensing: up-link and down-link use different frequencies (e.g. 6 GHz / 4 GHz) so the high-power transmitter does not swamp/de-sense the sensitive receiver.
L2: Distinguishes AM (amplitude varies, bandwidth $2 f_{\text{M}}$) and FM (frequency varies, bandwidth $2(\Delta f + f_{\text{M}})$, better noise immunity).
L3: Evaluates data capacity and bandwidth: optic fibre provides vastly higher carrier frequency and bandwidth/data capacity than copper wire or shared RF/satellite channels.

L3: Evaluates cost and security: optical fibre is secure with no radiated leakage but costly to install remotely. Radio and satellite links cover remote or mobile users widely at lower local cost, but need encryption.

parts.prompt: Describe the purpose of each stage in a real-time communication system block diagram. Explain why satellite transponders use different up-link and down-link frequencies. Compare optical fibre with satellite and radio transmission in terms of data capacity, cost, and security.
parts.expectedAnswer: An input transducer converts sound or data into an electrical signal. An encoder or modulator impresses it onto a carrier (AM or FM), and a transmitter boosts power into the medium. At the destination, a receiver, demodulator/decoder, and output transducer recover the original information. Satellites separate up-link (e.g. 6 GHz) and down-link (e.g. 4 GHz) bands so the strong outgoing signal does not de-sense the sensitive incoming receiver. Optical fibre gives very high bandwidth, high data capacity, low attenuation, and strong security because it is hard to tap. Satellites and radio cost less to reach remote or mobile users over wide areas, but they share finite RF bandwidth and have lower security.
workingSteps: Outline all real-time block-diagram stages: input transducer, encoder/modulator, transmitter, transmission medium, receiver, decoder/demodulator, output transducer.
Explain satellite frequency separation: strong re-transmitted down-link would overwhelm (de-sense) the satellite's sensitive up-link receiver if both used the same frequency.
Compare AM vs FM modulation principles and bandwidth requirements ($2 f_{\text{M}}$ vs $2(\Delta f + f_{\text{M}})$).
Compare transmission media (optic fibre vs copper wire vs radio/satellite) explicitly across data transmission rate/bandwidth, installation/operating cost, and security.

items.stem: Emerging at 131 W m⁻² from an ideal analyzer, a plane-polarized beam started at 160 W m⁻². Apply Malus's law (I = I₀ cos²θ) here. Determine the acute rotation angle θ.
items.workedSolution: Take square root of I = I₀ cos²θ: cos θ = √(131 / 160) = 0.906, yielding θ = arccos(0.906) = 25.0°.

items.stem: With sound speed 348 m s⁻¹, a resonance tube closed at one end and open at the other (0.28 m long) resonates in odd harmonic n = 3, treating the pipe as ideal.
items.workedSolution: (a) With L_eff = 0.280 m, lowest harmonic is f₁ = v / (4L_eff) = 311 Hz. (b) λ_3 = 4L_eff / 3 = 0.373 m. (c) f_3 = 3f₁ = 932 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies quarter-wave first-harmonic relation f₁ = v / (4L_eff).
Multiplies first-harmonic frequency by odd harmonic index 3 (or uses v / λ).

parts.prompt: Calculate the first-harmonic (n = 1) frequency of this closed-end air column.
workingSteps: For a pipe closed at one end, λ₁ = 4L so f₁ = v / (4L).

items.stem: Two identical progressive waves of wavelength 44 cm and amplitude 2.8 cm travel in opposite directions along a taut string. They superpose to form the stationary wave shown at t = 0, T/4, and T/2.
items.workedSolution: (a) 22.0 cm. (b) 5.60 cm. (c) At one quarter of a period, the two opposite progressive waves are in antiphase at every position. Their displacements cancel everywhere to give a flat line for an instant.

markScheme.criterion: States opposite progressive waves are in antiphase everywhere at t = T/4.
Notes wave energy is temporarily wholly kinetic so the string overshoots into t = T/2.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance between two adjacent nodes along the string.
Calculate the amplitude of oscillation at an antinode.
Explain why the resultant string profile is completely flat at t = T/4 yet continues oscillating at t = T/2.
parts.expectedAnswer: At one quarter of a period, the two opposite progressive waves are in antiphase at every position, so their displacements cancel to a flat line. However, particles at antinodes pass through equilibrium with maximum speed and kinetic energy, so oscillation continues.
workingSteps: At one quarter of a period, the two opposite waves are in antiphase everywhere, cancelling to a flat line for an instant.

items.stem: A nylon string of mass per unit length $\mu = 1.10 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$ runs over a bridge and bench pulley in Required Practical 1. Held taut by a 0.45 kg hanging mass ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²), what is its transverse wave speed?
items.workedSolution: With $T = mg = 0.45 \times 9.81 = 4.41 N$, wave speed $v = \sqrt{T/\mu} = 63.3 m s⁻¹$, $f_1 = v/(2L) = 25.3 Hz$, gradient $= v/2 = 31.7 m s⁻¹$, and $\%\Delta \mu = 1.2 + 2(0.7) + 2(0.4) = 3.40\%$. Answer: 63.3 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to take the square root in v = √(T/μ).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses mass m directly instead of tension T = mg.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Confuses wave speed v with the f₁ vs 1/L gradient v/2.

items.stem: An observatory upgrades from a 1.50 m primary mirror to a 6.00 m primary mirror operating at the same optical wavelength. By what factor does the collecting power increase?
items.workedSolution: Collecting power is proportional to collecting area and hence $D^2$: $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{6.00}{1.50}\right)^2 = 4^2 = 16.0$.

items.stem: Still air transmits sound at 343 m s⁻¹. A stationary observer detects waves from a train horn (750 Hz) moving towards the observer at 76 m s⁻¹. Calculate that frequency.
items.workedSolution: Doppler equation (towards detector): f' = fv / (v − v_s) = (750 × 343) / (343 − 76) = 963 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 963 Hz (D).

items.stem: A physics student mounts a flat screen 1.2 m behind two narrow parallel slits of spacing 0.5 mm. Coherent 405 nm light shines normally onto the slits.
items.workedSolution: (a) Young's spacing = λD / d = (4.05 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.2) / 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 9.72 × 10⁻⁴ m. (b) Half-spacing to first dark band = ½ × 9.72 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.86 × 10⁻⁴ m. (c) For n = 3: nλ = 3 × 4.05 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.22 × 10⁻⁶ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units and substitutes into λD / (slit separation).
Takes half of the bright-fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
Determine the distance on the screen from the central bright maximum to the centre of the first dark fringe.
workingSteps: First destructive minimum occurs halfway between the central and first-order bright maxima: y_dark,1 = 0.5 × fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the geometric path difference between waves arriving from the two slits at the order n = 3 bright fringe.
workingSteps: Constructive interference at order n requires path difference Δℓ = nλ.

items.stem: Long-distance digital PCM links use periodic regenerators, while long-distance analogue links use analogue amplifiers. Why does the digital link achieve a much better signal-to-noise ratio?
items.workedSolution: Digital regenerators compare the noisy waveform against a threshold and rebuild clean rectangular pulses. This removes accumulated noise, whereas an analogue amplifier amplifies noise along with the signal.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that digital regenerators restore clean digital logic levels and remove noise, whereas an analogue amplifier amplifies noise with the signal.

options.label: A
options.text: Digital pulses experience zero attenuation or dispersion inside cables.
options.distractorRationale: Digital pulses still attenuate and pick up noise, which is why regenerators are needed periodically.

options.label: B
options.text: Regenerators shift signals to a higher carrier frequency so noise vanishes completely.
options.distractorRationale: Regenerators reconstruct clean binary 0/1 levels in baseband.

options.label: C
options.text: Regenerator restores clean digital logic levels removing accumulated noise whereas an analogue amplifier amplifies noise with the signal.

options.label: D
options.text: Analogue amplifiers strip noise automatically whereas regenerators only boost voltage.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the fundamental distinction between analogue amplifiers and digital regenerators.

items.stem: At $4.0\text{ kHz}$, a patient with suspected hearing damage can only just hear a sound of intensity $1.00 \times 10^{-7}\text{ W m}^{-2}$. This threshold is shown as patient curve P on the equal-loudness graph. A normal ear has a threshold intensity of $1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $10\log_{10}(10^5) = 50.0 dB$. (b) noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz. (c) Age-related loss raises threshold steadily across all high frequencies without recovering above $4\text{ kHz}$.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz.
Describes progressive high-frequency threshold rise for age-related loss.
Notes lowered upper frequency cutoff rather than an isolated 4 kHz notch.

parts.prompt: Calculate the patient's threshold intensity level in dB at $4.0\text{ kHz}$.
Identify the cause of the hearing defect indicated by patient curve P.
parts.expectedAnswer: Exposure to excessive noise, since noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz.
workingSteps: Recognise the localised 4 kHz notch: noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz.

parts.prompt: Describe how the threshold curve for age-related hearing deterioration differs from patient curve P.
parts.expectedAnswer: Age-related hearing loss raises the threshold steadily across all high frequencies above about 4 kHz and lowers the upper audible frequency limit. It does not form a narrow notch around 4 kHz with recovery at higher frequencies.
workingSteps: Note progressive elevation across all higher frequencies.
Contrast with the localised 4 kHz notch of noise injury.

items.stem: An unpolarized beam of light of intensity 96 W m⁻² passes normally through an ideal vertical polarizer P₁. It then passes through an ideal linear analyzer A whose transmission axis is at θ = 20° to P₁. For plane-polarized light of intensity I₁, Malus's law gives I = I₁ cos²θ.
items.workedSolution: (a) After P₁, I₁ = ½ I₀ = 48.0 W m⁻². (b) After analyzer A, I = I₁ cos²(20°) = 42.4 W m⁻². (c) Overall fraction I / I₀ = ½ cos²(20°) = 0.442.

markScheme.criterion: Halves unpolarized incident intensity at ideal polarizer P₁.
Applies I = I₁ cos²θ to the polarized beam.
Divides final transmitted intensity by incident unpolarized intensity I₀.

items.stem: The diagram shows a stretched string fixed at both ends of vibrating length 0.9 m and linear mass density 0.0032 kg m⁻¹. It vibrates in harmonic mode n = 1 at a frequency of 69.44 Hz. The transverse wave speed on a taut string is v = √(T / μ). Determine the required tension T.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.9) / 1 = 1.80 m, so required wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 125 m s⁻¹. Rearranging v = √(T / μ) gives T = μv² = 0.0032 × (125)² = 50.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 2Lf_n / n and computes T = μv² = 50.0 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to square the wave speed when rearranging v = √(T / μ) to T = μv².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, halving v and underestimating T = μv² by a factor of 4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides v² by linear mass density μ instead of multiplying T = μv².

items.stem: A teacher demonstrates plane polarisation using a microwave transmitter, a rotatable metal-grille analyser, and a receiver. The teacher also sets up a second-harmonic stationary wave on a $0.90\text{ m}$ string.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda = 2L/2 = 0.900\text{ m}$. (b) Plane-polarised transverse waves restrict oscillations to one plane, whereas longitudinal waves cannot be polarised. The detected signal falls from maximum at $0^\circ$ to zero at $90^\circ$, then rises back to maximum at $180^\circ$.

markScheme.criterion: Identify second harmonic spans two half-wavelengths ($L = \lambda$).
L1 (Area 1): States emitted microwaves are plane-polarised in one plane perpendicular to direction of energy transfer.
L1 (Area 1): Notes maximum signal occurs when receiver aerial/detector aligns parallel to transmitted oscillation plane (0°).
L2 (Area 2): States signal falls steadily to zero / minimum at 90° rotation (crossed orientation).
L2 (Area 2): States signal rises back to maximum again at 180° rotation.
L3 (Area 3): Explains longitudinal oscillations are parallel to energy transfer so rotating the detector about the beam axis would produce no intensity variation.
L3 (Area 3): Concludes observed periodic variation proves microwaves are transverse waves.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of the second-harmonic stationary wave on the $0.90\text{ m}$ string.
workingSteps: For the second harmonic ($n = 2$), two loops fit in $L = 0.90\text{ m}$, so $\lambda = L = 0.900\text{ m}$.

parts.prompt: Describe and explain how the microwave receiver reading changes as the receiver is rotated smoothly through $180^\circ$ about the beam axis. Explain how this proves microwaves are transverse waves.
parts.expectedAnswer: The transmitter emits vertically plane-polarised waves whose electric field oscillates in one vertical plane perpendicular to energy transfer. Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised because their oscillations lie parallel to energy transfer and stay symmetric under rotation. At $0^\circ$, the receiver is parallel to the transmitted plane and gives a maximum signal. As it rotates towards $90^\circ$, the parallel component drops to zero (minimum reading). From $90^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, alignment is restored and the signal rises back to maximum.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): State emitted microwaves are plane-polarised transverse waves (oscillations in one plane perpendicular to energy transfer).
Area 2 (L2): Trace reading through 0° (max) -> 90° (zero/min) -> 180° (max) via dipole alignment.
Area 3 (L3): Prove transverse nature by contrasting with rotationally symmetric longitudinal waves.

items.stem: In the venous scan shown, blood flows steadily away from the angled ultrasound probe. How does the frequency of the reflected ultrasound returning to the probe compare with the emitted frequency?
items.workedSolution: When scatterers move away from the probe, the reflected wavelength increases and the received frequency is lower than f. Therefore the correct statement is: Blood moving away from the transducer reflects ultrasound at a lower received frequency than the emitted frequency.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: blood moving away from the transducer reflects ultrasound at a lower received frequency than the emitted frequency.

options.text: Blood moving away from the transducer reflects ultrasound at a lower received frequency than the emitted frequency.

options.label: B
options.text: Blood moving away from the transducer reflects ultrasound at a higher received frequency than the emitted frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Receding scatterers stretch the wavefront spacing, decreasing rather than increasing received frequency.

options.label: C
options.text: The received frequency equals the emitted frequency because the double shift cancels on the return path.
options.distractorRationale: Both shifts are in the same downward direction, doubling rather than cancelling the shift.

options.label: D
options.text: The received frequency alternates randomly above and below the emitted frequency for steady laminar flow.
options.distractorRationale: Steady flow away from the probe produces a consistent negative frequency shift.

items.stem: On an A-scan CRO trace, echoes from the front and rear surfaces of a kidney arrive at $42\,\mu\text{s}$ and $112\,\mu\text{s}$ respectively. Taking the speed of ultrasound inside the kidney to be 1560 m s⁻¹, what is the thickness of the kidney?
items.workedSolution: Time interval between echoes is $\Delta t = 112 - 42 = 70\,\mu\text{s}$. Using $2d = c\Delta t$, $d = \frac{1560 \times 70 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 0.0546\text{ m} = 54.6 mm$.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 575 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 450 lines mm⁻¹. Diffracted orders starting from n = 1 are observed across the forward semicircle.
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 2.22 × 10⁻⁶ m, so θ₁ = arcsin(λ / d) = 15.0°. (b) d / λ = 3.86, giving n_max = 3. (c) Total principal maxima = 2(3) + 1 = 7.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and applies sin θ₁ = λ / d.
Evaluates d / λ = 3.86 and rounds down.

items.workedSolution: (a) $f = 50.0 Hz$. (b) $v = 16.0 m s⁻¹$. (c) Particle P is moving upwards through equilibrium because the approaching crest lies immediately to its left.

items.stem: Monochromatic red laser light illuminates a single narrow vertical slit to form the intensity pattern shown. Which statement correctly describes the widths of the maxima?
items.workedSolution: The single-slit central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases (or wavelength increases). Therefore option C is correct: central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases.

options.label: A
options.text: In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum has the same width as every secondary maximum and narrows when slit width decreases
options.distractorRationale: Confuses single-slit diffraction with Young's double-slit equal-width fringes, and inverts the 1/a scaling.

options.label: B
options.text: In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum is half as wide as each secondary maximum
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the 2:1 ratio between central and secondary maxima.

options.label: C
options.text: In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases

options.label: D
options.text: In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum width depends only on laser intensity and not slit width
options.distractorRationale: Intensity scales peak height, whereas width scales as 2λD/a.

items.stem: White light containing wavelengths from 410 nm (violet) to 690 nm (red) illuminates a double slit of separation s = 0.45 mm placed D = 2.00 m from a screen.
items.workedSolution: (a) 1.82 mm. (b) 3.07 mm. (c) The central fringe is bright white. Outer fringes form continuous spectra with violet closest to the centre and red furthest out because w = lambda D / s increases with wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: Applies w = λD / s with SI conversions.
Substitutes λ = 690 nm into w = λD / s.
States central fringe is white because all colours have zero path difference.
States outer fringes are spectra with violet inner and red outer edges.

items.stem: Diffracted by a 600 lines mm⁻¹ grating, a green laser pointer produces $n = +1$ and $n = -1$ bright spots separated by $2h = 1.076$ m. The flat viewing screen stands $D = 1.60$ m from the grating.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\theta = \arctan(0.538/1.6) = 18.6^\circ$. (b) $\lambda = d\sin\theta/1 = 531 nm$. (c) $n_{\max} = \lfloor d/\lambda \rfloor = 3$. (d) Align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square. Measure the symmetric span between matching orders, and never look directly into the laser.

markScheme.criterion: Halves 2h to obtain h and applies $\tan\theta = h/D$.
Sets $\sin\theta \le 1$ to evaluate $d/\lambda$ and rounds down.
Aligns grating perpendicular to incident beam using a set square.
Measuring symmetric span 2h reduces % uncertainty and checks symmetry.

parts.prompt: Calculate the diffraction angle $\theta$ for the $n = 1$ order maximum.
Determine the wavelength $\lambda$ of the laser in nm.
Calculate the maximum diffraction order $n_{\max}$ observable on either side of the central maximum.
Explain how the student verifies normal incidence of the grating and why measuring $2h$ is superior to measuring $h$ alone.
parts.expectedAnswer: Align the grating perpendicular to the beam using a set square. Measure the symmetric span between matching orders, and never look directly into the laser.
workingSteps: Check 90° alignment with a set square against bench/screen and verify equal +n and −n distances.
Measuring 2h halves percentage uncertainty and averages out small zero-order alignment offsets.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 650 nm illuminates two narrow parallel slits of separation 0.4 mm. Each slit has finite width 0.08 mm, and the pattern forms on a screen 1.4 m away. Calculate the full width of the central single-slit diffraction envelope on the screen.
items.workedSolution: The first single-slit diffraction minima lie at θ = ±λ / b, so the full width of the central diffraction envelope on the screen is w_env = 2λD / b = (2 × 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.4) / 8.00 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.0227 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w_env = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0227 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the adjacent interference fringe spacing λD / d instead of the diffraction envelope width 2λD / b.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes slit separation d in place of individual slit width b, computing 2λD / d.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the half-width λD / b from the centre to one minimum instead of the full width 2λD / b.

items.stem: An emergency vehicle emits a constant siren tone of frequency $680\text{ Hz}$ while travelling directly toward a stationary pedestrian at $28.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Taking the speed of sound in air as $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$, what frequency does the pedestrian hear?
items.workedSolution: For a moving source approaching a stationary observer, $f' = f\frac{v}{v - u_{\text{s}}} = 680 \times \frac{340}{340 - 28.0} = 741 Hz$.

items.stem: Along a taut string (1.2 m long, clamped at both ends), waves move at 168 m s⁻¹. Find the frequency when it resonates in harmonic mode n = 5.
items.workedSolution: For n = 5 on a clamped string, λ_n = 2L / n = 2(1.2) / 5 = 0.480 m, yielding f_n = v / λ_n = 168 / 0.480 = 350 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f_n = nv / (2L) to obtain 350 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic frequency v / (2L) instead of multiplying by harmonic number n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the closed-one-end pipe formula nv / (4L) instead of fixed-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n, computing f = nv / L.

items.stem: During a Doppler demonstration, a student moves at 64 m s⁻¹ directly away from a stationary alarm set to 640 Hz. The speed of sound in still air is 340 m s⁻¹. Find the heard frequency.
items.workedSolution: Detected pitch: f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 640 × (340 − 64) / 340 = 520 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 520 Hz (A).

items.stem: A student reads 8.87 mm between the central maximum and the n = 5 bright fringe using 532 nm rays. The screen distance from two narrow parallel slits S₁ and S₂ is 1.4 m. Determine the slit separation.
items.workedSolution: Rearranging y_n = nλD / d yields d = nλD / y_n = (5 × 5.32 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.4) / 8.87 × 10⁻³ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁴ m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th bright fringe displacement as a single fringe spacing, omitting the factor of n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies dark-fringe factor (n − ½) instead of integer n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides total span by (n + 1) instead of n fringe intervals between n = 0 and order n.

items.stem: The displacement–position graph shows a sinusoidal wave travelling on a stretched string. The wave has amplitude 0.018 m, wavelength 0.32 m, and speed 2.56 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency of the wave.
items.workedSolution: Using f = v / λ with wave speed v = 2.56 m s⁻¹ and wavelength λ = 0.32 m gives f = 2.56 / 0.32 = 8.00 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges v = fλ to obtain f = v / λ = 8.00 Hz (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the oscillation period T = λ / v instead of the frequency f = v / λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength (vλ) instead of dividing v by λ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Mistakes two full cycles for one wavelength, halving the calculated frequency.

items.stem: Both ends are open on a resonance tube open at both ends (0.9 m long, ignoring end effects) in harmonic n = 5. With sound speed 330 m s⁻¹, calculate this frequency.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n.

items.stem: Measurements target the n = 3 principal maximum. A 650 nm beam passes normally through a 200 lines mm⁻¹ grating to a screen 1.15 m behind.
items.workedSolution: (a) Convert ruling: d = 10⁻³ / 200 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Grating law gives sin θ = nλ / d = 0.390, so θ = 23.0°. (c) Spot position: y = D tan θ = 1.15 × tan(23.0°) = 0.487 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises large-angle geometry y = D tan θ rather than small-angle D sin θ.

items.stem: A wave along a long stretched rope has wavelength 2 m, frequency 50 Hz, and amplitude 0.035 m. Find the phase difference in degrees between P at x₁ = 0.2 m and Q at x₂ = 0.8 m.
items.workedSolution: First find Δx = 0.8 m − 0.2 m = 0.6 m. Comparing against one cycle (2 m) gives 0.300 cycles, so Δφ = 360° × 0.300 = 108°.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 360° to get 108° (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in radians without converting to degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (180°) instead of a full cycle (360°) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

items.stem: Coherent 450 nm waves travel normally through a 0.25 mm single slit, forming a central peak and side minima 3.5 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Small-angle minimum: θ = λ / b = 1.80 × 10⁻³ rad. (b) y₁ = θD = 6.30 × 10⁻³ m. (c) Central band: w = 2y₁ = 0.0126 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies θ = λ / b in SI units.
Multiplies θ by screen distance D.
Doubles half-width to span both sides of the central peak.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular position θ (in radians) of the first diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Use the small-angle single-slit first-minimum relation θ = λ / b.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear distance on the screen from the centre of the pattern to the first dark minimum.
Calculate the full linear width of the central bright maximum on the screen.
workingSteps: The central maximum spans from −y₁ to +y₁: w = 2y₁.

items.stem: Water has a refractive index of 1.33 for yellow light ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$). What speed of light in water was predicted by Huygens' wave theory and later confirmed experimentally by Foucault in 1850?
items.workedSolution: Huygens' wave theory predicts light slows in optically denser water: $v_{\text{water}} = \frac{c}{n} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8}{1.33} = 2.26 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹$ (whereas Newton's corpuscular model predicted $nc = 3.99 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$).

items.stem: An instrumentation op-amp has a gain–bandwidth product of $4.80\text{ MHz}$ on its Bode plot. It is configured as a non-inverting amplifier with closed-loop gain $120$. Calculate the upper cutoff frequency (bandwidth) in kHz.
items.workedSolution: $\text{Bandwidth} = \frac{4.80 \times 10^3\text{ kHz}}{120} = 40.0 kHz$.

items.stem: An ideal linear analyzer is rotated by θ = 35° to the incoming polarization. A plane-polarized beam of 84 W m⁻² enters it normally. Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ for plane-polarized light.
items.workedSolution: (a) Amplitude fraction: E / E₀ = cos(35°) = 0.819. (b) Output intensity: I = I₀ cos²(35°) = 56.4 W m⁻². (c) Absorbed part = 84 − 56.4 = 27.6 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Projects electric-field vector via E / E₀ = cos θ.
Subtracts transmitted intensity from incident intensity.

parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio E / E₀ of the transmitted electric-field amplitude to the incident electric-field amplitude.
workingSteps: Only the electric-field component parallel to the analyzer axis is transmitted: E / E₀ = cos θ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity I of the beam emerging from the analyzer.
Determine the intensity removed (absorbed or rejected) from the beam by the analyzer.

items.stem: Monochromatic light illuminates a mask of $N$ identical equally spaced slits of fixed separation $d$ and fixed individual slit width $b$. How does the interference pattern change as $N$ is increased from $2$ to $5$?
items.workedSolution: With N coherent slits of fixed d, amplitudes add to NA so peak intensity I ∝ N². Principal peaks become sharper at fixed d sin θ = nλ, and N − 2 faint secondary maxima form. Therefore option A is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: increasing N keeps principal maxima at fixed angles, sharpens them, scales intensity as N squared, and adds N minus two secondary maxima.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the number of slits N keeps principal maxima at unchanged angles while narrowing them increasing peak intensity proportional to N squared and adding N minus two secondary maxima.

options.label: B
options.text: Principal maxima move further apart in angle while their peak intensity grows linearly with N and no secondary maxima appear.
options.distractorRationale: Angular positions obey d sin θ = nλ (unchanged for fixed d), intensity scales as N², and N − 2 secondary maxima appear.

options.label: C
options.text: Principal maxima become broader and dimmer while the single-slit envelope disappears completely.
options.distractorRationale: More slits sharpen principal maxima, boost peak intensity as N², and retain the fixed single-slit envelope for fixed b.

options.label: D
options.text: Principal maxima shift closer together while the number of secondary maxima between them equals N squared.
options.distractorRationale: Fixed slit separation d fixes principal maximum angles, and there are exactly N − 2 secondary maxima between adjacent principal peaks.

items.stem: A 0.85 m resonance tube is closed at one end (ignoring end effects) with wave speed 348 m s⁻¹. Find the next resonance above its first harmonic.
items.workedSolution: Closed-one-end pipes allow odd harmonics only (n = 1, 3, 5,...), so the next mode is n = 3: f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 3(348) / (4 × 0.85) = 307 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies odd harmonic n = 3 and computes f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 307 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic frequency v / (4L) instead of the next higher harmonic 3v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes an even n = 2 harmonic exists in a pipe closed at one end, computing 2f₁ = v / (2L) instead of 3f₁ = 3v / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the open-both-ends formula 3v / (2L) instead of closed-one-end 3v / (4L).

items.stem: An air-filled cylindrical pipe of length $1.20\text{ m}$ is sealed tightly at both ends. The speed of sound in air is $342\text{ m s}^{-1}$. What is the frequency of the third harmonic standing wave inside this pipe?
items.workedSolution: Two closed ends impose displacement nodes at both ends, so $f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}$. Thus $f_3 = \frac{3 \times 342}{2 \times 1.20} = 428 Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $f_3 = 3v/(2L) = 428 Hz$ for a two-closed pipe.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the closed–open pipe formula 3v/(4L) instead of the two-closed pipe formula 3v/(2L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first harmonic frequency instead of the third harmonic.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes the second harmonic instead of the third harmonic.

items.stem: A microwave probe moves 8.4 cm across 6 consecutive node-to-node intervals in front of a flat metal reflector. Taking c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the frequency of the microwave transmitter in GHz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats node-to-node spacing 1.4 cm as a full wavelength, doubling the frequency.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Halves the frequency erroneously.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the entire 8.4 cm span as one wavelength.

items.stem: During Required Practical 1, a student varies the vibrating length $L$ of a nylon string tensioned by a 0.45 kg hanging mass ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). A graph of first-harmonic frequency $f_1$ versus $1/L$ passes through the origin with gradient 31.7 m s⁻¹. Recorded percentage uncertainties are 1.2% (mass), 0.7% (frequency), and 0.4% (length).
items.workedSolution: (a) $v = 2 \times 31.7 = 63.3 m s⁻¹$. (b) $T = 4.41 N$, $\mu = T/v^2 = 1.10 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$. (c) $\%\Delta \mu = 1.2 + 2(0.7) + 2(0.4) = 3.40\%$. (d) measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $T = mg = 4.41 N$ and substitutes into $\mu = T/v^2$.
Mass per unit length $\mu = 1.10 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$.
Doubles percentage uncertainties in both $f_1$ and $L$ before adding $\%\Delta m$.
Measures vibrating length between wooden bridge and top of pulley (fixed nodes).
Links fixed-node span to first-harmonic condition $f_1 = v/(2L)$.

parts.prompt: Use the gradient of the $f_1$ against $1/L$ graph to determine the wave speed $v$ on the string.
Calculate the mass per unit length $\mu$ of the string.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $\mu$ from the stated measurement uncertainties.
Explain clearly between which two points $L$ must be measured to avoid a systematic error.
parts.expectedAnswer: measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length
workingSteps: Measure directly between the fixed nodes at the bridge apex and pulley top.
First harmonic has λ = 2L between those fixed nodes.

items.stem: A 45.0 m diameter wire-mesh radio telescope observes emissions at wavelength 0.180 m, while a 3.00 m optical reflector observes at wavelength 500 nm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda/20 = 9.00 × 10⁻³ m$. (b) $\theta_{\text{radio}} = 4.00 × 10⁻³ rad$. (c) $\theta_{\text{opt}} = 1.67 × 10⁻⁷ rad$, orders of magnitude finer than the radio dish.

markScheme.criterion: Correct optical resolution 1.67 × 10⁻⁷ rad and identifies superior optical detail.

items.workedSolution: (a) Rest wavelength: λ₀ = v / f = 0.607 m. (b) Shifted spacing near listener: λ′ = (v + v_s) / f = 0.714 m. (c) Heard pitch: f′ = v / λ′ = 476 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f′ = v / λ′ or exact moving-source Doppler formula.

items.stem: What is the separation of adjacent bright fringes on a screen 2.4 m behind a pair of narrow slits? The slit spacing is 0.36 mm and the wavelength is 445 nm.
items.workedSolution: Convert first: λ = 4.45 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ m. Young's formula yields λD / (slit separation) = (4.45 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.4) / 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.97 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) to obtain 2.97 × 10⁻³ m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit separation and divides by screen distance (λd / D) instead of λD / d.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the distance from the central bright fringe to the first dark minimum (½ λD / d) instead of bright fringe spacing.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2, confusing double-slit fringe spacing with single-slit central maximum width.

items.stem: An audiologist plots a factory worker's threshold of hearing (patient curve P on the equal-loudness chart). What characteristic defect is revealed by the sharp upward notch centred near $4\text{ kHz}$?
items.workedSolution: Prolonged loud noise damages cochlear hair cells tuned near $4\text{ kHz}$: noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz.

options.label: A
options.text: Normal healthy hearing, which always has its poorest sensitivity at 4 kHz.
options.distractorRationale: Normal hearing is actually most sensitive around 3–4 kHz, not least sensitive.

options.label: B
options.text: Purely age-related hearing loss, which only raises thresholds below 100 Hz.
options.distractorRationale: Age-related hearing loss raises thresholds progressively across all high frequencies rather than only below 100 Hz.

options.label: C
options.text: A flat 40 dB elevation at all frequencies caused exclusively by ear canal resonance.
options.distractorRationale: A sharp localised notch near 4 kHz is the hallmark of noise-induced hearing loss.

options.label: D
options.text: The trace shows that noise-induced hearing loss produces a pronounced dip around four kilohertz following prolonged exposure to loud industrial noise.

items.stem: Unpolarized light of initial intensity I₀ passes through ideal polarizer P₁ followed by analyzer A rotated by θ = 70° to P₁. The final transmitted intensity is 11.2 W m⁻², where plane-polarized transmission obeys I = I₁ cos²θ. Determine the incident unpolarized intensity I₀.
items.workedSolution: Since I = ½ I₀ cos²θ, rearranging gives I₀ = 2I / cos²(70°) = (2 × 11.2) / 0.117 = 192 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Solves I = ½ I₀ cos²θ to obtain I₀ = 192 W m⁻² (D).

The string is under a tension of 18.15 N and resonates in harmonic n = 4. Transverse waves travel along a string of tension T and mass per unit length μ at speed v = √(T / μ).

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T and μ into v = √(T / μ).
Divides wave speed from (a) by wavelength from (b).

Determine the wavelength of the n = 4 harmonic mode.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this standing wave.

items.stem: On the stationary wave envelope shown, points P and R lie in adjacent loops separated by a single node. How are the oscillations of P and R related in phase?
items.workedSolution: Points separated by one node oscillate in antiphase ($\pi\text{ rad}$ or $180^\circ$). Therefore option C is correct: antiphase or pi radians because points lie on opposite sides of a node.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: antiphase or pi radians because points lie on opposite sides of a node.

options.label: A
options.text: Points P and R oscillate in phase because every point on a stationary wave moves together
options.distractorRationale: Only points within the same loop (or separated by an even number of nodes) oscillate in phase.

options.label: B
options.text: Points P and R oscillate vaguely out of phase by an angle equal to their separation
options.distractorRationale: AQA explicitly rejects vague 'out of phase'; across one node the phase difference is exactly π rad (antiphase).

options.label: C
options.text: Points P and R oscillate in antiphase or pi radians because points lie on opposite sides of a node

options.label: D
options.text: Points P and R oscillate with identical amplitude and zero displacement at every instant
options.distractorRationale: Nodes have permanent zero displacement; P and R oscillate with non-zero amplitudes.

items.stem: During a medical scan, a 4.00 MHz Doppler ultrasound probe is held at 60.0° to a femoral vein. Blood flows away from the probe at 0.480 m s⁻¹, and the speed of ultrasound is $c = 1560\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δf = 1.23 × 10³ Hz. (b) 1.23 kHz. (c) Ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift because moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect the wave. (d) Acoustic coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound transmits into tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes f in Hz, v, cos θ, c, and factor of 2 into Δf = (2fv cos θ)/c.
Converts to 1.23 kHz and states received frequency is lower.
States moving red blood cells receive a Doppler-shifted frequency.
States the reflected wave experiences a second Doppler shift back to the probe as moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect it.
States gel displaces air from the gap between the probe and skin.
Explains acoustic impedance matching enables transmission into tissue rather than reflection at the skin.

parts.prompt: Using $\Delta f / f = (2v\cos\theta)/c$, calculate the Doppler frequency shift $\Delta f$ in hertz.
Express this frequency shift in kilohertz and state whether the received frequency is higher or lower than the emitted frequency.
workingSteps: Blood flows away from the probe, so the received frequency is lower.

parts.prompt: Explain why the factor of 2 appears in the Doppler ultrasound equation.
parts.expectedAnswer: The factor of 2 arises because ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift: moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect the wave.
workingSteps: Red blood cells act first as moving receivers of shifted wavefronts.
They then reflect the wave back as moving emitters, so the ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift.

parts.prompt: Explain why acoustic coupling gel must be applied between the probe and the patient's skin.
parts.expectedAnswer: Acoustic coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound enters tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.
workingSteps: Air has much lower acoustic impedance than skin and soft tissue, causing nearly total reflection.
Acoustic coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound transmits into tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.

items.stem: An eye A-scan records the front-surface echo of an eye lens at $26\,\mu\text{s}$ through aqueous humour ($c_1 = 1520\text{ m s}^{-1}$). The rear-surface echo arrives at $76\,\mu\text{s}$, with wave speed $c_2 = 1580\text{ m s}^{-1}$ inside the second layer.
items.workedSolution: (a) $d_1 = 19.8 mm$. (b) $\Delta t = 50\,\mu\text{s} \Rightarrow d_2 = 39.5 mm$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $2d_1 = c_1 t_1$ with factor of 2.

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 640 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 200 lines mm⁻¹. Including the central zero-order maximum, how many total principal maxima emerge across the forward semicircle (−90° ≤ θ ≤ +90°)?
items.workedSolution: d = 10⁻³ / 200 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ m, so d / λ = 7.81 and n_max = 7. Including ±1..±7 and n = 0 gives 2(7) + 1 = 15 principal maxima.

items.stem: A tuning fork produces a longitudinal sound wave of frequency $850\text{ Hz}$ travelling through air at $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$. What is the distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of the immediately adjacent rarefaction?
items.workedSolution: $\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340}{850} = 0.400\text{ m} = 40.0 cm$. Compression to adjacent rarefaction is $\frac{\lambda}{2} = 20.0 cm$.

markScheme.criterion: Finds $\lambda = 40.0 cm$ and halves it to obtain $20.0 cm$.

items.stem: An outdoor warning horn radiates 1.20 W of acoustic power equally in all directions. Taking $I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$, what is the minimum safe distance from the horn so the sound intensity level does not exceed 80.0 dB?
items.workedSolution: At 80.0 dB, $I = 1.0 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^{8.0} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ W m}^{-2}$. Rearranging $I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2}$ gives $r = \sqrt{\frac{1.20}{4\pi \times 1.0 \times 10^{-4}}} = 30.9 m$.

items.stem: A red diode laser illuminates a double slit ($s = 0.38$ mm) located $D = 2.10$ m from a matte screen during Required Practical 2. The centre-to-centre span across 9 consecutive bright fringes (8 fringe spaces) is 28.4 mm. Calculate the wavelength of this light.
items.workedSolution: With 9 bright fringes there are 8 spaces, so fringe spacing $w = 28.4 / 8 = 3.55 mm$. Using $\lambda = ws / D = (3.55 \times 10^{-3})(0.38 \times 10^{-3}) / 2.1 = 642 nm$.

items.stem: In the diffraction grating part of Required Practical 2, the grating is checked with a set square. Why is this done, and why is distance measured symmetrically between the $+n$ and $-n$ maxima?
items.workedSolution: Align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square to keep orders symmetric. Measure the symmetric span between matching orders to cut uncertainty, and never look directly into the laser.

markScheme.criterion: Aligns the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square, measures the symmetric span between matching orders, and avoids looking into the laser.

options.text: Measuring from the +n spot to the −n spot doubles sin θ directly so no trigonometry is required.
options.distractorRationale: You must halve the symmetric span (h = 2h/2) before applying tan θ = h/D and sin θ.

options.label: B
options.text: Align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square measure the symmetric span between matching orders and never look directly into the laser.

options.label: C
options.text: Tilting the grating slightly improves fringe sharpness and cancels any error in grating ruling N.
options.distractorRationale: Any tilt breaks symmetry between +n and −n orders and invalidates d sin θ = nλ.

options.label: D
options.text: A diffraction grating produces wider, dimmer fringes than a double slit, making angles harder to resolve.
options.distractorRationale: A grating produces much sharper, brighter, and more widely separated maxima than a double slit.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 488 nm is incident normally on two narrow parallel slits S₁ and S₂. Each slit has a width of 0.09 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.54 mm. The diffraction-modulated interference pattern is observed on a screen 2.6 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Interference fringe spacing Δy = λD / d = 2.35 × 10⁻³ m. (b) Central envelope full width w_env = 2λD / b = 0.0282 m. (c) First missing order n = d / b = 6.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λD / d with slit separation d.
Uses 2λD / b with individual slit width b.
Equates interference maximum angle to first diffraction minimum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent double-slit interference maxima near the centre of the pattern.
Calculate the full width of the central single-slit diffraction envelope on the screen.
Determine the lowest positive interference order n that is missing due to coincidence with a single-slit diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Equate nλ / d = λ / b => n = d / b.

items.stem: A high-speed train sounds a $510\text{ Hz}$ horn while travelling at a constant speed of $30.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ past a stationary platform observer. The speed of sound in still air is $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f'_{\text{app}} = 510 \times \frac{340}{340 - 30.0} = 559 Hz$. (b) $f'_{\text{rec}} = 510 \times \frac{340}{340 + 30.0} = 469 Hz$. (c) $\lambda' = \frac{340 - 30.0}{510} = 0.608 m$. (d) Train motion compresses wavefronts to a shorter wavelength ahead of the source. Because $f'$ depends inversely on $v \mp u_{\text{s}}$, the upward shift is larger in magnitude than the downward shift.

markScheme.criterion: Explains compressed wavefronts with shorter wavelength ahead of the moving source.
Notes the asymmetric change in $1/(v \mp u_{\text{s}})$ produces a larger upward shift than downward shift.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency heard by the stationary observer as the train approaches.
workingSteps: Substitute $f = 510\text{ Hz}$, $v = 340\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $u_{\text{s}} = 30.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to obtain 559 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency heard by the stationary observer after the train has passed and is receding.
Determine the wavelength of the sound waves in air directly ahead of the moving train.
Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why the observer hears a higher pitch during approach and why the upward frequency shift exceeds the downward shift.
parts.expectedAnswer: Forward motion of the train compresses wavefronts to a shorter wavelength ahead of the moving source. Because $f' \propto \frac{1}{v \mp u_{\text{s}}}$, subtracting $u_{\text{s}}$ raises $f'$ more than adding $u_{\text{s}}$ lowers $f'$.
workingSteps: Describe compressed wavefronts with shorter wavelength ahead of the moving source.
Compare the denominators $(v - u_{\text{s}})$ and $(v + u_{\text{s}})$ in the inverse relationship.

items.stem: The transverse speed is 192 m s⁻¹ on a taut string (1.2 m, clamped at both ends) vibrating steadily in its 5th harmonic.
items.workedSolution: (a) Wavelength: λ_5 = 2L / n = 2(1.2) / 5 = 0.480 m. (b) Resonant frequency: f_5 = v / λ_5 = 192 / 0.480 = 400 Hz. (c) Base harmonic: f₁ = f_5 / 5 = 80.0 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of this n = 5 harmonic standing wave.
workingSteps: For a string fixed at both ends, λ_n = 2L / n.

parts.prompt: Determine the oscillation frequency of this standing wave.
Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string when kept at the same tension.

items.stem: A 780 Hz sound wave leaves a fixed warning horn in still air (wave speed 343 m s⁻¹). A listener moves towards the source at 72 m s⁻¹. What frequency is heard?
items.workedSolution: By the Doppler formula, f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 780 × (343 + 72) / 343 = 944 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 944 Hz (C).
