items.stem: A student examines the n = 4 bright maximum during a Young's slits experiment. Coherent 560 nm rays cross a pair of narrow slits S₁ and S₂ (0.55 mm apart) to a wall 3 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δℓ = nλ = 4 × 5.60 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.24 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Angular location: θ_4 = arcsin(nλ / d) = 0.233°. (c) Linear height: y_4 = nλD / d = 0.0122 m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the path difference between waves from S₁ and S₂ arriving at the n = 4 bright fringe.
workingSteps: For constructive interference at order n, Δℓ = nλ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deflection θ_4 (in degrees) of the n = 4 bright fringe from the central axis.
Determine the linear distance from the central bright fringe to the n = 4 bright fringe on the screen.

items.stem: A progressive sinusoidal wave travels to the left on a stretched string, as shown by the instantaneous displacement–position graph y(x). The wave has amplitude 0.03 m, wavelength 0.48 m, and frequency 55 Hz.
items.workedSolution: (a) Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 55 = 0.0182 s. (b) Wave speed v = fλ = 55 × 0.48 = 26.4 m s⁻¹. (c) Crest-to-trough distance = 2A = 0.0600 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = 1 / f with given frequency.
Substitutes into v = fλ or v = λ / T.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period of oscillation of a point in the medium.
Determine the propagation speed of the progressive wave.
workingSteps: Apply v = fλ (or v = λ / T).

parts.prompt: Determine the total vertical distance moved by a medium particle in travelling from a wave crest to an adjacent trough.
workingSteps: Crest-to-trough vertical span equals twice the wave amplitude, Δy = 2A.

items.stem: Air carries sound at 343 m s⁻¹ inside an open air pipe (0.42 m long, treating the open pipe as ideal). Find its resonant frequency in mode n = 5.
items.workedSolution: Open-open harmonic law with L = 0.42 m and n = 5 gives f_n = nv / (2L) = (5 × 343) / (2 × 0.42) = 2.04 × 10³ Hz.

options.distractorRationale: Computes the first-harmonic frequency f₁ instead of the n-th harmonic.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n.

items.stem: At θ = 57.1° from the axis, order n = 3 emerges from a 500 lines mm⁻¹ grating lit normally. Calculate the light wavelength.
items.workedSolution: Grating pitch: d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Solving d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(57.1°) / 3 = 5.60 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.60 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Given a 25 Hz wave along a long stretched rope with wavelength 2 m and amplitude 0.028 m, points P and Q sit at x₁ = 0.3 m and x₂ = 0.6 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Propagation speed: v = fλ = 25 × 2 = 50.0 m s⁻¹. (b) Cycle period: T = 1 / 25 = 0.0400 s. (c) Offset Δx = 0.300 m yields Δφ = 2π Δx / λ = 0.942 rad.

parts.prompt: Calculate the propagation speed of the wave.
Determine the oscillation period of particle P.
Calculate the phase difference, in radians, between the oscillations at P and Q.

items.stem: Testing a 0.1 mm single slit with a screen 2.2 m away, a teacher uses 488 nm light normally. Find the full linear width across the central peak.
items.workedSolution: At θ = ±λ / b, offset is y₁ = λD / b = 0.0107 m, giving total central width w = 2λD / b = 0.0215 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0215 m (C).

items.stem: A parallel beam of monochromatic light strikes an air–glass boundary (refractive index $n = 1.50$) at an angle of incidence of 50.0°. Take $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\theta_2 = 30.7 °$. (b) $v = 2.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹$. (c) Newton corpuscular theory predicted light travels faster in water whereas Huygens wave theory predicted light slows down in water confirmed by Foucault.

markScheme.criterion: States Newton predicted greater speed in optically denser medium.
States Huygens predicted lower speed, later confirmed by Foucault.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angle of refraction inside the glass.
Calculate the speed of light inside the glass predicted by Huygens' wave model.
Contrast Newton's corpuscular prediction with Huygens' wave prediction for refraction into water or glass.
parts.expectedAnswer: Historically, Newton corpuscular theory predicted light travels faster in water whereas Huygens wave theory predicted light slows down in water confirmed by Foucault.
workingSteps: Newton assumed perpendicular attraction accelerated corpuscles toward the normal ($v_{\text{dense}} > c$).
Huygens showed slower wave speed in denser media turns wavefronts toward the normal ($v_{\text{dense}} < c$).

items.stem: From a modulated radio $V$–$t$ waveform, a student measures one carrier cycle period $T_{\text{c}} = 6.25\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ and one modulating information cycle period $T_{\text{M}} = 0.125\text{ ms}$. The same audio signal is alternatively transmitted by FM with frequency deviation $\Delta f = 32.0\text{ kHz}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_{\text{c}} = 160 kHz$. (b) $f_{\text{M}} = 8.00\text{ kHz} \Rightarrow \text{BW}_{\text{AM}} = 16.0 kHz$. (c) $\text{BW}_{\text{FM}} = 2(32.0 + 8.00) = 80.0 kHz$; FM rejects amplitude noise better at the cost of wider channel bandwidth.

markScheme.criterion: Finds $f_{\text{M}} = 8.00\text{ kHz}$ and doubles for AM.
Notes FM resists amplitude noise better while AM uses narrower bandwidth allowing more stations.

parts.prompt: Calculate the carrier frequency $f_{\text{c}}$ in kHz.
Find the information frequency $f_{\text{M}}$ and hence calculate the required AM bandwidth.
Calculate the FM channel bandwidth for $\Delta f = 32.0\text{ kHz}$ and state one trade-off between AM and FM.
parts.expectedAnswer: 80.0 kHz. FM offers much better noise immunity than AM because noise mainly spikes amplitude. However, FM needs a much wider bandwidth, so fewer channels fit in a given frequency band.
workingSteps: Contrast FM noise immunity with AM bandwidth economy.

items.stem: An ideal analyzer cuts plane-polarized light from 96 W m⁻² to 78.9 W m⁻². For plane-polarized light, use I = I₀ cos²θ. Calculate the acute angle θ to the incident polarization.
items.workedSolution: Solve I = I₀ cos²θ: cos θ = √(78.9 / 96) = 0.906; hence θ = arccos(0.906) = 25.0°.

options.distractorRationale: Forgets to take the square root of I / I₀ before taking arccos, solving cos θ = I / I₀ instead of cos²θ = I / I₀.

options.distractorRationale: Computes the complement angle 90° − θ (using arcsin √(I / I₀) instead of arccos √(I / I₀)).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda = 500\text{ nm}$ illuminates $3$ rectangular slits of individual width $b = 20.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ and centre-to-centre separation $d = 100\text{ }\mu\text{m}$. The modulated intensity pattern is projected onto a screen $D = 2.40\text{ m}$ away.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\theta = 25.0 mrad$. (b) Central width $= 120 mm$. (c) $s = 12.0 mm$, missing order $n = d/b = 5.00$. (d) finite slit width b imposes a single-slit diffraction envelope whose first minimum at theta equals lambda over b modulates the multiple-slit peaks.

markScheme.criterion: Applies θ = λ/b with b = 20.0 μm.
Calculates fringe spacing s = λD/d = 12.0 mm.
Equates d sin θ = nλ with b sin θ = λ ⇒ n = d/b.
States multi-slit intensity is multiplied by single-slit diffraction envelope.
Explains the single-slit envelope minimum at θ = λ/b suppresses order d/b because finite slit width b modulates the multiple-slit peaks.

parts.prompt: Using $\theta = \lambda / b$, calculate the angular position of the first minimum of the single-slit diffraction envelope in $\text{mrad}$.
Calculate the full linear width of the central maximum of the single-slit envelope on the screen.
Determine the separation $s = \lambda D / d$ of principal maxima and hence deduce which order $n$ is the first missing principal maximum.
parts.expectedAnswer: Fringe spacing s = 12.0 mm; first missing order n = 5.00.

parts.prompt: Explain qualitatively why the intensity of successive principal maxima falls off away from the centre and why order $n = d/b$ is missing.
parts.expectedAnswer: Finite slit width b imposes a single-slit diffraction envelope over the multiple-slit peaks. Its first minimum at theta equals lambda over b suppresses order n = d/b.
workingSteps: finite slit width b imposes a single-slit diffraction envelope whose first minimum at theta equals lambda over b modulates the multiple-slit peaks.

items.stem: Sealed at one end, a resonance tube (0.24 m long, neglecting open-end effects) carries sound at 348 m s⁻¹. The air column enters odd harmonic n = 7.
items.workedSolution: (a) L_eff = 0.240 m, so f₁ = v / (4L_eff) = 363 Hz. (b) Harmonic wavelength: λ_7 = 4L_eff / 7 = 0.137 m. (c) Frequency: f_7 = 7f₁ = 2.54 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies quarter-wave first-harmonic relation f₁ = v / (4L_eff).
Multiplies first-harmonic frequency by odd harmonic index 7 (or uses v / λ).

parts.prompt: Calculate the first-harmonic (n = 1) frequency of this closed-end air column.
workingSteps: For a pipe closed at one end, λ₁ = 4L so f₁ = v / (4L).

parts.prompt: Determine the wavelength of the n = 7 harmonic standing wave.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this n = 7 harmonic mode.

items.stem: An elastic string of length $L = 0.900\text{ m}$ carries waves at speed $108\text{ m s}^{-1}$. One end is clamped firmly, while the other end is attached to a light ring sliding freely on a smooth vertical rod.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_1 = 30.0 Hz$. (b) $f_3 = 90.0 Hz$, $f_5 = 150 Hz$. (c) A string with one fixed end and one free end has a displacement node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end. This supports only odd harmonics. (d) Increasing damping lowers the peak resonance amplitude, broadens the response curve, and slightly reduces the resonant frequency.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies node at fixed end and antinode at free end.
Links odd quarter-wavelengths (node at fixed end, antinode at free end) to odd harmonics only.
States lower peak amplitude and broader peak.
States a slight downward shift in resonant frequency as damping lowers the peak and broadens the response curve.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the first harmonic of this fixed–free string.
Calculate the frequencies of the third harmonic and the next allowed harmonic above it (the fifth harmonic).
parts.expectedAnswer: Third harmonic f₃ = 90.0 Hz; fifth harmonic f₅ = 150 Hz.

parts.prompt: Explain in terms of displacement nodes and antinodes why this string cannot support even harmonics.
parts.expectedAnswer: A string with one fixed end and one free end forms a displacement node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end. Only odd harmonics satisfy these boundary conditions.
workingSteps: One fixed end forms a displacement node and one free end forms an antinode. Only odd harmonics fit these boundary conditions.

parts.prompt: When a sinusoidal vibrator drives this string through air of increasing viscosity, describe the three qualitative changes to the resonance amplitude–frequency curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: Increasing damping decreases the peak resonance amplitude, broadens the response curve, and slightly reduces the resonant frequency.
workingSteps: increasing damping decreases the peak resonance amplitude broadens the response curve and slightly reduces the resonant frequency.

items.stem: A stretched string supports a stationary wave of wavelength 64 cm with transverse wave speed 128 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) 32.0 cm. (b) 200 Hz. (c) All points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase with each other. Points in neighbouring loops across a node oscillate in antiphase with a phase difference of pi radians.

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = λ / 2 for the first harmonic.
States points within the same loop oscillate in phase (0 rad).
States points in adjacent loops across a node oscillate in antiphase (π rad).

parts.prompt: State the vibrating length of string needed for this wavelength to correspond to the first harmonic.
Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string.
The string is then made to vibrate in its third harmonic. Compare the phase of two points in the same loop and two points in adjacent loops.
parts.expectedAnswer: All points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase with each other. Points in neighbouring loops across a node oscillate in antiphase with a phase difference of pi radians.
workingSteps: Points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase. Points in neighbouring loops across a node oscillate in antiphase (phase difference pi radians).

items.stem: Between the wooden bridge and the top of the bench pulley, a student measures vibrating length $L$ in Required Practical 1. Why is this span measured rather than the full length from vibration generator to hanging mass?
items.workedSolution: Measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes. The first harmonic frequency equals the wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Measures vibrating length between the bridge and pulley nodes, since first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the vibration generator produces an antinode at the pulley and doubles the wave speed.
options.distractorRationale: Both the wooden bridge and the pulley contact point act as fixed nodes.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the hanging section of string vibrates at twice the first harmonic frequency of the horizontal section.
options.distractorRationale: Only the taut section bounded by the bridge and pulley forms the measured stationary wave.

options.label: C
options.text: Because tension is zero between the vibration generator and the wooden bridge.
options.distractorRationale: Tension is nearly uniform along the string; the bridge simply establishes a clean fixed node.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

items.stem: A steerable radio dish of diameter 64.0 m monitors neutral hydrogen emission at a wavelength of 0.210 m. What is the minimum angular resolution of this single radio dish?
items.workedSolution: Using $\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D} = \frac{0.210}{64.0} = 3.28 × 10⁻³ rad$.

items.stem: When an ambulance siren moves towards a stationary observer at 82 m s⁻¹, its emitted 620 Hz tone shifts. Given sound speed 336 m s⁻¹, determine the detected frequency.
items.workedSolution: Observed pitch (towards observer): f' = fv / (v − v_s) = (620 × 336) / (336 − 82) = 820 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 820 Hz (D).

options.distractorRationale: Uses the moving-observer formula AND reverses the sign of the Doppler frequency shift.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the wrong sign in the denominator, using v + v_s for an approaching source (or v − v_s for a receding source).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the moving-observer equation f(v ± v_s) / v instead of the moving-source equation fv / (v ∓ v_s).

items.stem: A 445 nm light beam hits two narrow parallel slits (separation 0.45 mm) normally, projecting Young's interference fringes onto a screen 1.5 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Bright separation = λD / d = (4.45 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.5) / 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.48 × 10⁻³ m. (b) First dark fringe lies at ½ × 1.48 × 10⁻³ = 7.42 × 10⁻⁴ m. (c) At n = 2, path difference = nλ = 2 × 4.45 × 10⁻⁷ = 8.90 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units and substitutes into λD / (slit separation).
Takes half of the bright-fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
Determine the distance on the screen from the central bright maximum to the centre of the first dark fringe.
workingSteps: First destructive minimum occurs halfway between the central and first-order bright maxima: y_dark,1 = 0.5 × fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the geometric path difference between waves arriving from the two slits at the order n = 2 bright fringe.
workingSteps: Constructive interference at order n requires path difference Δℓ = nλ.

items.stem: A medium-wave AM allocation spans a total frequency band of 180 kHz. If each AM speech station carries audio up to $f_{\mathrm{M}} = 4.50\text{ kHz}$, what is the maximum number of non-overlapping AM stations that can fit inside this band?
items.workedSolution: Each AM station occupies $\mathrm{BW}_{\mathrm{AM}} = 2 f_{\mathrm{M}} = 2(4.50) = 9.00\text{ kHz}$. Maximum stations $= \frac{180}{9.00} = 20$.

items.stem: An acoustic engineer measures a steady tone of intensity $5.00 \times 10^{-6}\text{ W m}^{-2}$ while calibrating equal-loudness curves using a $1.0\text{ kHz}$ reference tone ($I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $\text{Level} = 10\log_{10}(5.00 \times 10^6) = 67.0 dB$. (b) Subjects match the loudness of test tones at different frequencies to a fixed $1\text{ kHz}$ reference tone. (c) Unweighted dB measures raw physical intensity level, while the dBA scale weights frequencies to match human ear sensitivity.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a 1 kHz reference tone at fixed dB level.
Matches perceived loudness across frequencies and plots required intensity level against frequency.
Notes dB is unweighted across frequency.
Explains dBA scale weights frequencies to match human ear sensitivity.

parts.prompt: Calculate the sound intensity level in dB for an intensity of $5.00 \times 10^{-6}\text{ W m}^{-2}$.
Outline how an equal-loudness curve (e.g. 40 phon) is produced experimentally.
parts.expectedAnswer: A listener compares a pure test tone at each frequency with a 1 kHz reference tone at a fixed level (e.g. 40 dB). They adjust the test tone's intensity until both sound equally loud, and plot the required dB against log frequency.
workingSteps: Use a 1 kHz reference tone fixed at a known dB level.
Adjust intensity of test tones across frequencies until perceived loudness matches the reference and plot dB vs frequency.

parts.prompt: Explain the difference between the unweighted dB scale and the dBA scale used in environmental noise meters.
parts.expectedAnswer: Unweighted dB treats all frequencies equally. The dBA scale weights frequencies to match human ear sensitivity, reducing very low and very high frequencies where hearing is less sensitive.
workingSteps: Note dB has flat frequency response across all frequencies.
State dBA scale weights frequencies to match human ear sensitivity.

items.stem: The diagram shows unpolarized light of intensity 220 W m⁻² incident on two ideal polarizing filters. The beam passes first through polarizer P₁ and then through analyzer A tilted at θ = 20° to P₁. For plane-polarized light, transmitted intensity obeys I = I₁ cos²θ.
items.workedSolution: (a) After P₁, I₁ = ½ I₀ = 110 W m⁻². (b) After analyzer A, I = I₁ cos²(20°) = 97.1 W m⁻². (c) Overall fraction I / I₀ = ½ cos²(20°) = 0.442.

markScheme.criterion: Halves unpolarized incident intensity at ideal polarizer P₁.
Applies I = I₁ cos²θ to the polarized beam.
Divides final transmitted intensity by incident unpolarized intensity I₀.

parts.prompt: State and calculate the intensity I₁ of the plane-polarized beam between polarizer P₁ and analyzer A.
workingSteps: Averaging cos²φ = ½ over all random polarization orientations reduces unpolarized intensity by half: I₁ = ½ I₀.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity I emerging from analyzer A.
workingSteps: Apply Malus's law I = I₁ cos²θ.

parts.prompt: Determine the overall fraction I / I₀ of the original unpolarized intensity transmitted by the two-filter combination.
workingSteps: Overall transmission fraction = I / I₀ = ½ cos²θ.

items.stem: The diagram shows a stretched string fixed at both ends of vibrating length 0.9 m and linear mass density 0.0012 kg m⁻¹. It vibrates in harmonic mode n = 3 at a frequency of 208.3 Hz. The transverse wave speed on a taut string is v = √(T / μ). Determine the required tension T.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.9) / 3 = 0.600 m, so required wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 125 m s⁻¹. Rearranging v = √(T / μ) gives T = μv² = 0.0012 × (125)² = 18.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 2Lf_n / n and computes T = μv² = 18.8 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to square the wave speed when rearranging v = √(T / μ) to T = μv².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, halving v and underestimating T = μv² by a factor of 4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides v² by linear mass density μ instead of multiplying T = μv².

items.stem: Refer to the stationary wave diagram showing points P, Q, and R along a vibrating string.
items.workedSolution: (a) P–Q: $0\text{ rad}$ (in phase); P–R: antiphase or pi radians because points lie on opposite sides of a node. (b) Stationary wave has varying amplitude and no net transfer of energy along a stationary wave; progressive wave has equal amplitude and transfers energy.

markScheme.criterion: P and Q are in phase ($0\text{ rad}$).
P and R are in antiphase ($\pi\text{ rad}$ / $180^\circ$; reject vague 'out of phase').
Stationary amplitude varies from zero at nodes to max at antinodes (progressive constant).
No net transfer of energy along a stationary wave (progressive transfers energy).

parts.prompt: State the phase difference between P and Q, and between P and R.
parts.expectedAnswer: P and Q are in phase ($0\text{ rad}$), whereas P and R are in antiphase or pi radians because points lie on opposite sides of a node.
workingSteps: Same loop = 0 rad; separated by one node = π rad (antiphase).

parts.prompt: Compare amplitude variation and energy transfer in a stationary wave with those in an undamped progressive wave.
parts.expectedAnswer: In a stationary wave, amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes, with no net transfer of energy along the wave. In a progressive wave, amplitude is constant and energy is transferred in the direction of propagation.
workingSteps: Contrast amplitude profile and net energy transfer.

items.stem: A diagnostic ultrasound probe uses a piezoelectric crystal that vibrates at its first-harmonic resonant frequency of 5.00 MHz. If longitudinal waves travel through the crystal at 4200 m s⁻¹, what is the required thickness of the crystal ($\lambda / 2$)?
items.workedSolution: Wavelength in the crystal is $\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{4200}{5.00 \times 10^6} = 8.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m} = 0.840\text{ mm}$. Resonant thickness is $\frac{\lambda}{2} = 0.420 mm$.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 532 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 500 lines mm⁻¹. Diffracted orders starting from n = 1 are observed across the forward semicircle (−90° < θ < +90°).
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m, so θ₁ = arcsin(λ / d) = 15.4°. (b) d / λ = 3.76, giving n_max = 3. (c) Total principal maxima = 2(3) + 1 = 7.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and applies sin θ₁ = λ / d.
Evaluates d / λ = 3.76 and rounds down.

items.stem: A transverse travelling wave moves to the left along a flexible cord. It has wavelength $\lambda = 18.0\text{ cm}$ and period $T = 12.0\text{ ms}$, as shown by the $y(x)$ and $y(t)$ graphs.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f = 83.3 Hz$. (b) $v = 15.0 m s⁻¹$. (c) Particle P moves downwards through equilibrium because the approaching trough lies immediately to its right. (d) Travelling waves transfer energy while particles oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions with zero net transport of matter. In a transverse wave, particles oscillate perpendicular to energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave, they oscillate parallel to energy transfer.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = fλ = λ/T in SI units.
Deduces particle P is moving downwards through equilibrium because the approaching trough lies immediately to its right.
States energy propagates through local coupling between neighbouring oscillators.
States particles oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions with zero net transport of matter while energy travels across space.
Defines transverse oscillation perpendicular to energy transfer.
Defines longitudinal oscillation as parallel to energy transfer (contrasted with perpendicular oscillation in a transverse wave).

Determine the speed of the wave along the cord.
Predict the instantaneous direction of motion of particle P (at $x = \lambda/2$) given that the wave travels to the left.
parts.expectedAnswer: Particle P is moving downwards through equilibrium because the approaching trough lies immediately to its right.
workingSteps: moving downwards through equilibrium because the approaching trough lies immediately to its right.

parts.prompt: Explain how a travelling wave transfers energy across the cord without causing a net displacement of matter, and contrast transverse with longitudinal particle oscillation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Travelling waves transfer energy across space while medium particles oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions with zero net transport of matter. In addition, particles oscillate perpendicular to energy transfer in a transverse wave, whereas they oscillate parallel to energy transfer in a longitudinal wave.
workingSteps: travelling waves transfer energy across space while particles of the medium oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions with zero net transport of matter.
in a transverse wave particles oscillate perpendicular to energy transfer whereas in a longitudinal wave particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer.

items.stem: A small loudspeaker emits sound uniformly at 0.200 W in an open courtyard. Take $I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 9.95 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻²$, $L_1 = 90.0 dB$. (b) $L_2 = 84.0 dB$. (c) dBA is frequency weighted to match human ear sensitivity peaking near three kilohertz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies inverse-square drop of $6.02\text{ dB}$ for doubling distance.
States ear sensitivity peaks around 3 kHz and is much lower at 100 Hz.
Explains dBA weighting accounts for this frequency response.

parts.prompt: Calculate the sound intensity and intensity level in dB at a distance of 4.00 m.
Calculate the new intensity level when the listener moves to 8.00 m.
workingSteps: Doubling distance cuts intensity by a factor of 4, reducing level by $10\lg(4) = 6.02\text{ dB}$.

parts.prompt: Explain why a sound measured at 60 dB at 100 Hz sounds much quieter than 60 dB at 3 kHz, referring to the dBA scale.
parts.expectedAnswer: The human ear is much less sensitive at 100 Hz than at 3 kHz. The dBA scale is frequency weighted to match human ear sensitivity, which peaks near three kilohertz.
workingSteps: Note equal-loudness curves slope upward strongly at low frequencies.
Explain dBA applies frequency weighting matching peak ear sensitivity around 3 kHz.

items.stem: Why is a diffraction grating with hundreds of slits per millimetre preferred over Young's double slit for measuring an unknown laser wavelength accurately?
items.workedSolution: Many slits produce narrower, brighter, and more widely separated maxima, reducing percentage uncertainty in angle measurement. Therefore option A is correct: many slits produce narrower brighter and more widely separated maxima.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: many slits produce narrower brighter and more widely separated maxima.

options.label: B

options.distractorRationale: Gratings make maxima sharper (narrower) and brighter, not dimmer or broader.

options.label: C
options.text: Compared with two slits, a grating eliminates the central zero-order maximum completely
options.distractorRationale: The bright central n = 0 maximum is always present and serves as the angular reference.

options.label: D
options.text: Compared with two slits, a grating works even if the light is completely incoherent white noise
options.distractorRationale: Diffraction gratings still rely on coherent superposition across slits.

items.stem: Why do astronomers and analytical chemists use a transmission diffraction grating rather than a Young's double slit to measure atomic spectral wavelengths?
items.workedSolution: Many narrow slits superpose together to produce intense, razor-sharp maxima at large diffraction angles θ, minimizing uncertainty in λ. Diffraction gratings produce sharper, brighter, and more widely dispersed maxima than double slits for accurate spectral analysis. Therefore option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: diffraction gratings produce sharper, brighter, and more widely dispersed maxima than double slits for spectral analysis.

options.label: A
options.text: Diffraction gratings require no coherent light and display only a single zero-order white image.
options.distractorRationale: Spectral analysis relies specifically on the dispersed higher-order maxima n = 1, 2,... where d sin θ = nλ.

options.label: B
options.text: Diffraction gratings reduce the angular separation between red and violet so the whole spectrum fits into a 1° camera aperture.
options.distractorRationale: Grating spacing d is tiny, giving much larger angular dispersion θ and lower percentage uncertainty in θ.

options.label: C
options.text: Double slits cannot diffract visible wavelengths shorter than 550 nm.
options.distractorRationale: Double slits diffract all visible wavelengths, but their broad, dim fringes yield poorer wavelength resolution.

options.label: D
options.text: Because thousands of narrow slits superpose simultaneously, diffraction gratings produce sharper, brighter, and more widely dispersed maxima than double slits, allowing accurate analysis of stellar absorption and emission spectra.

items.stem: In a double-slit experiment, a student measures from the centre of the first bright fringe to the centre of the eleventh bright fringe. Why is this better than measuring a single fringe spacing?
items.workedSolution: Dividing the span of ten fringe spaces by ten cuts percentage uncertainty tenfold. In addition, avoid looking directly into the laser beam, remove reflective surfaces, and measure across many fringe spaces to reduce percentage uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Dividing ten fringe spaces by ten cuts percentage uncertainty tenfold; also avoids looking into the laser beam and removes reflective surfaces.

options.text: Dividing the span of ten fringe spaces by ten cuts percentage uncertainty tenfold; alongside this, avoid looking directly into the laser beam remove reflective surfaces and measure across many fringe spaces to reduce percentage uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: Eleven bright fringes span eleven fringe spaces, eliminating all systematic error in slit separation s.
options.distractorRationale: Eleven bright fringes span ten spaces (not eleven), and averaging fringes does not fix systematic error in s.

options.label: C
options.text: Fringe spacing increases rapidly at outer fringes so measuring across ten spaces is required for linearity.
options.distractorRationale: For small angles in Young's double slit, fringe spacing w = λD/s is uniform across the central pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Measuring edge-to-edge of a single bright fringe has lower uncertainty than centre-to-centre across ten spaces.
options.distractorRationale: Single-fringe edges are diffuse and give much higher percentage uncertainty.

items.stem: Why does a diffraction grating generally give a more precise wavelength measurement than Young's double slits in RP2?
items.workedSolution: Maxima are sharper and separated by larger angles, reducing percentage uncertainty. Align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square, measure the symmetric span between matching orders, and never look directly into the laser.

markScheme.criterion: Notes maxima are sharper and at larger angles; aligns grating with a set square, measures symmetric spans, and avoids looking into the laser.

options.text: Because a diffraction grating allows the small-angle approximation w = λD/d to hold exactly up to 90°.
options.distractorRationale: Large diffraction angles require exact tan θ = h/D and d sin θ = nλ; the small-angle formula fails.

options.label: B
options.text: Because a diffraction grating eliminates the need to measure grating-to-screen distance D.
options.distractorRationale: Distance D is still required to find tan θ = h/D unless using a spectrometer vernier scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Maxima are sharper and separated by larger angles; still, align the grating perpendicular to the beam with a set square measure the symmetric span between matching orders and never look directly into the laser.

options.label: D
options.text: Because a grating eliminates laser eye hazards by dispersing energy harmlessly.
options.distractorRationale: The zero-order and diffracted laser beams remain hazardous; never look into any beam.

items.stem: Coherent light of wavelength 450 nm strikes two narrow parallel slits of separation 0.3 mm. The interference pattern is viewed on a screen 2.6 m away. If the first minimum of the single-slit diffraction envelope suppresses the n = 4 interference maximum, calculate the width b of each slit.
items.workedSolution: The first single-slit minimum occurs at θ = λ / b while the n-th double-slit maximum is at θ = nλ / d. Coincidence at n = 4 gives b = d / 4 = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ / 4 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁵ m.

markScheme.criterion: Equates λ / b = nλ / d to obtain b = d / 4 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁵ m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides slit separation by (n + 1) instead of missing order n = d / b.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the highest visible order inside the central envelope (n − 1) instead of the missing order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2 from the full angular width of the central envelope.

items.stem: The diagram compares a laboratory reference absorption spectrum with the observed absorption spectrum of a star. What does the displacement of the dark lines tell an astronomer about the star's radial motion relative to Earth?
items.workedSolution: All characteristic absorption lines are shifted toward the red (longer-wavelength) end of the spectrum. This redshift shows that the star is receding from Earth.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that redshift toward longer wavelength indicating the star is receding.

options.label: D

items.stem: On a 0.6 m taut string (fixed at both ends), waves travel at 192 m s⁻¹ in harmonic mode n = 3. Calculate the consecutive node separation.
items.workedSolution: With L = 0.6 m divided into n half-waves (n = 3), consecutive nodes lie at d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n = 0.6 / 3 = 0.200 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n to obtain 0.200 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the node-to-adjacent-antinode distance λ / 4 instead of adjacent node spacing λ / 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides string length L by the total number of nodes (n + 1) instead of the number of loops n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates a full wavelength λ = 2L / n instead of the half-wavelength node-to-node spacing λ / 2.

items.stem: Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹ through still air. A fixed warning horn produces a steady 860 Hz note, and an observer travels towards it at 72 m s⁻¹. Find the observed frequency.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 1.04 × 10³ Hz (C).

options.label: B

items.stem: How far is the n = 5 bright fringe from the central bright fringe when 488 nm light crosses two narrow parallel slits (0.28 mm apart) to a screen 1.4 m away?
items.workedSolution: One spacing = λD / d = 2.44 × 10⁻³ m. Offset from n = 0 to n = 5: y_5 = 5 × λD / d = 0.0122 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates single adjacent fringe spacing λD / d instead of multiplying by order n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies destructive half-integer factor (n − ½) instead of constructive integer order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Counts one extra interval, multiplying fringe spacing by (n + 1) fringes instead of n intervals from n = 0.

items.stem: A progressive wave travels to the left along a stretched string at a speed of 6 m s⁻¹. From its displacement–position graph, the amplitude is 0.018 m and the wavelength is 1.2 m. Determine the frequency of oscillation.
items.workedSolution: Using f = v / λ with wave speed v = 6 m s⁻¹ and wavelength λ = 1.2 m gives f = 6 / 1.2 = 5.00 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges v = fλ to obtain f = v / λ = 5.00 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the oscillation period T = λ / v instead of the frequency f = v / λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Mistakes two full cycles for one wavelength, halving the calculated frequency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength (vλ) instead of dividing v by λ.

items.stem: What resonant frequency corresponds to mode n = 3 in an open air pipe (1.26 m long, ignoring end effects) if sound speed in air is 346 m s⁻¹?
items.workedSolution: Open-open harmonic law with L = 1.26 m and n = 3 gives f_n = nv / (2L) = (3 × 346) / (2 × 1.26) = 412 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the first-harmonic frequency f₁ instead of the n-th harmonic.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n.

items.stem: Using 430 nm coherent light and a 600 lines mm⁻¹ grating at right angles, a class views maxima 0.85 m away. Focus on n = 1.
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 10⁻³ / 600 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) First find sin θ = nλ / d = 0.258; thus θ = 15.0°. (c) Linear displacement: y = D tan θ = 0.85 × tan(15.0°) = 0.227 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises large-angle geometry y = D tan θ rather than small-angle D sin θ.

items.stem: Calculate the phase difference in degrees between P and Q (x₁ = 0.072 m, x₂ = 0.306 m) on a sinusoidal wave along a slinky spring (wavelength 0.36 m, frequency 25 Hz, amplitude 0.022 m).
items.workedSolution: With Δx = 0.306 m − 0.072 m = 0.234 m and one complete cycle = 0.36 m, fraction is 0.650 cycles; thus Δφ = 360° × 0.650 = 234°.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 360° to get 234° (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in radians without converting to degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (180°) instead of a full cycle (360°) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

items.stem: Using a 650 nm laser and a 0.08 mm single slit, a class views the central bright peak on a screen 1.8 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Small-angle minimum: θ = λ / b = 8.13 × 10⁻³ rad. (b) y₁ = θD = 0.0146 m. (c) Central band: w = 2y₁ = 0.0293 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies θ = λ / b in SI units.
Multiplies θ by screen distance D.
Doubles half-width to span both sides of the central peak.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular position θ (in radians) of the first diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Use the small-angle single-slit first-minimum relation θ = λ / b.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear distance on the screen from the centre of the pattern to the first dark minimum.
Calculate the full linear width of the central bright maximum on the screen.
workingSteps: The central maximum spans from −y₁ to +y₁: w = 2y₁.

items.stem: In 1850, Foucault measured the speed of light in water. How did this measurement settle the rivalry between Newton's corpuscular model and Huygens' wave model of refraction?
items.workedSolution: To bend toward the normal, Newton's corpuscular theory predicted light travels faster in water than in air. Huygens' wave theory predicted light slows down in water, which Foucault's experiment confirmed.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that Newton corpuscular theory predicted light travels faster in water whereas Huygens wave theory predicted light slows down in water confirmed by Foucault.

options.distractorRationale: Reverses the two historical predictions: Newton argued attractive forces accelerated corpuscles into water.

options.label: B
options.text: It resolved the dispute because Newton corpuscular theory predicted light travels faster in water whereas Huygens wave theory predicted light slows down in water confirmed by Foucault.

options.label: C
options.text: Both models predicted equal speeds in water and air, so Foucault's test proved both wrong.
options.distractorRationale: The two models made opposite predictions (v_water > v_air vs v_water < v_air), allowing a decisive test.

options.label: D
options.text: Foucault showed that light does not refract at an air-water boundary unless polarised.
options.distractorRationale: Refraction occurs for all unpolarised light; Foucault measured the speed inside water directly.

items.stem: Normal-incidence vertically plane-polarized light (240 W m⁻²) meets an ideal linear analyzer angled at θ = 30° from the vertical. The transmitted intensity obeys I = I₀ cos²θ.
items.workedSolution: (a) Field ratio: E / E₀ = cos(30°) = 0.866. (b) Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²(30°) = 180 W m⁻². (c) Absorbed = 240 − 180 = 60.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Projects electric-field vector via E / E₀ = cos θ.
Subtracts transmitted intensity from incident intensity.

workingSteps: Only the electric-field component parallel to the analyzer axis is transmitted: E / E₀ = cos θ.

items.stem: Coherent monochromatic light illuminates $N = 4$ identical parallel slits, each individually producing intensity $I_1$ at the centre of a distant screen. What is the ratio $I_{\max} / I_1$ of the central principal maximum intensity to the single-slit intensity?
items.workedSolution: At the central principal maximum all $4$ waves arrive in phase, so amplitude is $4A_1$ and intensity $I_{\max} = N^2 I_1 = 4^2 I_1 = 16.0 I_1$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes peak intensity scales linearly as N instead of quadratically as N².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses 2N rather than N² for coherent amplitude superposition.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Cubes N instead of squaring the summed amplitude NA.

items.stem: Air inside a 0.24 m cylindrical pipe (closed at one end, neglecting open-end effects) carries sound at 336 m s⁻¹. Work out the next mode frequency above the first harmonic.
items.workedSolution: Only odd modes (n = 1, 3, 5,...) resonate here; next above the first harmonic is n = 3, giving f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 3(336) / (4 × 0.24) = 1.05 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies odd harmonic n = 3 and computes f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 1.05 × 10³ Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic frequency v / (4L) instead of the next higher harmonic 3v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes an even n = 2 harmonic exists in a pipe closed at one end, computing 2f₁ = v / (2L) instead of 3f₁ = 3v / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the open-both-ends formula 3v / (2L) instead of closed-one-end 3v / (4L).

items.stem: A uniform string of length $L = 1.20\text{ m}$ carries transverse waves at $144\text{ m s}^{-1}$. One end is clamped fixed, and the other end is attached to a light frictionless sliding ring (free boundary). What is the frequency of the third harmonic ($n = 3$)?
items.workedSolution: For one fixed and one free end, $\lambda_n = \frac{4L}{n}$ for odd $n$. At $n = 3$, $\lambda_3 = \frac{4(1.20)}{3} = 1.60\text{ m}$, so $f_3 = \frac{144}{1.60} = 90.0 Hz$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Applies the fixed–fixed formula nv/(2L) instead of the fixed–free formula nv/(4L).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first harmonic frequency instead of the third harmonic frequency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses n = 4 instead of n = 3 in nv/(4L).

items.stem: Which statement accurately contrasts energy transfer in a stationary wave vibrating in its first harmonic against a progressive wave of the same frequency?
items.workedSolution: Zero net energy transfer and spatially varying amplitude (0 at nodes, maximum at antinodes) define a stationary wave. Unlike a progressive wave, a stationary wave stores energy locally between nodes and transfers zero net energy along the wave. Therefore option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: a stationary wave stores energy locally between nodes and transfers zero net energy along the wave.

options.label: A
options.text: A stationary wave transfers energy at twice the wave speed because two progressive waves carry energy together.
options.distractorRationale: The two opposite progressive waves carry equal energy fluxes in opposite directions, giving zero net energy transfer.

options.label: B
options.text: A stationary wave has zero kinetic and potential energy at every instant because the wave profile does not advance.
options.distractorRationale: Energy oscillates continuously between kinetic and potential forms within each loop.

options.label: C
options.text: Every point along a stationary wave oscillates with the same maximum amplitude as a progressive wave.
options.distractorRationale: Amplitude varies continuously from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes in a stationary wave.

options.label: D
options.text: Considering energy flow along the medium, unlike a progressive wave, a stationary wave stores energy locally in vibrating pockets between nodes and transfers zero net energy along the wave.

items.stem: A hanging mass of 0.55 kg ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²) tensions a braided cotton cord during Required Practical 1. Varying vibrating length $L$ and plotting $f_1$ against $1/L$ gives a straight line through the origin of gradient 23.7 m s⁻¹. Percentage uncertainties are 1.4% in mass, 0.8% in frequency, and 0.6% in length.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v = 2 \times 23.7 = 47.4 m s⁻¹$. (b) $T = 5.40 N$, $\mu = T/v^2 = 2.40 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$. (c) $\%\Delta \mu = 1.4 + 2(0.8) + 2(0.6) = 4.20\%$. (d) measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $T = mg = 5.40 N$ and substitutes into $\mu = T/v^2$.
Mass per unit length $\mu = 2.40 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$.
Doubles percentage uncertainties in both $f_1$ and $L$ before adding $\%\Delta m$.
Measures vibrating length between wooden bridge and top of pulley (fixed nodes).
Links fixed-node span to first-harmonic condition $f_1 = v/(2L)$.

parts.prompt: Use the gradient of the $f_1$ against $1/L$ graph to determine the wave speed $v$ on the string.
Calculate the mass per unit length $\mu$ of the string.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $\mu$ from the stated measurement uncertainties.
Explain clearly between which two points $L$ must be measured to avoid a systematic error.
parts.expectedAnswer: measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length
workingSteps: Measure directly between the fixed nodes at the bridge apex and pulley top.
First harmonic has λ = 2L between those fixed nodes.

items.stem: Modern astrophysics combines data from giant ground-based radio dishes and high-altitude optical reflectors.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: Collecting power is proportional to diameter squared, while minimum angular resolution equals wavelength divided by diameter. Radio wavelengths are orders of magnitude longer than visible wavelengths. Therefore, radio dishes are huge wire-mesh structures ($\lambda/20$ surface tolerance) yet still have poorer single-dish resolution than mountain-top optical reflectors. Both use ground atmospheric windows but have different siting needs.

markScheme.criterion: States that both telescopes use parabolic reflectors with collecting power proportional to $D^2$.
Applies $\theta \approx \lambda / D$ to explain why radio telescopes have much poorer angular resolution than optical telescopes despite far larger diameters.
Explains why radio dishes can use lightweight wire mesh (mesh spacing smaller than $\lambda / 20$) whereas optical mirrors need sub-wavelength smooth glass.
Identifies that both bands pass through Earth's atmospheric windows allowing ground-based operation.
Explains optical siting requirements: high, dry, dark sites to minimise cloud cover, atmospheric turbulence, and light pollution.
Explains radio siting advantages and constraints: operates in daylight/clouds at sea level, but must avoid terrestrial radio interference.

parts.prompt: Compare the structure, siting, collecting power, and resolving power of a single-dish radio telescope and a ground-based optical reflecting telescope.
parts.expectedAnswer: Both telescopes use parabolic reflectors where collecting power is proportional to diameter squared and minimum angular resolution equals wavelength divided by diameter. Radio wavelengths (centimetres to metres) are roughly $10^5$ to $10^6$ times longer than visible wavelengths. A radio dish therefore needs a much larger diameter, yet even a huge single dish has poorer angular resolution than a modest optical mirror. Radio dishes can use lightweight wire mesh because surface precision only needs to be better than about $\lambda / 20$. Optical mirrors require glass polished smoothly to fractions of a micrometre. Both bands pass through atmospheric windows. Optical reflectors need high, dry, dark mountains away from clouds, turbulence, and light pollution. Radio telescopes work day and night in cloudy weather at lower altitudes, sited away from human radio interference.
workingSteps: State both rely on parabolic reflecting surfaces with collecting power proportional to diameter squared.
Compare minimum resolvable angle $\theta \approx \lambda / D$ across radio vs visible wavelengths.
Explain why radio dishes can use open wire mesh ($\sim \lambda / 20$ tolerance) vs precision-polished optical mirrors.
Explain atmospheric windows allowing ground operation for both bands.
Contrast siting constraints: high dry dark mountains for optical vs radio-quiet valleys for radio (24-hour, cloud-penetrating).
Note linking multiple radio dishes in a wide array overcomes single-dish resolution limits.

items.stem: The figure shows wavefronts around an ambulance siren sounding at 680 Hz as it approaches a stationary listener at 56 m s⁻¹. Sound moves at 343 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Rest wavelength: λ₀ = v / f = 0.504 m. (b) Shifted spacing near listener: λ′ = (v − v_s) / f = 0.422 m. (c) Heard pitch: f′ = v / λ′ = 813 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f′ = v / λ′ or exact moving-source Doppler formula.

items.stem: During a Young's slits test, a student directs 589 nm light onto two narrow parallel slits S₁ and S₂ separated by 0.24 mm. With the screen 1.5 m away, calculate the fringe width.
items.workedSolution: Write lengths in metres (λ = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ m); then separation = λD / (slit separation) = (5.89 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.5) / 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.68 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) to obtain 3.68 × 10⁻³ m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit separation and divides by screen distance (λd / D) instead of λD / d.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the distance from the central bright fringe to the first dark minimum (½ λD / d) instead of bright fringe spacing.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2, confusing double-slit fringe spacing with single-slit central maximum width.

items.stem: Global communications use both guided media (copper cables and optical fibres) and unguided radio paths. The radio paths include ground waves, sky waves, and space waves.
items.workedSolution: Optical fibres give lower attenuation, higher bandwidth, and immunity to electromagnetic interference compared with copper cables. Ground waves (LF/MF) diffract along Earth's surface, while sky waves (HF) refract from the ionosphere for long-range links. Space waves (VHF/UHF/microwave) pass through the ionosphere for high-bandwidth line-of-sight and satellite links.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that optical fibres have lower attenuation per kilometre than copper, allowing greater spacing between signal boosters.
Explains that optical fibres offer vastly higher bandwidth and immunity to electromagnetic interference / crosstalk (plus notes a trade-off such as specialist splicing).
Describes ground-wave propagation (LF/MF) diffracting around Earth's surface curvature for regional range.
Describes sky-wave propagation (HF, 3–30 MHz) refracting from the ionosphere for long-distance links (noting ionospheric variability).
Describes space-wave propagation (VHF/UHF/microwave, >30 MHz) penetrating the ionosphere for line-of-sight terrestrial or satellite links.
Connects higher carrier frequencies explicitly to greater available bandwidth for high-data-rate communications.

parts.prompt: Compare optical fibre with copper cabling as a high-capacity guided transmission medium. Explain how carrier frequency determines whether unguided radio waves travel mainly as ground waves, sky waves, or space waves.
parts.expectedAnswer: Optical fibres carry infrared pulses by total internal reflection with lower attenuation per kilometre than copper cables, allowing wider spacing between signal boosters. They also provide much higher bandwidth, negligible crosstalk, immunity to electromagnetic interference, and stronger security against tapping. However, splicing fibres requires careful alignment, and fibres cannot carry DC power. In unguided radio links, LF and MF ground waves (below a few MHz) diffract around Earth's curvature for regional coverage. HF sky waves (roughly 3–30 MHz) refract and reflect from ionised layers in the ionosphere for intercontinental links, though they suffer fading. VHF, UHF, and microwave space waves (above 30 MHz) pass straight through the ionosphere, requiring line-of-sight masts or satellite relays while giving huge bandwidth for television, mobile networks, and satellite data.
workingSteps: L1: Contrast copper cables with optical fibres on attenuation (booster spacing) and bandwidth capacity.
L1: Note optical fibre immunity to electromagnetic interference / crosstalk and security vs splicing/power trade-off.
L2: Explain ground waves (LF/MF, below ~3 MHz): diffract around hills and Earth's curvature, modest bandwidth.
L2: Explain sky waves (HF, ~3–30 MHz): refract from the ionosphere for long-range global links, affected by solar/diurnal fading.
L3: Explain space waves (VHF/UHF/microwave, >30 MHz): penetrate the ionosphere, travel line-of-sight to tall masts or satellites.
L3: Link higher carrier frequencies directly to higher available channel bandwidth for high-bit-rate data.

items.stem: Almost all airborne sound energy would be reflected if waves hit the fluid-filled cochlea directly without the middle ear. Why does this happen, and how do the ossicles and oval window overcome it?
items.workedSolution: Air and cochlear fluid have a large acoustic impedance mismatch. The ossicles lever increases force, and the smaller oval window amplifies pressure into the cochlear fluid.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that ossicles lever increases force and smaller oval window amplifies pressure into cochlea fluid.

options.label: A
options.text: The ossicles reduce force while spreading vibration over a wider oval window to slow the sound wave down.
options.distractorRationale: The ossicles increase force and concentrate it onto a much smaller oval window area.

options.label: B
options.text: Because air and fluid have mismatched acoustic impedances, the ossicles lever increases force and smaller oval window amplifies pressure into cochlea fluid to drive fluid vibrations efficiently.

options.label: C
options.text: The ossicles convert longitudinal air waves directly into transverse electrical pulses before the oval window.
options.distractorRationale: Transduction to nerve impulses happens inside the cochlea hair cells, not in the bony ossicles.

options.label: D
options.text: The ossicles act as a low-pass filter blocking all frequencies above 1 kHz from entering the cochlea.
options.distractorRationale: Human hearing peaks in sensitivity around 3 kHz and extends up to ~20 kHz.

items.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity 36 W m⁻² passes first through an ideal vertical polarizer P₁. It then strikes an ideal analyzer A whose transmission axis is rotated by θ = 65° relative to P₁. Using I = I₁ cos²θ for plane-polarized light of intensity I₁, calculate the emerging intensity.
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 18.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(65°) = ½(36) cos²(65°) = 3.21 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(65°) = 3.21 W m⁻² (A).

The string is under a tension of 110.3 N and resonates in harmonic n = 4. Transverse waves travel along a string of tension T and mass per unit length μ at speed v = √(T / μ).

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T and μ into v = √(T / μ).
Divides wave speed from (a) by wavelength from (b).

Determine the wavelength of the n = 4 harmonic mode.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this standing wave.

items.stem: Why can light waves and microwaves be plane-polarised whereas sound waves in air cannot?
items.workedSolution: Longitudinal sound waves cannot be polarised because oscillations are parallel to energy transfer. Therefore option C is correct: longitudinal sound waves cannot be polarised because oscillations are parallel to energy transfer.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: longitudinal sound waves cannot be polarised because oscillations are parallel to energy transfer.

options.distractorRationale: Progressive sound waves transfer energy through compressions and rarefactions.

options.label: C
options.text: Polarisation applies only to transverse waves because longitudinal sound waves cannot be polarised because oscillations are parallel to energy transfer

options.label: D
options.text: Polarisation applies only to transverse waves because sound waves already travel in a single plane
options.distractorRationale: Longitudinal oscillations lie along a single line parallel to propagation, so no transverse plane can be selected.

items.stem: Hospital vascular clinics use handheld Doppler ultrasound probes to check for narrowing (stenosis) in leg and neck arteries.
items.workedSolution: Piezoelectric ultrasound coupled through gel experiences a double Doppler shift proportional to the blood velocity component along the beam. Acoustic coupling gel matches tissue acoustic impedance to prevent air reflection at the skin. The piezoelectric crystal transmits MHz pulses and detects reflected echoes from moving red blood cells. Moving cells both receive and re-emit the wave, which produces the factor of 2. Only the velocity component v cos θ along the beam contributes to Δf. Flow speed is obtained non-invasively in real time with zero ionising radiation.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Identifies piezoelectric probe generating and detecting MHz ultrasound waves.
L1: States that acoustic coupling gel removes air pockets and matches acoustic impedance at the skin.
L2: Explains the factor of 2 arises from a double Doppler shift (cells act as moving receivers then moving reflectors).
L2: Explains cos θ selects the blood velocity component parallel to the ultrasound beam (zero shift at 90°).
L3: Links higher received frequency to flow towards probe (lower for away) and rearrangement v = cΔf/(2f cos θ).
L3: Identifies non-invasive real-time measurement with zero ionising radiation hazard.

parts.prompt: Explain how a Doppler ultrasound probe measures blood flow speed in an artery. Include the role of the piezoelectric probe and coupling gel. Also explain why the factor of 2 and cos θ appear in Δf/f = (2v cos θ)/c, and state two clinical advantages over invasive methods. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Piezoelectric ultrasound coupled through gel experiences a double Doppler shift proportional to the blood velocity component along the beam. Acoustic coupling gel matches tissue acoustic impedance to prevent air reflection at the skin. The piezoelectric crystal transmits MHz pulses and detects reflected echoes from moving red blood cells. Moving cells both receive and re-emit the wave, which produces the factor of 2. Only the velocity component v cos θ along the beam contributes to Δf. Flow speed is obtained non-invasively in real time with zero ionising radiation.
workingSteps: Describe piezoelectric generation/reception of MHz ultrasound and impedance-matching coupling gel.
Derive/explain the double Doppler shift (factor of 2) and beam-angle projection (cos θ).
State clinical benefits: non-invasive, real-time, portable, no ionising radiation.

items.stem: Medical ultrasound probes use a single piezoelectric crystal both to generate high-frequency acoustic pulses and to detect faint returning echoes from tissue boundaries.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: An alternating potential difference makes the piezoelectric crystal vibrate at resonance to emit ultrasound pulses. Returning echoes deform the crystal to produce measurable voltage spikes. Covers $\lambda/2$ resonance thickness, damping backing for short pulses, gel impedance matching, and attenuation of deeper echoes.

markScheme.criterion: Explains alternating pd causes the piezoelectric crystal to vibrate and emit an ultrasound pulse.
Notes crystal thickness equals $\lambda / 2$ for resonance to maximise vibration amplitude.
Explains the damping backing block stops crystal ringing quickly, producing short pulses for improved axial resolution.
Explains coupling gel displaces air and matches acoustic impedance of skin to allow transmission.
Explains detection: returning echoes deform the crystal, generating a measurable potential difference across its faces.
Explains why deeper echoes are weaker (tissue attenuation, beam spreading, partial reflections) requiring gain compensation.

parts.prompt: Explain how a piezoelectric probe transmits and detects ultrasound pulses. Include the roles of resonant crystal thickness, the damping backing material, and coupling gel. Also explain why echoes from deeper boundaries have smaller amplitudes.
parts.expectedAnswer: An alternating potential difference across the piezoelectric crystal causes resonant vibrations that transmit ultrasound pulses. The crystal thickness equals $\lambda / 2$ so its natural frequency matches the drive frequency. A heavily absorbing backing block damps crystal vibrations as soon as the drive pulse stops. This gives a very short pulse length so echoes from closely spaced boundaries do not overlap, improving axial resolution. Coupling gel between the probe face and skin removes air and matches soft-tissue acoustic impedance, preventing nearly total reflection at the skin. Between pulses, returning echoes stress the crystal and generate small alternating voltages via the inverse piezoelectric effect, with depth found from $2d = c\Delta t$. Echoes from deeper boundaries are weaker due to absorption in tissue, beam spreading, and earlier partial reflections, so time-gain compensation is applied.
workingSteps: Describe transmission: alternating pd across piezoelectric crystal causes resonant vibration (thickness $\lambda / 2$).
Explain damping backing material shortening pulse length for good axial resolution.
Explain coupling gel matching acoustic impedance to eliminate air-skin reflection.
Describe reception: returning echoes compress/stretch crystal, inducing alternating voltage spikes.
Link echo arrival time to depth via $2d = c\Delta t$.
Explain smaller echo amplitude from deeper boundaries (attenuation, spreading, earlier reflections) and time-gain amplification.

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 545 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 480 lines mm⁻¹. What is the largest integer order n for which a principal maximum is formed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 480 = 2.08 × 10⁻⁶ m. Since sin θ ≤ 1, n ≤ d / λ = 2.08 × 10⁻⁶ / 5.45 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.82. Taking the floor gives n_max = 3.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 3.82 and takes floor to get n_max = 3 (A).

items.stem: A loudspeaker emits a steady sinusoidal sound wave through air as illustrated by the particle positions and displacement graph. How does a compression differ from a rarefaction?
items.workedSolution: At a compression, particles on each side move inward, bunching molecules at maximum pressure. The opposite happens at a rarefaction, where particles spread furthest apart at minimum pressure. Therefore option C is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: a compression has particles closest together at maximum pressure, and a rarefaction has them furthest apart at minimum pressure.

options.label: A
options.text: At a compression air particles have maximum positive displacement from equilibrium whereas at a rarefaction displacement is maximum negative.
options.distractorRationale: Both compressions and rarefactions occur at zero-displacement points where neighbouring particles converge or diverge.

options.label: B
options.text: A compression is a region of minimum air density and pressure whereas a rarefaction is a region of maximum pressure.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the definitions of compression (high pressure/density) and rarefaction (low pressure/density).

options.label: C
options.text: A compression has particles displaced closest together at maximum pressure whereas a rarefaction has particles spread furthest apart at minimum pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: The distance between a compression and the immediately adjacent rarefaction equals two full wavelengths.
options.distractorRationale: Adjacent compression and rarefaction centres are separated by half a wavelength (λ/2).

items.stem: Cones packed at a patient's fovea have diameter 2.00 μm, and the distance from the eye lens to the retina is 17.0 mm. Resolution requires at least one unstimulated cone between two stimulated cones. What is the smallest separation between two bright dots on a chart 8.50 m away that the eye can resolve?
items.workedSolution: Minimum retinal image separation is $2 d_{\text{cone}} = 4.00\,\mu\text{m}$. By similar triangles, $s = \frac{4.00 \times 10^{-6}}{17.0 \times 10^{-3}} \times 8.50 = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 2.00 mm$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses single cone diameter d_cone instead of twice the cone diameter (forgetting the unstimulated cone between them).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the minimum separation unnecessarily.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Makes a tenfold unit conversion slip between micrometres and millimetres.

items.stem: A green diode laser ($\lambda = 532\text{ nm}$) illuminates a single narrow slit of width $a = 0.15\text{ mm}$ at a distance $2.10\text{ m}$ from a screen.
items.workedSolution: (a) $W = 2\lambda D / a = 14.9 mm$. (b) central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum and widens when slit width decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitute SI values into $W = 2\lambda D / a$.
Central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
Narrowing the slit widens the diffraction pattern (and reduces brightness).

parts.prompt: Calculate the width of the central diffraction maximum (between the two first-order minima) in millimetres using $W \approx 2\lambda D / a$.
Compare the width of the central maximum with a secondary maximum, and state what happens to the pattern if the slit is made narrower.
parts.expectedAnswer: The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum. Narrowing the slit widens the pattern and reduces peak intensity because less light passes through.
workingSteps: State 2:1 width ratio and inverse scaling with slit width a.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 633 nm is incident normally on two narrow parallel slits S₁ and S₂. Each slit has a width of 0.075 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.3 mm. The diffraction-modulated interference pattern is observed on a screen 2.6 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Interference fringe spacing Δy = λD / d = 5.49 × 10⁻³ m. (b) Central envelope full width w_env = 2λD / b = 0.0439 m. (c) First missing order n = d / b = 4.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λD / d with slit separation d.
Uses 2λD / b with individual slit width b.
Equates interference maximum angle to first diffraction minimum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent double-slit interference maxima near the centre of the pattern.
Calculate the full width of the central single-slit diffraction envelope on the screen.
Determine the lowest positive interference order n that is missing due to coincidence with a single-slit diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Equate nλ / d = λ / b => n = d / b.

items.stem: A stationary fire-station siren emits sound of frequency $800\text{ Hz}$ in still air where the speed of sound is $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$. A cyclist rides directly toward the siren and detects an apparent frequency of $840\text{ Hz}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda = \frac{340}{800} = 0.425 m$. (b) From $f' = f\frac{v + u_{\text{o}}}{v}$, $u_{\text{o}} = 340\left(\frac{840}{800} - 1\right) = 17.0 m s⁻¹$. (c) Motion of the observer results in an unchanged wavelength in the medium while the observer encounters wavefronts at a higher rate.

markScheme.criterion: States wavelength in air is unchanged because the source is at rest.
Explains unchanged wavelength in the medium while the observer encounters wavefronts at a higher rate.

Determine the speed $u_{\text{o}}$ of the cyclist.
Explain why the detected frequency rises even though the source is stationary.
parts.expectedAnswer: The wavelength in the medium stays unchanged because the source is at rest. However, the observer meets wavefronts at a higher rate because the relative wave speed becomes $v + u_{\text{o}}$.
workingSteps: State that a stationary source produces evenly spaced circular wavefronts in air.
Explain that the wavelength in the medium is unchanged while the observer encounters wavefronts at a higher rate.

items.stem: Along a 0.84 m taut string clamped at both ends, waves move at 192 m s⁻¹. A standing wave forms in its 4th harmonic.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_4 = 2L / n = 2(0.84) / 4 = 0.420 m. (b) Using wave speed: f_4 = v / λ_4 = 192 / 0.420 = 457 Hz. (c) Lowest mode: f₁ = f_4 / 4 = 114 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of this n = 4 harmonic standing wave.
workingSteps: For a string fixed at both ends, λ_n = 2L / n.

parts.prompt: Determine the oscillation frequency of this standing wave.
Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string when kept at the same tension.

items.stem: Moving directly away from a fixed siren at 72 m s⁻¹, a listener hears sound emitted at 920 Hz. Calculate the detected frequency if the speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: By the Doppler formula, f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 920 × (330 − 72) / 330 = 719 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 719 Hz (A).

items.stem: Bright interference bands from 460 nm light fall 1.4 m beyond a pair of narrow slits spaced 0.28 mm apart. Data are logged at the n = 5 bright fringe.
items.workedSolution: (a) Wave path gap: Δℓ = nλ = 5 × 4.60 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.30 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Off-axis angle: θ_5 = arcsin(nλ / d) = 0.471°. (c) Distance from centre: y_5 = nλD / d = 0.0115 m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the path difference between waves from S₁ and S₂ arriving at the n = 5 bright fringe.
workingSteps: For constructive interference at order n, Δℓ = nλ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deflection θ_5 (in degrees) of the n = 5 bright fringe from the central axis.
Determine the linear distance from the central bright fringe to the n = 5 bright fringe on the screen.

items.stem: The displacement–position graph shows a progressive wave travelling along a long stretched rope at a single instant. The wave has an amplitude of 0.075 m and a wavelength of 0.32 m. The source oscillates at a steady frequency of 15 Hz.
items.workedSolution: (a) Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 15 = 0.0667 s. (b) Wave speed v = fλ = 15 × 0.32 = 4.80 m s⁻¹. (c) Crest-to-trough distance = 2A = 0.150 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = 1 / f with given frequency.
Substitutes into v = fλ or v = λ / T.

parts.prompt: Calculate the time period of oscillation of a point in the medium.
Determine the propagation speed of the progressive wave.
workingSteps: Apply v = fλ (or v = λ / T).

parts.prompt: Determine the total vertical distance moved by a medium particle in travelling from a wave crest to an adjacent trough.
workingSteps: Crest-to-trough vertical span equals twice the wave amplitude, Δy = 2A.

items.stem: Containing air with sound speed 334 m s⁻¹, a resonance tube open at both ends (0.78 m long, treating the open pipe as ideal) vibrates in harmonic n = 4. Calculate its frequency.

options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

items.stem: Using a 500 lines mm⁻¹ grating at right angles, a class finds order n = 2 at θ = 36.1°. Determine the light wavelength.
items.workedSolution: Line spacing: d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. From d sin θ = nλ, λ = d sin(36.1°) / 2 = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Marked at x₁ = 0.3 m and x₂ = 0.72 m are points P and Q on a wave along a slinky spring. The wave has frequency 4 Hz, amplitude 0.045 m, and wavelength 1.2 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Wave equation: v = fλ = 4 × 1.2 = 4.80 m s⁻¹. (b) Time period: T = 1 / 4 = 0.250 s. (c) Separation Δx = 0.420 m, so Δφ = 2π Δx / λ = 2.20 rad.

parts.prompt: Calculate the propagation speed of the wave.
Determine the oscillation period of particle P.

items.stem: Light of wavelength 670 nm passes through a single slit and forms a 22.3 mm central peak on a screen 2.5 m away. Work out the slit width b.

items.stem: In a UHF Hertz radio demonstration ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$), a sliding probe detects six consecutive nodes spanning a total distance of 0.900 m (adjacent spacing 0.180 m). At an antinode the peak dipole signal is 200 mV.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of the UHF radio waves.
workingSteps: Adjacent node spacing is $\lambda/2 = 0.180\text{ m} \Rightarrow \lambda = 0.360 m$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the transmitter frequency in megahertz.
Calculate the detected amplitude when the dipole is rotated $30°$ from alignment.

items.stem: An FM broadcast transmitter carries high-fidelity audio up to $f_{\text{M}} = 15.0\text{ kHz}$ with a maximum carrier frequency deviation of $\Delta f = 60.0\text{ kHz}$. Using the AQA Data Sheet equation $\text{bandwidth} = 2(\Delta f + f_{\text{M}})$, calculate the required FM channel bandwidth.
items.workedSolution: FM bandwidth $= 2(\Delta f + f_{\text{M}}) = 2(60.0 + 15.0) = 150 kHz$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of $2$ outside the bracket.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies only $\Delta f$ by $2$, failing to double $f_{\text{M}}$.

items.stem: In a polarization test, a plane-polarized beam drops from 160 W m⁻² to 40.0 W m⁻² through an ideal analyzer. Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ for plane-polarized light. Work out the acute angle θ.
items.workedSolution: Isolate cosine in I = I₀ cos²θ: cos θ = √(40.0 / 160) = 0.500; thus θ = arccos(0.500) = 60.0°.
