items.stem: Coherent monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda = 620\text{ nm}$ is incident normally on $N = 5$ parallel identical slits separated by $d = 155\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ (each of width $b = 31.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$). The interference pattern is viewed on a screen $D = 2.00\text{ m}$ away.
items.workedSolution: (a) $s = 8.00 mm$. (b) $I_{\max}/I_1 = 25.0$. (c) $N - 2 = 3.00$ secondary maxima. (d) Increasing the number of slits N keeps principal maxima at the same angles while making them narrower. Peak intensity rises proportional to N squared, and N minus two secondary maxima appear.

markScheme.criterion: Applies s = λD/d in SI units.
Notes principal maxima stay at same angles d sin θ = nλ.
Notes principal peaks become sharper/narrower and scale as I ∝ N².
Notes N − 2 faint secondary maxima appear while principal maxima stay at the same angles, narrow, and grow proportional to N squared.

parts.prompt: Using $s = \lambda D / d$, calculate the separation $s$ between adjacent principal maxima near the centre of the screen.
Determine the ratio $I_{\max} / I_1$ of the central maximum intensity to the intensity from one slit alone.
State the number of secondary maxima located between two adjacent principal maxima.
Explain how increasing $N$ from $2$ to $5$ at fixed $d$ and $b$ alters the intensity distribution of the pattern.
parts.expectedAnswer: Increasing the number of slits N keeps principal maxima at unchanged angles while making them narrower. Peak intensity increases proportional to N squared, and N minus two secondary maxima appear between adjacent principal peaks.
workingSteps: Increasing N keeps principal maxima at unchanged angles and makes them narrower. Peak intensity scales as N squared, with N minus two secondary maxima.

items.stem: In odd harmonic n = 5, standing waves form inside a resonance tube closed at one end. Its length is 0.34 m, sound speed 336 m s⁻¹, with zero end effect.
items.workedSolution: (a) Effective length L_eff = 0.340 m gives first harmonic f₁ = v / (4L_eff) = 247 Hz. (b) Wavelength: λ_5 = 4L_eff / 5 = 0.272 m. (c) Mode frequency: f_5 = 5f₁ = 1.24 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies quarter-wave first-harmonic relation f₁ = v / (4L_eff).
Multiplies first-harmonic frequency by odd harmonic index 5 (or uses v / λ).

parts.prompt: Calculate the first-harmonic (n = 1) frequency of this closed-end air column.
workingSteps: For a pipe closed at one end, λ₁ = 4L so f₁ = v / (4L).

parts.prompt: Determine the wavelength of the n = 5 harmonic standing wave.
Calculate the resonant frequency of this n = 5 harmonic mode.

items.stem: A rigid cylindrical acoustic duct of length $L = 1.70\text{ m}$ is closed at both ends and filled with air in which the speed of sound is $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) a pipe closed at both ends forms a displacement node at each closed end and supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n. (b) $f_1 = 100 Hz$. (c) $\lambda_2 = 1.70 m$, $f_2 = 200 Hz$. (d) destructive resonance drives dangerously large oscillation amplitudes when periodic forcing matches structural natural frequency so damping is introduced to dissipate energy.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies displacement nodes at both rigid closed ends.
States λ_n = 2L/n allows all integer harmonics because both closed ends form displacement nodes.
Links matching driving and natural frequencies to large energy accumulation.
Notes excessive oscillation amplitudes cause fatigue or collapse.
Explains that damping dissipates vibrational energy to prevent dangerously large resonance amplitudes when periodic forcing matches the natural frequency.

parts.prompt: State the displacement boundary conditions at the ends of a pipe closed at both ends and explain why all integer harmonics are permitted.
parts.expectedAnswer: A pipe closed at both ends forms a displacement node at each closed end. It supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.
workingSteps: a pipe closed at both ends forms a displacement node at each closed end and supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the first harmonic in this closed–closed pipe.
Determine the wavelength and frequency of the second harmonic.
parts.expectedAnswer: Wavelength λ₂ = 1.70 m; frequency f₂ = 200 Hz.

parts.prompt: Explain how periodic external vibrations can cause destructive resonance in ducts or bridges, and outline how engineers prevent structural failure.
parts.expectedAnswer: In mechanical structures, destructive resonance drives dangerously large oscillation amplitudes when periodic forcing matches structural natural frequency so damping is introduced to dissipate energy.
workingSteps: destructive resonance drives dangerously large oscillation amplitudes when periodic forcing matches structural natural frequency so damping is introduced to dissipate energy.

items.stem: Inspect the middle snapshot at t = T/4 in the superposition diagram. Why is the resultant stationary wave completely flat for an instant?
items.workedSolution: During T/4, each opposite progressive wave shifts by λ/4 in opposite directions, placing crests directly over troughs. At one quarter of a period, the two opposite waves are in antiphase everywhere. Their displacements cancel to give a flat line for an instant, so option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: at one quarter of a period the opposite waves are in antiphase everywhere, cancelling to a flat line.

options.label: A
options.text: At t = T/4 both progressive waves momentarily stop oscillating and lose all their mechanical energy to the supports.
options.distractorRationale: At t = T/4 the antinode particles have maximum transverse speed, storing the wave's full energy as kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.text: From the principle of superposition, at one quarter of a period the two oppositely travelling progressive waves are in antiphase at every position, so their displacements cancel everywhere to give a momentarily flat line.

options.label: C
options.text: At t = T/4 every point along the string becomes a permanent node for the rest of the oscillation.
options.distractorRationale: One quarter-period later (t = T/2) the antinodes reach maximum opposite displacement.

options.label: D
options.text: At t = T/4 the two opposite progressive waves arrive in phase everywhere, doubling the displacement to zero.
options.distractorRationale: In-phase arrival doubles the amplitude (t = 0 and t = T/2); cancellation at t = T/4 occurs because they are in antiphase.

items.stem: A stainless steel wire of length 1.10 m between bridge and pulley has linear density 1.90 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹ under a hanging mass of 0.75 kg ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). Calculate its first harmonic frequency.
items.workedSolution: With $T = mg = 0.75 \times 9.81 = 7.36 N$, wave speed $v = \sqrt{T/\mu} = 62.2 m s⁻¹$, $f_1 = v/(2L) = 28.3 Hz$, gradient $= v/2 = 31.1 m s⁻¹$, and $\%\Delta \mu = 0.9 + 2(0.6) + 2(0.5) = 3.10\%$. Answer: 28.3 Hz.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ = L instead of λ = 2L for the first harmonic.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits g = 9.81 m s⁻² when calculating tension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies an erroneous factor of one half during algebraic rearrangement.

items.stem: Why have charge-coupled devices (CCDs) largely replaced direct visual observation by the unaided human eye at research optical observatories?
items.workedSolution: CCDs convert roughly seventy to eighty percent of incident photons into electron-hole pairs, compared with roughly one percent for the eye. They offer much higher quantum efficiency, a linear response, and wider spectral sensitivity than the human eye.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that much higher quantum efficiency linear response and wider spectral sensitivity than the human eye.

items.stem: A Doppler shift turns an 820 Hz signal from a loudspeaker on a car into 1.11 × 10³ Hz at a fixed listener. As the source moves towards the listener in air (wave speed 340 m s⁻¹), find its speed.
items.workedSolution: From f' = fv / (v − v_s), isolate the denominator: v − v_s = vf / f' = (340 × 820) / 1.11 × 10³, giving v_s = 88.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: During a class optics test, a student shines 405 nm monochromatic light onto a pair of narrow slits spaced 0.16 mm apart. The screen sits 1.8 m behind.
items.workedSolution: (a) Young's spacing = λD / d = (4.05 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.8) / 1.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.56 × 10⁻³ m. (b) Half-spacing to first dark band = ½ × 4.56 × 10⁻³ = 2.28 × 10⁻³ m. (c) For n = 3: nλ = 3 × 4.05 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.22 × 10⁻⁶ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units and substitutes into λD / (slit separation).
Takes half of the bright-fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
Determine the distance on the screen from the central bright maximum to the centre of the first dark fringe.
workingSteps: First destructive minimum occurs halfway between the central and first-order bright maxima: y_dark,1 = 0.5 × fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the geometric path difference between waves arriving from the two slits at the order n = 3 bright fringe.
workingSteps: Constructive interference at order n requires path difference Δℓ = nλ.

items.stem: What occurs if an analogue audio signal containing frequencies up to $f_{\max}$ is sampled by an ADC at a sampling frequency lower than $2 f_{\max}$?
items.workedSolution: Nyquist's theorem requires $f_{\mathrm{s}} \ge 2 f_{\max}$; sampling below twice the maximum signal frequency produces false lower-frequency aliasing distortion.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that sampling below twice the maximum signal frequency produces false lower-frequency aliasing distortion.

options.label: A
options.text: Quantisation resolution improves automatically because fewer samples require more bits.
options.distractorRationale: Resolution $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n$ is set by bit depth $n$, not sampling rate.

options.label: B
options.text: Sampling below twice the maximum signal frequency produces false lower-frequency aliasing distortion.

options.label: C
options.text: Signal amplitude saturates at the supply rails while frequency remains exact.
options.distractorRationale: Undersampling causes frequency-domain aliasing, not amplitude clipping.

options.label: D
options.text: All frequency components above half the sampling rate are cleanly boosted in fidelity.
options.distractorRationale: Undersampled high frequencies fold down into false lower frequencies.

items.stem: A mammal's middle ear has an eardrum area of $72.0\text{ mm}^2$, an oval window area of $3.60\text{ mm}^2$, and an ossicles lever force gain of $1.50$. By what factor is acoustic pressure amplified between the eardrum and the oval window?
items.workedSolution: Pressure amplification $= 1.50 \times \frac{72.0}{3.60} = 1.50 \times 20.0 = 30.0$.

items.stem: The diagram shows unpolarized light of intensity 192 W m⁻² incident on two ideal polarizing filters. The beam passes first through polarizer P₁ and then through analyzer A tilted at θ = 70° to P₁. For plane-polarized light, transmitted intensity obeys I = I₁ cos²θ.
items.workedSolution: (a) After P₁, I₁ = ½ I₀ = 96.0 W m⁻². (b) After analyzer A, I = I₁ cos²(70°) = 11.2 W m⁻². (c) Overall fraction I / I₀ = ½ cos²(70°) = 0.0585.

markScheme.criterion: Halves unpolarized incident intensity at ideal polarizer P₁.
Applies I = I₁ cos²θ to the polarized beam.
Divides final transmitted intensity by incident unpolarized intensity I₀.

parts.prompt: State and calculate the intensity I₁ of the plane-polarized beam between polarizer P₁ and analyzer A.
workingSteps: Averaging cos²φ = ½ over all random polarization orientations reduces unpolarized intensity by half: I₁ = ½ I₀.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity I emerging from analyzer A.
workingSteps: Apply Malus's law I = I₁ cos²θ.

parts.prompt: Determine the overall fraction I / I₀ of the original unpolarized intensity transmitted by the two-filter combination.
workingSteps: Overall transmission fraction = I / I₀ = ½ cos²θ.

items.stem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.9 m and mass per unit length 0.0032 kg m⁻¹. Its n = 1 harmonic resonates at 102.8 Hz. The transverse wave speed on a taut string is v = √(T / μ). Calculate the tension T in the string.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.9) / 1 = 1.80 m, so required wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 185 m s⁻¹. Rearranging v = √(T / μ) gives T = μv² = 0.0032 × (185)² = 110 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 2Lf_n / n and computes T = μv² = 110 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to square the wave speed when rearranging v = √(T / μ) to T = μv².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, halving v and underestimating T = μv² by a factor of 4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides v² by linear mass density μ instead of multiplying T = μv².

items.stem: A student investigates unpolarised light using two Polaroid filters and then wears Polaroid sunglasses while observing fish beneath a sunlit pond.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Plane-polarised transverse waves restrict oscillations to a single plane, whereas longitudinal waves cannot be polarised. Rotating an analyser from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ cuts intensity from maximum to zero. Vertically aligned Polaroid sunglasses absorb horizontally polarised glare reflected from water.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): States unpolarised transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer in many planes (reject 'wave motion').
L1 (Area 1): Defines plane-polarised wave as having oscillations restricted to a single plane containing the direction of propagation.
L2 (Area 2): Explains longitudinal waves cannot be polarised because their oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
L2 (Area 2): Explains rotating a second Polaroid (analyser) through 90° from parallel to perpendicular reduces transmitted intensity from maximum to zero.
L3 (Area 3): States light reflected off horizontal water is partially horizontally polarised.
L3 (Area 3): Explains vertically aligned Polaroid sunglasses absorb horizontal glare while transmitting the vertical component of unpolarised light from underwater objects.

parts.prompt: Explain what is meant by a plane-polarised wave and why polarisation proves light is transverse rather than longitudinal. Explain how rotating an analyser changes transmitted intensity, and how Polaroid sunglasses reduce water glare.
parts.expectedAnswer: An unpolarised transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer in many planes. A plane-polarised transverse wave restricts oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised because their oscillations are parallel to energy transfer. A first polariser limits light to its transmission axis; rotating a second Polaroid (analyser) by $90^\circ$ cuts transmitted intensity smoothly from maximum to zero. Sunlight reflected from horizontal water is partially horizontally polarised. Vertically aligned Polaroid sunglasses absorb this horizontal glare while transmitting the vertical component of unpolarised light from beneath the water.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Define unpolarised vs plane-polarised transverse waves (oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer in one plane).
Area 2 (L2): Explain why longitudinal waves cannot be polarised and how rotating an analyser by 90° cuts intensity from max to zero.
Area 3 (L3): Apply to water glare: horizontal reflection polarisation absorbed by vertical Polaroid axis while unpolarised underwater light passes.

items.stem: Inside an ultrasound probe, an epoxy-tungsten backing block is bonded directly behind the piezoelectric crystal. What is its primary physical function?
items.workedSolution: A heavily damped backing block stops crystal vibrations quickly to produce short pulses. This improves axial resolution so echoes from closely spaced boundaries do not overlap.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that damps crystal vibrations rapidly to produce short pulses improving axial resolution.

options.label: A
options.text: It amplifies the voltage of the AC drive signal to increase crystal ringing duration.
options.distractorRationale: Long ringing degrades axial resolution and prevents receiving echoes from shallow boundaries.

options.label: B
options.text: It reflects backward-travelling ultrasound waves to create continuous standing waves in tissue.
options.distractorRationale: Pulse-echo imaging requires ultra-short damped pulses, not continuous waves.

options.label: C
options.text: The backing block damps crystal vibrations rapidly to produce short pulses improving axial resolution.

options.label: D
options.text: It shields the patient from ionising gamma photons emitted by the crystal.
options.distractorRationale: Ultrasound probes emit non-ionising mechanical vibrations, never gamma radiation.

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 590 nm strikes a diffraction grating ruled with 600 lines mm⁻¹ at normal incidence. Principal maxima beginning at n = 1 are measured across the forward semicircle (−90° < θ < +90°).
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m, so θ₁ = arcsin(λ / d) = 20.7°. (b) d / λ = 2.82, giving n_max = 2. (c) Total principal maxima = 2(2) + 1 = 5.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and applies sin θ₁ = λ / d.
Evaluates d / λ = 2.82 and rounds down.

items.stem: A signal generator drives a loudspeaker at $425\text{ Hz}$, sending a longitudinal sound wave through air at $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda = 0.800\text{ m}$. (b) $d = \lambda/2 = 0.400\text{ m}$. (c) In a compression, air particles are closest together at maximum pressure. In a rarefaction, particles are furthest apart at minimum pressure.

markScheme.criterion: Describes compression as closer particle spacing / maximum pressure.
Describes rarefaction as wider particle spacing / minimum pressure.
Links particle oscillation parallel to wave travel: particles crowd together at maximum pressure in a compression and spread apart at minimum pressure in a rarefaction.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of the sound wave in air.
Determine the distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of the adjacent rarefaction.
Distinguish between a compression and a rarefaction in terms of air particle spacing and local pressure.
parts.expectedAnswer: In a longitudinal sound wave, a compression has particles closest together at maximum pressure. A rarefaction has particles spread furthest apart at minimum pressure.
workingSteps: A compression has particles closest together at maximum pressure, while a rarefaction has particles furthest apart at minimum pressure.

items.stem: An eye test chart sits 5.10 m from a patient whose foveal cones have diameter 3.00 μm at an eye-lens-to-retina distance of 17.0 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\theta = 3.53 × 10⁻⁴ rad$. (b) $s = 1.80 mm$. (c) cones at the fovea have individual nerve connections for sharp colour vision in bright light whereas rods share connections for dim light sensitivity.

markScheme.criterion: Explains rods share optic nerve pathways (summing weak signals in dim light).
Contrasts with 1-to-1 foveal cones needed for high acuity and colour vision.

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum angular resolution in radians limited by foveal cone spacing.
Hence calculate the smallest separation between two lines on the chart 5.10 m away.
Explain why peripheral vision is far more sensitive in dim starlight yet cannot read fine chart lettering.
parts.expectedAnswer: Cones at the fovea have individual nerve connections for sharp colour vision in bright light. Rods share nerve connections, giving higher dim-light sensitivity but lower detail.
workingSteps: Peripheral rods pool signals from several rods onto one nerve fibre, raising dim-light sensitivity.
Shared nerve connections prevent the brain from localising individual photons, reducing spatial acuity.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength $620\text{ nm}$ strikes a diffraction grating with $450\text{ lines mm}^{-1}$ at normal incidence. What is the highest order $n_{\max}$ of diffraction maximum observable?
items.workedSolution: $d = 10^{-3}/450 = 2.222 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$; $d/\lambda = 2.222 \times 10^{-6} / 620 \times 10^{-9} = 3.58$, so highest integer order $n_{\max} = 3$. Option D (3.00) matches.

items.stem: How do the colours appear in the first-order fringes on either side of the central white maximum in a white-light Young's double-slit experiment?
items.workedSolution: From w = λD/s, shorter-wavelength violet has the smallest fringe spacing (inner edge) and longer-wavelength red has the widest (outer edge). Outer fringes form continuous spectra with violet closest to the centre and red furthest out. Therefore option A is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: outer fringes form continuous spectra with violet closest to the centre and red furthest out because w = lambda D / s increases with wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: Away from the centre, outer fringes form continuous spectra with violet closest to the centre and red furthest out because fringe spacing w = lambda D / s increases with wavelength.

options.label: B
options.text: Outer fringes show red on the inner edge and violet on the outer edge because violet has a higher frequency and bends more.
options.distractorRationale: Diffraction/interference angle increases with *wavelength* (w = λD/s), not frequency, so red lies further from the centre.

options.label: C
options.text: Every outer fringe remains pure white because all colours share the same speed in air.
options.distractorRationale: Equal speed in air does not make wavelengths equal; longer wavelengths have larger fringe spacing w.

options.label: D
options.text: Only violet and red lines appear with complete darkness between them because intermediate colours cancel out.
options.distractorRationale: White light contains a continuous visible spectrum, producing a continuous rainbow across each outer fringe before higher orders overlap.

items.stem: Coherent light of wavelength 450 nm strikes two narrow parallel slits of separation 0.45 mm. The interference pattern is viewed on a screen 1.4 m away. If the first minimum of the single-slit diffraction envelope suppresses the n = 6 interference maximum, calculate the width b of each slit.
items.workedSolution: The first single-slit minimum occurs at θ = λ / b while the n-th double-slit maximum is at θ = nλ / d. Coincidence at n = 6 gives b = d / 6 = 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ / 6 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁵ m.

markScheme.criterion: Equates λ / b = nλ / d to obtain b = d / 6 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁵ m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides slit separation by (n + 1) instead of missing order n = d / b.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the highest visible order inside the central envelope (n − 1) instead of the missing order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2 from the full angular width of the central envelope.

items.stem: A star approaches an observer on Earth with a radial speed of $460\text{ km s}^{-1}$. A spectral absorption line has a laboratory wavelength of $486.0\text{ nm}$. What is the magnitude of the wavelength shift $\Delta\lambda$ observed?
items.workedSolution: Convert $v = 4.60 \times 10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Then $\Delta\lambda \approx \lambda\frac{v}{c} = 486.0 \times \frac{4.60 \times 10^5}{3.00 \times 10^8} = 0.745 nm$.

items.stem: Between rigid ends 0.72 m apart, a stretched string holds harmonic mode n = 3 (speed 126 m s⁻¹). Find adjacent node separation.
items.workedSolution: Mode n = 3 fits n loops along L = 0.72 m (L), so node spacing is d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n = 0.72 / 3 = 0.240 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n to obtain 0.240 m (C).

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates a full wavelength λ = 2L / n instead of the half-wavelength node-to-node spacing λ / 2.

items.stem: Because a listener travelling in a car moves directly away from a stationary alarm emitting 400 Hz, the detected pitch shifts to 309 Hz. Take sound speed as 343 m s⁻¹ and find the observer speed.
items.workedSolution: With a fixed emitter, f′ = f(v − v_o) / v, so v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 343 × |309 / 400 − 1| = 78.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 78.0 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A progressive wave travels across a ripple tank at a speed of 26.25 m s⁻¹. From its displacement–position graph, the amplitude is 0.048 m and the wavelength is 0.75 m. Determine the frequency of oscillation.
items.workedSolution: Using f = v / λ with wave speed v = 26.25 m s⁻¹ and wavelength λ = 0.75 m gives f = 26.25 / 0.75 = 35.0 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges v = fλ to obtain f = v / λ = 35.0 Hz (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the oscillation period T = λ / v instead of the frequency f = v / λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Mistakes two full cycles for one wavelength, halving the calculated frequency.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength (vλ) instead of dividing v by λ.

items.stem: At 1237 Hz, a cylindrical pipe open at both ends enters its n = 4 harmonic (treating the open pipe as ideal). Given sound speed 334 m s⁻¹, calculate the length of the pipe.
items.workedSolution: Open-open resonance yields L = nv / (2f_n) = (4 × 334) / (2 × 1.24 × 10³) = 0.540 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = nv / (2f_n) to obtain 0.540 m (C).

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies the closed-one-end pipe relation L = nv / (4f_n) instead of open-both-ends L = nv / (2f_n).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in L = nλ / 2.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises large-angle geometry y = D tan θ rather than small-angle D sin θ.

items.stem: With frequency 8 Hz, amplitude 0.014 m, and wavelength 0.8 m, a wave runs along a stretched string. A plot marks t₁ = 0.025 s (P) and t₂ = 0.0625 s (Q). Determine the phase difference in radians.
items.workedSolution: Gap Δt = 0.0625 s − 0.025 s = 0.0375 s over cycle span 1 / f = 0.125 s equals 0.300 cycles. Therefore Δφ = 2π × 0.300 = 1.88 rad.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 2π rad to get 1.88 rad (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (π rad) instead of a full cycle (2π rad) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in degrees instead of radians.

items.stem: During a physics lesson, 650 nm monochromatic light crosses a 0.12 mm single slit to form a diffraction pattern 3 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) First dark fringe: θ = λ / b = 5.42 × 10⁻³ rad. (b) Offset from centre: y₁ = θD = 0.0163 m. (c) Central span: w = 2y₁ = 0.0325 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies θ = λ / b in SI units.
Multiplies θ by screen distance D.
Doubles half-width to span both sides of the central peak.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular position θ (in radians) of the first diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Use the small-angle single-slit first-minimum relation θ = λ / b.

parts.prompt: Determine the linear distance on the screen from the centre of the pattern to the first dark minimum.
Calculate the full linear width of the central bright maximum on the screen.
workingSteps: The central maximum spans from −y₁ to +y₁: w = 2y₁.

items.stem: In Fizeau's toothed-wheel measurement of the speed of light ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$), a wheel with 720 teeth reflects a light pulse off a mirror 8630 m away. Using $c = 4 n f d$, calculate the lowest wheel rotation frequency $f$ at which the returning beam is first blocked by the next tooth.
items.workedSolution: During the round trip $2d / c$, the wheel turns by half a tooth-gap spacing ($\frac{1}{2n}$ revolution), so $c = 4nfd \Rightarrow f = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8}{4 \times 720 \times 8630} = 12.1 Hz$.

items.stem: Two modulated radio signals are displayed on voltage–time ($V$–$t$) graphs. How do you distinguish an AM waveform from an FM waveform visually?
items.workedSolution: Comparing $V$–$t$ traces directly shows that AM varies carrier amplitude while FM varies carrier frequency at the information frequency.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that AM varies carrier amplitude while FM varies carrier frequency at the information frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: On a $V$–$t$ trace, AM varies carrier amplitude while FM varies carrier frequency at the information frequency while keeping peak-to-peak amplitude constant.

options.label: B
options.text: AM maintains constant amplitude with bunching crests, whereas FM varies the outer envelope height.
options.distractorRationale: That reverses AM and FM completely.

options.label: C
options.text: AM consists exclusively of digital binary pulses whereas FM uses continuous sine waves.
options.distractorRationale: Both standard AM and FM modulate continuous sinusoidal carriers.

options.label: D
options.text: AM has zero carrier cycles inside the envelope while FM has constant wavelength throughout.
options.distractorRationale: AM has uniform carrier frequency inside a varying envelope, while FM compresses and stretches carrier cycles.

items.stem: Light that is vertically plane-polarized (32 W m⁻²) hits an ideal analyzer at right angles. Its pass axis lies at θ = 25° from the vertical. Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ for plane-polarized light.
items.workedSolution: (a) E / E₀ = cos(25°) = 0.906. (b) Squaring scales intensity: I = I₀ cos²(25°) = 26.3 W m⁻². (c) Absorbed intensity = 32 − 26.3 = 5.72 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Projects electric-field vector via E / E₀ = cos θ.
Subtracts transmitted intensity from incident intensity.

items.stem: Water waves of fixed wavelength travel towards a harbour barrier containing an opening of adjustable width $b$. Under what condition is diffraction spreading beyond the gap most pronounced?
items.workedSolution: Significant angular spreading occurs whenever the aperture or obstacle size is close to (or smaller than) the wavelength λ. Therefore option C is correct: diffraction spreading is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: diffraction spreading is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: Diffraction spreading is greatest when the aperture width is hundreds of times larger than the wavelength.
options.distractorRationale: When b ≫ λ waves pass almost straight through with minimal spreading at the edges.

options.label: B
options.text: Diffraction occurs only when the wave speed changes across the aperture and is independent of wavelength.
options.distractorRationale: Wave speed does not change across an open aperture; diffraction depends critically on the ratio λ/b.

options.label: C
options.text: Diffraction spreading through an aperture or around an obstacle is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle width is comparable to the wavelength.

options.label: D
options.text: Diffraction vanishes completely around solid obstacles and occurs exclusively through narrow slits.
options.distractorRationale: Waves diffract both through apertures and around obstacles whose dimensions are comparable to λ.

items.stem: Excited at 1518 Hz, a cylindrical pipe closed at one end of length 0.28 m enters odd harmonic n = 5, assuming ideal end conditions. Calculate the speed of sound.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength for n = 5 gives λ_n = 4L / n = 4(0.28) / 5 = 0.224 m. Wave speed: v = f_n λ_n = 340 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = 4Lf_n / n to obtain 340 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses open-pipe wavelength 2L / n instead of closed-pipe 4L / n, halving the speed of sound.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes an even harmonic index (n − 1) instead of the odd harmonic n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th harmonic frequency as the first-harmonic mode v = 4Lf.

items.stem: A cylindrical pipe of length $0.680\text{ m}$ is closed at one end and open at the other (speed of sound $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$, neglecting end effects). What is the next resonant frequency immediately above the first harmonic?
items.workedSolution: First harmonic $f_1 = \frac{v}{4L} = \frac{340}{4(0.680)} = 125 Hz$. Because only odd harmonics form in a closed–open pipe, the next allowed mode is the third harmonic: $f_3 = 3f_1 = 375 Hz$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the second harmonic (2f₁) is allowed in a closed–open pipe; only odd harmonics exist.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first harmonic frequency f₁ rather than the next allowed harmonic (third harmonic 3f₁).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Skips ahead to the fifth harmonic instead of the third harmonic.

items.stem: Two identical progressive waves, each of amplitude 3.4 cm, travel in opposite directions along a string and superpose to form the stationary wave shown. What is the maximum amplitude of oscillation at an antinode?
items.workedSolution: At an antinode, both waves arrive in phase at t = 0 and t = T/2, giving A_antinode = 2 × 3.4 = 6.80 cm.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes antinode amplitude equals a single progressive wave amplitude.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Confuses amplitude with peak-to-peak excursion (4A_p).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a √2 factor instead of direct constructive superposition 2A_p.

items.stem: Which practical procedure reduces friction bias in tension and ensures sharp node identification during Required Practical 1?
items.workedSolution: Use a low-friction pulley and wear safety goggles in case the taut wire snaps. Measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes, where first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a low-friction pulley with safety goggles for snap hazards, and measures length between the bridge and pulley nodes.

options.label: A
options.text: Clamp the pulley wheel fixed so the string cannot slip, eliminating tension uncertainty.
options.distractorRationale: A seized pulley introduces friction so tension in the horizontal section no longer equals mg.

options.label: B
options.text: Set the oscillator to maximum power so the string vibrates with very large amplitude.
options.distractorRationale: Excessive amplitude stretches the string nonlinearly and alters tension during each cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a low-friction pulley with safety goggles for taut wire snap hazards, and measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the wooden bridge with a soft foam pad so energy is absorbed at the node.
options.distractorRationale: A rigid sharp bridge edge creates a well-defined node with minimal damping.

items.stem: A 0.40 m visual telescope is viewed by a human eye with quantum efficiency 1.0%. It is compared with a 2.00 m observatory telescope fitted with a cooled CCD camera of quantum efficiency 80%.
items.workedSolution: (a) Collecting power ratio $= (2.00/0.40)^2 = 25.0$. (b) QE ratio $= 80.0$. (c) Beyond QE, much higher quantum efficiency linear response and wider spectral sensitivity than the human eye.

markScheme.criterion: States wider spectral sensitivity (e.g. near-IR / UV).
States linear response or digital storage / long-exposure image stacking.

items.stem: Wavefronts spread at 332 m s⁻¹ from a loudspeaker on a car set to 820 Hz. The source travels directly away from a fixed microphone at 56 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Unshifted value: λ₀ = v / f = 0.405 m. (b) Motion changes wavelength to λ′ = (v + v_s) / f = 0.473 m. (c) Wave equation gives f′ = v / λ′ = 702 Hz.

items.stem: Separated by 0.6 mm, two narrow parallel slits are lit by coherent 650 nm light. Calculate the spacing between neighbouring bright fringes 2.4 m away.
items.workedSolution: Using λ = 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m, adjacent bright-fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) = (6.50 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.4) / 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.60 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) to obtain 2.60 × 10⁻³ m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit separation and divides by screen distance (λd / D) instead of λD / d.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the distance from the central bright fringe to the first dark minimum (½ λD / d) instead of bright fringe spacing.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2, confusing double-slit fringe spacing with single-slit central maximum width.

items.stem: Using a 12 bits per sample ADC across an 8.19 V input span, a digital acoustic recorder captures 6 independent microphone channels. Each audio channel contains frequencies up to 20.0 kHz and is sampled at 44.0 kHz prior to TDM interleaving.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}}/2^n = 2.00 mV$. (b) Minimum Nyquist rate $2 f_{\max} = 40.0 kHz$. (c) TDM total bit rate $= 3.17 × 10³ kbit s⁻¹$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the voltage resolution of the ADC in mV.
State the minimum theoretical Nyquist sampling frequency required to avoid aliasing (in kHz).
Calculate the aggregate bit rate transmitted across the TDM link in $\text{kbit s}^{-1}$.
workingSteps: Total bit rate $= N \times f_{\mathrm{s}} \times n = 6 \times 44.0 \times 12 = 3.17 × 10³ kbit s⁻¹$.

items.stem: At a $1.0\text{ kHz}$ reference tone, the acoustic intensity reaching a listener's ear is $3.16 \times 10^{-5}\text{ W m}^{-2}$. Taking the threshold of hearing $I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$, calculate the sound intensity level in decibels.
items.workedSolution: $\text{Intensity level} = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{3.16 \times 10^{-5}}{1.0 \times 10^{-12}}\right) = 10\log_{10}(3.16 \times 10^7) = 75.0 dB$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes $\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ in bels rather than multiplying by 10 for decibels.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses natural logarithm $\ln$ instead of base-10 logarithm $\log_{10}$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 20 (amplitude) instead of 10 (intensity).

items.stem: The diagram shows an unpolarized beam of intensity 36 W m⁻² passing through ideal polarizer P₁ and then analyzer A. The axis of A makes an angle θ = 50° with P₁, and polarized light obeys I = I₁ cos²θ. What intensity emerges from analyzer A?
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 18.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(50°) = ½(36) cos²(50°) = 7.44 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(50°) = 7.44 W m⁻² (A).

items.stem: Before placing a Doppler ultrasound probe against a patient's neck over the carotid artery, a sonographer applies a thin layer of water-based gel. What is the primary physical role of this gel?
items.workedSolution: Air has an acoustic impedance roughly four orders of magnitude below soft tissue, so air gaps reflect almost 100% of incident ultrasound. Coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound transmits into tissue rather than reflecting at the skin.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: coupling gel removes air and matches acoustic impedance so ultrasound transmits into tissue.

options.text: It absorbs reflected ultrasound echoes so that only the transmitted beam reaches the arterial wall.
options.distractorRationale: Reflected echoes are essential for measuring the Doppler shift and must transmit back into the probe.

options.label: B
options.text: It cools the skin so that the speed of ultrasound in red blood cells drops by half.
options.distractorRationale: Coupling gel is used for acoustic impedance matching, not for significantly changing wave speed in blood.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: It refracts the ultrasound beam to 90° so that the beam strikes the blood flow perpendicularly.
options.distractorRationale: A 90° beam gives cos 90° = 0 and therefore zero Doppler frequency shift.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 680 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating ruled with 250 lines mm⁻¹. Determine the maximum observable diffraction order n_max.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 250 = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Since sin θ ≤ 1, n ≤ d / λ = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ / 6.80 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.88. Taking the floor gives n_max = 5.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 5.88 and takes floor to get n_max = 5 (A).

items.stem: Astronauts outside a spacecraft communicate via radio signals rather than shouting through space. Which physical difference between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves explains this?
items.workedSolution: Mechanical waves depend on restoring forces between particles of a medium. Electromagnetic waves are transverse oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel through vacuum. Therefore option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: mechanical waves need a material medium, whereas electromagnetic waves are transverse electric and magnetic fields travelling through vacuum.

options.text: Electromagnetic waves are longitudinal pressure disturbances that travel faster in vacuum than in solids.
options.distractorRationale: Electromagnetic waves are transverse electric and magnetic field oscillations, not pressure waves.

options.label: B
options.text: Mechanical waves require no medium and travel at the speed of light whereas electromagnetic waves require air molecules.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the essential requirement of a material medium between mechanical and electromagnetic waves.

options.label: C
options.text: Both sound and radio waves propagate freely across empty space, but sound has a wavelength too long to detect.
options.distractorRationale: Sound cannot propagate across vacuum at all because there are no particles to transmit compressions.

options.label: D
options.text: Mechanical waves require a material medium and transfer energy via particle interactions whereas electromagnetic waves consist of transverse oscillating electric and magnetic fields propagating through vacuum.

items.stem: Why do workplace noise meters measure perceived loudness on the dBA scale rather than the unweighted dB intensity scale?
items.workedSolution: Perceived loudness varies strongly with frequency, so the dBA scale is frequency weighted to match human ear sensitivity peaking near three kilohertz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that frequency weighted to match human ear sensitivity peaking near three kilohertz.

options.text: Because the dBA scale ignores sound intensity and measures only acoustic frequency.
options.distractorRationale: dBA combines logarithmic intensity with frequency-dependent ear sensitivity weighting.

options.text: Because human ears are most sensitive near twenty hertz and insensitive around three kilohertz.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses human ear response: sensitivity peaks around 3 kHz and drops sharply at low frequencies.

items.stem: Sodium light of wavelength $589\text{ nm}$ is incident normally on a diffraction grating ruled with $300\text{ lines mm}^{-1}$. Calculate the diffraction angle $\theta$ of the second-order ($n = 2$) maximum.
items.workedSolution: $d = 10^{-3}/300 = 3.33 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$; $\sin\theta = 2 \times 589 \times 10^{-9} / d = 0.3534$, giving $\theta = 20.7 °$. Option C (20.7 °) matches.

items.stem: Monochromatic laser light in Young's double-slit apparatus is replaced by a white-light source as shown. Why is the central (n = 0) fringe pure white?
items.workedSolution: At the exact centre of the screen, Δl = 0 for every wavelength λ. All colours travel equal path lengths and interfere constructively together to form a bright white central fringe. Therefore option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: the central fringe is bright white because all wavelengths travel equal path lengths to the centre and interfere constructively together.

options.text: The central fringe is white because white light does not diffract until it reaches the first-order angle.
options.distractorRationale: All wavelengths diffract through both slits; it is zero path difference that brings all colours into constructive overlap at the centre.

options.distractorRationale: Zero path difference produces constructive interference for every visible wavelength at the same point.

options.label: C
options.text: The central fringe is white because the slit separation s equals the average wavelength of visible white light.
options.distractorRationale: Slit separation s (~0.4 mm) is nearly a thousand times larger than visible wavelengths.

options.label: D
options.text: At the central axis of symmetry, the central fringe is bright white because all wavelengths travel equal path lengths to the centre and interfere constructively together.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 488 nm is incident normally on two narrow parallel slits. Each slit has a width of 0.06 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.3 mm. The diffraction-modulated interference pattern is observed on a screen 3.2 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Interference fringe spacing Δy = λD / d = 5.21 × 10⁻³ m. (b) Central envelope full width w_env = 2λD / b = 0.0521 m. (c) First missing order n = d / b = 5.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λD / d with slit separation d.
Uses 2λD / b with individual slit width b.
Equates interference maximum angle to first diffraction minimum.

Calculate the full width of the central single-slit diffraction envelope on the screen.
Determine the lowest positive interference order n that is missing due to coincidence with a single-slit diffraction minimum.
workingSteps: Equate nλ / d = λ / b => n = d / b.

items.stem: A stationary loudspeaker emits sound waves uniformly in all directions while Observer O moves directly toward it. How does this moving-observer situation differ physically from a moving-source Doppler shift?
items.workedSolution: Because the source is stationary, the wavefronts remain evenly spaced with an unchanged wavelength in the medium. The moving observer meets wavefronts at a higher rate, which raises the observed frequency.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that unchanged wavelength in the medium while the observer encounters wavefronts at a higher rate.

options.text: The wavelength of the sound in the air becomes shorter ahead of the observer while relative wave speed stays unchanged.
options.distractorRationale: Wavelength in the air changes only when the source moves, not when the observer moves.

options.label: B
options.text: The stationary source produces concentric wavefronts of unchanged wavelength in the medium while the observer encounters wavefronts at a higher rate because the relative speed between wave and observer increases.

options.label: C
options.text: No Doppler shift is detected because the source itself remains at rest in the air.
options.distractorRationale: Moving through stationary wavefronts changes the rate of wavefront arrival, producing a Doppler shift.

options.label: D
options.text: The observer detects a lower pitch because advancing toward the source increases the period between crests.

items.stem: With wave speed 216 m s⁻¹, a stretched string (fixed at both ends, length 0.96 m) sustains a stationary wave in its 4th harmonic.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_4 = 2L / n = 2(0.96) / 4 = 0.480 m. (b) Using wave speed: f_4 = v / λ_4 = 216 / 0.480 = 450 Hz. (c) Lowest mode: f₁ = f_4 / 4 = 113 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of this n = 4 harmonic standing wave.
workingSteps: For a string fixed at both ends, λ_n = 2L / n.

parts.prompt: Determine the oscillation frequency of this standing wave.
Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string when kept at the same tension.

items.stem: Using a stationary loudspeaker at 860 Hz in still air (speed 330 m s⁻¹), a car carrying a microphone moving towards it records 1.03 × 10³ Hz. Calculate the observer's speed.
items.workedSolution: From f′ = f(v + v_o) / v, rearrange directly: v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 330 × |1.03 × 10³ / 860 − 1| = 64.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 64.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: At sound speed 330 m s⁻¹, standing waves in harmonic n = 3 fill a cylindrical pipe open at both ends (0.9 m long, assuming zero end effects). What is this frequency?
items.workedSolution: Substitute L = 0.9 m and n = 3 into the open-pipe relation: f_n = nv / (2L) = (3 × 330) / (2 × 0.9) = 550 Hz.

items.workedSolution: Convert ruling: d = 10⁻³ / 400 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. By d sin θ = nλ, λ = d sin(20.1°) / 2 = 4.30 × 10⁻⁷ m.

items.workedSolution: (a) Wave speed: v = fλ = 40 × 0.24 = 9.60 m s⁻¹. (b) Period: T = 1 / 40 = 0.0250 s. (c) Gap Δx = 0.0360 m, giving Δφ = 2π Δx / λ = 0.942 rad.

items.stem: Coherent 488 nm light crosses a narrow slit (0.25 mm wide) towards a screen 1.8 m behind. Determine the full linear width of the central bright maximum.
items.workedSolution: First dark bands lie at θ = ±λ / b, so half-width is y₁ = λD / b = 3.51 × 10⁻³ m; doubling gives w = 2λD / b = 7.03 × 10⁻³ m.

items.stem: Green laser light of wavelength $\lambda = 540\text{ nm}$ illuminates $5$ parallel slits spaced by $d = 180\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ (each of width $b = 30.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$), forming an interference pattern on a screen $D = 2.50\text{ m}$ away. What is the spacing $s$ between adjacent principal maxima near the centre of the screen?
items.workedSolution: Principal maxima occur at the same positions as double-slit fringes: $s = \frac{\lambda D}{d} = \frac{(540 \times 10^{-9})(2.50)}{180 \times 10^{-6}} = 7.50 mm$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $s = \lambda D / d$ independent of $N$ to obtain $7.50 mm$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses individual slit width b instead of slit separation d in s = λD/d.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides fringe spacing by the number of slits N = 5, confusing fringe width with fringe separation.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an extraneous factor of one-half.

items.stem: One end is sealed on a cylindrical pipe of length 0.24 m, with an ideal open end. It vibrates in odd harmonic n = 3 with sound speed 343 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Acoustic length L_eff = 0.240 m yields f₁ = v / (4L_eff) = 357 Hz. (b) Standing wavelength: λ_3 = 4L_eff / 3 = 0.320 m. (c) Resonant pitch: f_3 = 3f₁ = 1.07 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies quarter-wave first-harmonic relation f₁ = v / (4L_eff).
Multiplies first-harmonic frequency by odd harmonic index 3 (or uses v / λ).

parts.prompt: Calculate the first-harmonic (n = 1) frequency of this closed-end air column.
workingSteps: For a pipe closed at one end, λ₁ = 4L so f₁ = v / (4L).

items.stem: The resonance response graph compares a lightly damped oscillator with a more heavily damped oscillator driven at constant force amplitude. How does increasing damping modify the resonance curve?
items.workedSolution: Heavier damping reduces maximum steady-state amplitude at all driving frequencies, flattens/broadens the peak, and shifts peak frequency slightly below f₀. Therefore the correct statement is: Increasing damping decreases the peak resonance amplitude broadens the response curve and slightly reduces the resonant frequency.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: increasing damping decreases the peak resonance amplitude broadens the response curve and slightly reduces the resonant frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing damping decreases the peak resonance amplitude broadens the response curve and slightly reduces the resonant frequency.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing damping raises the peak amplitude, makes the peak sharper, and shifts the resonant frequency upwards.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses all three effects of damping on a driven oscillator's amplitude-frequency response.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing damping lowers the peak amplitude while keeping the resonant frequency strictly unchanged and narrowing the peak.
options.distractorRationale: Damping broadens the resonance peak and slightly lowers the frequency at which maximum amplitude occurs.

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing damping leaves the peak height unchanged at f₀ while increasing amplitude at every other driving frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Greater damping dissipates more energy per cycle, lowering amplitude across the resonance region.

items.stem: Transverse waves travel along a taut guitar string of vibrating length 37.5 cm at speed 105 m s⁻¹. Calculate the first-harmonic frequency of the string.
items.workedSolution: For the first harmonic on a string fixed at both ends, λ = 2L = 0.750 m; f₁ = v / λ = 105 / 0.750 = 140 Hz.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Sets λ = L instead of λ = 2L for the first harmonic.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Sets λ = 4L (closed-pipe condition) instead of λ = 2L.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength instead of dividing.

items.stem: While slowly sweeping the signal generator frequency upward in Required Practical 1, three clear antinode loops appear between the bridge and pulley. How does the student verify accurate length and harmonic measurement?
items.workedSolution: Three loops correspond to the third harmonic (f = 3f₁). Measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes. The first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

markScheme.criterion: States three loops give the third harmonic (f = 3f₁). Length is measured between the bridge and pulley nodes, where first harmonic frequency equals wave speed over twice that length.

options.label: A
options.text: Three loops correspond to a wavelength equal to three times the bridge-to-pulley distance.
options.distractorRationale: Three half-wavelength loops give L = 3λ/2, so λ = 2L/3.

options.label: B
options.text: Three loops correspond to the third harmonic (f = 3f₁), and the student must measure the vibrating length between the wooden bridge and pulley nodes because the first harmonic frequency equals wave speed divided by twice that length.

options.label: C
options.text: The vibrating length should be measured from the first antinode to the final antinode.
options.distractorRationale: Length L is always measured between the two outer fixed nodes (bridge to pulley).

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing the signal-generator amplitude shifts the first harmonic frequency upward.
options.distractorRationale: Amplitude does not change the resonant frequency of a linear taut string.

items.stem: An optical reflecting telescope with an aperture diameter of 2.70 m observes a close binary star system at a mean wavelength of 540 nm. Using the Rayleigh criterion $\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D}$, what is the minimum angular separation the telescope can resolve?
items.workedSolution: Applying the AQA Rayleigh criterion $\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D} = \frac{5.40 \times 10^{-7}}{2.70} = 2.00 × 10⁻⁷ rad$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses aperture radius instead of diameter in theta = lambda / D.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the diameter erroneously.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the Rayleigh formula as D / lambda.

items.stem: Directly towards a fixed listener, a train horn travels at 88 m s⁻¹ while sounding at 750 Hz. With sound moving at 332 m s⁻¹, what is the observed frequency?
items.workedSolution: Source moving towards a fixed listener: f' = fv / (v − v_s) = (750 × 332) / (332 − 88) = 1.02 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 1.02 × 10³ Hz (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the moving-observer formula AND reverses the sign of the Doppler frequency shift.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the wrong sign in the denominator, using v + v_s for an approaching source (or v − v_s for a receding source).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the moving-observer equation f(v ± v_s) / v instead of the moving-source equation fv / (v ∓ v_s).

items.stem: Light of wavelength 612 nm from a coherent source enters two narrow parallel slits (0.16 mm apart). An interference pattern forms on a screen 2.1 m behind.
items.workedSolution: (a) Bright separation = λD / d = (6.12 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.1) / 1.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.03 × 10⁻³ m. (b) First dark fringe lies at ½ × 8.03 × 10⁻³ = 4.02 × 10⁻³ m. (c) At n = 3, path difference = nλ = 3 × 6.12 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.84 × 10⁻⁶ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units and substitutes into λD / (slit separation).
Takes half of the bright-fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fringe spacing between adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
Determine the distance on the screen from the central bright maximum to the centre of the first dark fringe.
workingSteps: First destructive minimum occurs halfway between the central and first-order bright maxima: y_dark,1 = 0.5 × fringe spacing.

parts.prompt: Calculate the geometric path difference between waves arriving from the two slits at the order n = 3 bright fringe.
workingSteps: Constructive interference at order n requires path difference Δℓ = nλ.

items.stem: A digital communications link multiplexes 16 voice channels using time-division multiplexing (TDM). Each channel is sampled at 32.0 kHz and encoded into a PCM word of 12 bits. Calculate the total transmitted bit rate in $\text{kbit s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: Single-channel PCM bit rate $= f_{\mathrm{s}} \times n = 32.0\text{ kHz} \times 12 = 384\text{ kbit s}^{-1}$. Across 16 TDM channels: $16 \times 384 = 6.14 × 10³ kbit s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Total TDM bit rate equals 6.14 × 10³ kbit s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates bit rate for a single channel without multiplying by 16 TDM channels.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides by word length 12 instead of multiplying.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies sampling rate by $2^{12}$ levels instead of 12 bits per sample.

items.stem: Workshop machinery exposes an unprotected operator to a $4.0\text{ kHz}$ sound wave of intensity $2.50 \times 10^{-4}\text{ W m}^{-2}$. Using $I_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ W m}^{-2}$, find the intensity level in dB.
items.workedSolution: $\text{Intensity level} = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{2.50 \times 10^{-4}}{1.0 \times 10^{-12}}\right) = 84.0 dB$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 10 converting bels to decibels.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses natural log instead of $\log_{10}$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect threshold value $10^{-10}\text{ W m}^{-2}$.

items.stem: An unpolarized beam of light of intensity 160 W m⁻² passes normally through an ideal vertical polarizer P₁. It then passes through an ideal linear analyzer A whose transmission axis is at θ = 35° to P₁. For plane-polarized light of intensity I₁, Malus's law gives I = I₁ cos²θ.
items.workedSolution: (a) After P₁, I₁ = ½ I₀ = 80.0 W m⁻². (b) After analyzer A, I = I₁ cos²(35°) = 53.7 W m⁻². (c) Overall fraction I / I₀ = ½ cos²(35°) = 0.336.

markScheme.criterion: Halves unpolarized incident intensity at ideal polarizer P₁.
Applies I = I₁ cos²θ to the polarized beam.
Divides final transmitted intensity by incident unpolarized intensity I₀.

parts.prompt: State and calculate the intensity I₁ of the plane-polarized beam between polarizer P₁ and analyzer A.
workingSteps: Averaging cos²φ = ½ over all random polarization orientations reduces unpolarized intensity by half: I₁ = ½ I₀.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity I emerging from analyzer A.
workingSteps: Apply Malus's law I = I₁ cos²θ.

parts.prompt: Determine the overall fraction I / I₀ of the original unpolarized intensity transmitted by the two-filter combination.
workingSteps: Overall transmission fraction = I / I₀ = ½ cos²θ.

items.stem: The diagram shows a taut string fixed at both ends of vibrating length 0.64 m and linear mass density 0.0032 kg m⁻¹. It vibrates in harmonic mode n = 3 at a frequency of 199.2 Hz. The transverse wave speed on a taut string is v = √(T / μ). Determine the required tension T.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.64) / 3 = 0.427 m, so required wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 85.0 m s⁻¹. Rearranging v = √(T / μ) gives T = μv² = 0.0032 × (85.0)² = 23.1 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 2Lf_n / n and computes T = μv² = 23.1 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to square the wave speed when rearranging v = √(T / μ) to T = μv².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, halving v and underestimating T = μv² by a factor of 4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides v² by linear mass density μ instead of multiplying T = μv².

items.stem: Which statement matches the AQA definition of a transverse progressive wave?
items.workedSolution: AQA requires 'oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer' (avoiding imprecise 'vibrations' or 'wave motion'). Therefore option B is correct: oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

items.stem: Cortical bone has density 1900 kg m⁻³ and transmits ultrasound waves at a speed of 4080 m s⁻¹. Calculate the specific acoustic impedance $Z$ of cortical bone.
items.workedSolution: Specific acoustic impedance is $Z = \rho c = 1900 \times 4080 = 7.75 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 7.75 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹.

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 480 nm strikes a diffraction grating ruled with 550 lines mm⁻¹ at normal incidence. Principal maxima beginning at n = 1 are measured across the forward semicircle (−90° < θ < +90°).
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 1.82 × 10⁻⁶ m, so θ₁ = arcsin(λ / d) = 15.3°. (b) d / λ = 3.79, giving n_max = 3. (c) Total principal maxima = 2(3) + 1 = 7.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and applies sin θ₁ = λ / d.
Evaluates d / λ = 3.79 and rounds down.

items.stem: What retinal photoreceptor condition must be satisfied for the brain to resolve two closely spaced bright points as distinct objects?
items.workedSolution: To resolve two points, at least one unstimulated cone must lie between two stimulated cones. This gives a minimum centre-to-centre image separation of $2d_{\text{cone}}$.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that at least one unstimulated cone must lie between two stimulated cones.

options.label: A
options.text: To resolve two images, at least one unstimulated cone must lie between two stimulated cones.

options.label: B
options.text: Both images must land on adjacent touching cones with no gap between them.
options.distractorRationale: Adjacent stimulated cones cannot be distinguished from a single wider bright spot.

options.label: C
options.text: Both images must fall exclusively on peripheral rods outside the fovea.
options.distractorRationale: Peripheral rods share nerve pathways and yield poor spatial resolution compared with foveal cones.

options.label: D
options.text: At least ten rods must sit between two stimulated cones at the fovea.
options.distractorRationale: The central fovea contains densely packed cones rather than rods, and one unstimulated cone suffices.

items.stem: To observe a stable interference pattern in optical experiments, the superposing light waves must be coherent. What is meant by coherent waves?
items.workedSolution: AQA definition of coherence: waves having a constant phase difference and the same frequency and wavelength. Therefore option D is correct: waves having a constant phase difference and the same frequency and wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: waves having a constant phase difference and the same frequency and wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: Coherent sources emit waves of identical amplitude travelling at different frequencies
options.distractorRationale: Different frequencies cause phase difference to drift rapidly, washing out interference fringes.

options.label: B
options.text: Coherent sources emit plane-polarised waves of very high intensity regardless of phase
options.distractorRationale: Coherence requires a constant phase difference, not merely polarisation or brightness.

options.label: C
options.text: Coherent sources emit white light containing every visible wavelength simultaneously
options.distractorRationale: White light is polychromatic and only produces localised interference near zero path difference.

options.label: D
options.text: Coherent sources emit waves having a constant phase difference and the same frequency and wavelength

items.stem: One slit is covered so that white light now illuminates a single narrow slit. Which description matches the resulting single-slit white-light diffraction pattern on the screen?
items.workedSolution: A single slit illuminated by white light produces a broad white central maximum twice as wide as the dimmer outer coloured fringes. Each outer spectrum has violet on the inner edge and red on the outer edge. Therefore option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: white light through a single slit gives a wide white central maximum and dimmer coloured outer fringes (violet inner, red outer).

options.text: A single slit produces equally wide, equally bright white fringes across the entire screen with no colour separation.
options.distractorRationale: Single-slit diffraction has a central maximum twice as wide as outer maxima, rapidly dropping intensity, and coloured outer fringes.

options.label: B
options.text: Compared with double-slit fringes, a single slit illuminated by white light produces a wide white central maximum twice as wide as the dimmer outer coloured fringes, which have violet on the inner edge and red on the outer edge.

options.label: C
options.text: A single slit eliminates all diffraction so only a sharp white geometric shadow of the slit appears.
options.distractorRationale: A narrow slit produces a broad diffraction envelope with coloured outer fringes.

options.label: D
options.text: A single slit makes the central fringe dark while the first-order fringes are twice as wide and brightest.
options.distractorRationale: The central maximum is always the brightest and widest feature of a single-slit pattern.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 514 nm illuminates two narrow parallel slits with centre-to-centre separation 0.375 mm, forming fringes on a screen 1.4 m away. Single-slit diffraction makes the n = 5 order the first missing bright fringe. Determine the width b of each slit.
items.workedSolution: The first single-slit minimum occurs at θ = λ / b while the n-th double-slit maximum is at θ = nλ / d. Coincidence at n = 5 gives b = d / 5 = 3.75 × 10⁻⁴ / 5 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁵ m.

markScheme.criterion: Equates λ / b = nλ / d to obtain b = d / 5 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁵ m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides slit separation by (n + 1) instead of missing order n = d / b.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the highest visible order inside the central envelope (n − 1) instead of the missing order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2 from the full angular width of the central envelope.

items.stem: A stationary coastal foghorn sounds continuously at $440\text{ Hz}$ while a boat moves directly away from it at $34.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Given the speed of sound in air is $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$, what frequency is detected on the boat?
items.workedSolution: For a moving observer receding from a stationary source, $f' = f\frac{v - u_{\text{o}}}{v} = 440 \times \frac{340 - 34.0}{340} = 396 Hz$.

items.stem: With transverse speed 90 m s⁻¹, a 0.96 m taut string fixed at both ends resonates in harmonic mode n = 6. Work out the node-to-node distance.
items.workedSolution: Because n = 6 places n loops across L = 0.96 m, node separation is d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n = 0.96 / 6 = 0.160 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n to obtain 0.160 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the node-to-adjacent-antinode distance λ / 4 instead of adjacent node spacing λ / 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides string length L by the total number of nodes (n + 1) instead of the number of loops n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates a full wavelength λ = 2L / n instead of the half-wavelength node-to-node spacing λ / 2.

items.stem: A fixed warning horn sends out a steady 520 Hz sound in still air where sound moves at 336 m s⁻¹. Moving towards it, an observer in a vehicle detects 613 Hz. Calculate the observer speed.
items.workedSolution: Apply f′ = f(v + v_o) / v; isolating speed gives v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 336 × |613 / 520 − 1| = 60.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 60.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: What spacing between a pair of narrow slits puts the n = 5 bright maximum at 25.6 mm from the central bright fringe? The screen is 2 m away and the wavelength is 460 nm.
items.workedSolution: Make slit spacing the subject of y_n = nλD / d: d = nλD / y_n = (5 × 4.60 × 10⁻⁷ × 2) / 0.0256 = 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th bright fringe displacement as a single fringe spacing, omitting the factor of n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies dark-fringe factor (n − ½) instead of integer n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides total span by (n + 1) instead of n fringe intervals between n = 0 and order n.

items.stem: The displacement–position graph shows a sinusoidal wave travelling on a stretched string. The wave has amplitude 0.015 m, wavelength 0.8 m, and speed 68 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency of the wave.
items.workedSolution: Using f = v / λ with wave speed v = 68 m s⁻¹ and wavelength λ = 0.8 m gives f = 68 / 0.8 = 85.0 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges v = fλ to obtain f = v / λ = 85.0 Hz (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the oscillation period T = λ / v instead of the frequency f = v / λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Mistakes two full cycles for one wavelength, halving the calculated frequency.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength (vλ) instead of dividing v by λ.

items.stem: Inside a resonance tube open at both ends (0.54 m long, with ideal open-end conditions), sound moves at 343 m s⁻¹. Find the frequency when it vibrates in mode n = 5.
items.workedSolution: Substitute L = 0.54 m and n = 5 into the open-pipe relation: f_n = nv / (2L) = (5 × 343) / (2 × 0.54) = 1.59 × 10³ Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the first-harmonic frequency f₁ instead of the n-th harmonic.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n.

items.stem: Perpendicular rays cross a 300 lines mm⁻¹ diffraction grating, placing order n = 2 at θ = 20.7°. Calculate the wavelength.
items.workedSolution: First find d = 10⁻³ / 300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m; rearranging d sin θ = nλ yields λ = d sin(20.7°) / 2 = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: A student inspects a 10 Hz wave along a slinky spring (wavelength 2 m, amplitude 0.045 m) at x₁ = 0.5 m (P) and x₂ = 1.8 m (Q). Work out the phase difference in radians.
items.workedSolution: Gap Δx = 1.8 m − 0.5 m = 1.3 m over cycle span 2 m equals 0.650 cycles. Therefore Δφ = 2π × 0.650 = 4.08 rad.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 2π rad to get 4.08 rad (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (π rad) instead of a full cycle (2π rad) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in degrees instead of radians.

items.stem: Diffracted by a 0.1 mm single slit, 514 nm light strikes a screen 3.5 m behind. Work out the full linear width of the central bright maximum.
items.workedSolution: First dark bands lie at θ = ±λ / b, so half-width is y₁ = λD / b = 0.0180 m; doubling gives w = 2λD / b = 0.0360 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0360 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit width b and divides by screen distance D instead of 2λD / b.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates λD / b (the distance from the centre to one first-order minimum) instead of the full central maximum width 2λD / b.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 4 instead of 2 when doubling the first-minimum half-width.

items.stem: In a version of Hertz's standing-wave radio experiment, a dipole detector moves towards a flat metal reflector. Adjacent signal minima (nodes) are spaced 0.300 m apart. Taking $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, calculate the frequency of the radio waves.
items.workedSolution: Adjacent standing-wave nodes are separated by $\frac{\lambda}{2} = 0.300\text{ m}$, so $\lambda = 0.600\text{ m}$. Hence $f = \frac{c}{\lambda} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8}{0.600} = 5.00 \times 10^8\text{ Hz} = 500 MHz$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats adjacent node spacing as one full wavelength lambda instead of lambda / 2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides frequency by two erroneously.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies c by node spacing instead of dividing c / (2 d).

items.stem: The Bode frequency-response curve of a real operational amplifier shows a constant gain–bandwidth product (GBP) of $1.50\text{ MHz}$. When wired with negative feedback to give a closed-loop voltage gain of $75.0$, what is its usable bandwidth in kHz?
items.workedSolution: Since $\text{gain} \times \text{bandwidth} = \text{constant}$, $\text{bandwidth} = \frac{1.50 \times 10^3\text{ kHz}}{75.0} = 20.0 kHz$.

items.stem: A student records plane-polarized light falling from 144 W m⁻² to 47.4 W m⁻² across an ideal analyzer. Apply Malus's law (I = I₀ cos²θ) here. Calculate the acute axis angle θ.
items.workedSolution: Solve I = I₀ cos²θ: cos θ = √(47.4 / 144) = 0.574; hence θ = arccos(0.574) = 55.0°.

items.stem: Plane wavefronts of monochromatic light cross at an angle from air into glass of higher refractive index, as shown. How are rays oriented relative to wavefronts, and how do the wave properties change inside glass?
items.workedSolution: Rays point perpendicular to wavefronts. In a higher-n medium, wave speed v decreases at fixed frequency f, so λ decreases and rays refract towards the normal. Therefore option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: rays are perpendicular to wavefronts and bend towards the normal as speed and wavelength decrease at constant frequency.
