items.stem: Resonating one mode above its first harmonic, a 0.64 m air column is closed at one end (treating the pipe as ideal). At 348 m s⁻¹, calculate this frequency.
items.workedSolution: Only odd modes (n = 1, 3, 5,...) resonate here; next above the first harmonic is n = 3, giving f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 3(348) / (4 × 0.64) = 408 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies odd harmonic n = 3 and computes f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 408 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic frequency v / (4L) instead of the next higher harmonic 3v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes an even n = 2 harmonic exists in a pipe closed at one end, computing 2f₁ = v / (2L) instead of 3f₁ = 3v / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the open-both-ends formula 3v / (2L) instead of closed-one-end 3v / (4L).

items.stem: Air oscillates inside a cylindrical pipe sealed firmly at both ends, neglecting end effects. Which statement correctly describes the displacement boundary conditions and allowed harmonics?
items.workedSolution: Closed walls force zero air displacement (nodes) at both ends, giving L = n(λ/2) and λ_n = 2L/n for all harmonics n = 1, 2, 3,... Therefore option C is correct: both closed ends are displacement nodes, supporting all integer harmonics.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: both closed ends form displacement nodes, supporting all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.

options.label: A
options.text: A pipe closed at both ends forms displacement antinodes at both rigid caps and supports only odd harmonics.
options.distractorRationale: Air particles cannot move through rigid walls, so closed ends are displacement nodes and all integer harmonics are supported.

options.label: B
options.text: A pipe closed at both ends cannot form standing waves because sound waves cannot reflect from rigid boundaries.
options.distractorRationale: Sound waves reflect strongly from rigid closed caps, establishing node–node standing waves with λ_n = 2L/n.

options.label: C
options.text: A pipe closed at both ends forms a displacement node at each closed end and supports all integer harmonics with wavelength two L over n.

options.label: D
options.text: A pipe closed at both ends forms a displacement node at one end and an antinode at the other with wavelength four L.
options.distractorRationale: Node–antinode symmetry applies to a pipe closed at one end and open at the other, not a two-closed pipe.

items.stem: In the microwave stationary-wave setup shown, a probe moves 8.0 cm between the 1st minimum and the 6th minimum (spanning 5 consecutive node-to-node intervals). Calculate the wavelength λ of the microwaves.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Confuses node-to-node separation (λ/2) with full wavelength λ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by the number of minima (6) instead of the number of intervals (5).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the entire 8.0 cm span equals two wavelengths.

items.stem: A student determines mass per unit length $\mu = T / (4 f_1^2 L^2)$ of an enamelled copper string. The percentage uncertainties are 1.1% in hanging mass, 0.5% in resonant frequency $f_1$, and 0.3% in length $L$. What is the total percentage uncertainty in $\mu$?

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Fails to double the percentage uncertainties of squared terms f₁² and L².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Doubles %f₁ but forgets to double %L.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only %v instead of %μ.

items.stem: Which statement correctly explains how Earth's atmosphere determines the siting of telescopes across the electromagnetic spectrum?
items.workedSolution: Earth's atmosphere absorbs high-energy and most infrared wavelengths. Optical and radio waves pass through atmospheric windows, whereas infrared, ultraviolet, and X-rays are absorbed.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that optical and radio waves pass through atmospheric windows whereas infrared ultraviolet and X-rays are absorbed.

items.stem: Emitting a constant 560 Hz note, a loudspeaker on a car moves away from a stationary microphone and produces an observed pitch of 467 Hz. With sound speed 343 m s⁻¹, find the source speed.
items.workedSolution: Using f' = fv / (v + v_s) gives v + v_s = vf / f' = (343 × 560) / 467; therefore v_s = 68.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves f' = fv / (v ∓ v_s) for v_s = 68.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.distractorRationale: Halves the source speed as if applying a two-way radar reflection formula.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the low-speed / moving-observer relation v|f'/f − 1| instead of rearranging the exact moving-source formula f' = fv / (v ∓ v_s).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Stops at the effective denominator speed v(f / f') without taking the difference from v.

items.stem: In a double-slit test, two narrow parallel slits spaced 0.2 mm apart cast fringes 3.65 mm wide onto a screen 1.8 m away. Find the wavelength of the light.
items.workedSolution: Invert Δy = λD / d in SI units: λ = Δy × d / D = (3.64 × 10⁻³ × 2.00 × 10⁻⁴) / 1.8 = 4.05 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges double-slit relation to obtain λ = 4.05 × 10⁻⁷ m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes an extra factor of ½ from single-slit central-width formulas.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats bright-to-bright fringe spacing as half-wavelength path difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies fringe spacing by screen distance D and divides by slit separation instead of multiplying by slit separation / D.

items.stem: A VHF FM radio station broadcasts audio with maximum modulating frequency $f_{\mathrm{M}} = 15.0\text{ kHz}$ and maximum frequency deviation $\Delta f = 75.0\text{ kHz}$. Calculate the total channel bandwidth required by this FM broadcast.
items.workedSolution: For FM broadcasts, $\mathrm{BW}_{\mathrm{FM}} = 2(\Delta f + f_{\mathrm{M}}) = 2(75.0 + 15.0) = 180 kHz$.

items.stem: In a model of the human middle ear, the eardrum has effective area $A_1 = 64.0\text{ mm}^2$ and the oval window has area $A_2 = 3.20\text{ mm}^2$. The ossicles act as a lever that increases force by $F_2 / F_1 = 1.30$. Calculate the overall pressure amplification factor $P_{\text{oval}} / P_{\text{drum}}$.
items.workedSolution: $\frac{P_{\text{oval}}}{P_{\text{drum}}} = \left(\frac{F_2}{F_1}\right)\left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right) = 1.30 \times \frac{64.0}{3.20} = 26.0$.

items.stem: The diagram shows an unpolarized beam of intensity 220 W m⁻² passing through ideal polarizer P₁ and then analyzer A. The axis of A makes an angle θ = 25° with P₁, and polarized light obeys I = I₁ cos²θ. What intensity emerges from analyzer A?
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 110 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(25°) = ½(220) cos²(25°) = 90.4 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(25°) = 90.4 W m⁻² (B).

items.stem: The diagram shows a taut string clamped at both ends of vibrating length 1.25 m and linear mass density 0.0015 kg m⁻¹. It vibrates in harmonic mode n = 3 at a frequency of 168 Hz. The transverse wave speed on a taut string is v = √(T / μ). Determine the required tension T.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength λ_n = 2L / n = 2(1.25) / 3 = 0.833 m, so required wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 140 m s⁻¹. Rearranging v = √(T / μ) gives T = μv² = 0.0015 × (140)² = 29.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 2Lf_n / n and computes T = μv² = 29.4 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to square the wave speed when rearranging v = √(T / μ) to T = μv².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, halving v and underestimating T = μv² by a factor of 4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides v² by linear mass density μ instead of multiplying T = μv².

items.stem: The diagram shows a stationary wave on a stretched string with labelled points P, Q, and R. What is the phase difference between points P and Q, which lie between the same two adjacent nodes?
items.workedSolution: All points between two adjacent nodes reach maximum displacement at the same instant and have zero phase difference. Therefore option B is correct: points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: zero phase difference because all points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase.

options.label: A
options.text: Points P and Q have a progressive phase lag proportional to their separation along the string
options.distractorRationale: Classic AQA trap: progressive waves show continuous phase lag 2πΔx/λ, whereas stationary points within one loop oscillate in phase.

options.label: B
options.text: Points P and Q have zero phase difference because all points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase

options.label: C
options.text: Points P and Q have antiphase oscillation because one is climbing while the other falls
options.distractorRationale: Points on opposite sides of a node are in antiphase; P and Q lie inside the same loop.

options.label: D
options.text: Points P and Q have a quarter-cycle phase difference because they sit on opposite sides of the antinode
options.distractorRationale: Crossing an antinode does not invert phase; only crossing a node introduces a π phase jump.

items.stem: A clinician tilts a Doppler ultrasound probe from 65° to 35° relative to the axis of a blood vessel carrying steady blood flow. Which statement correctly explains how the angle affects the measured frequency shift?
items.workedSolution: Since Δf = (2 f v cos θ)/c, lowering θ increases cos θ and enlarges the component v cos θ along the ultrasound beam. Only the blood velocity component parallel to the beam produces a Doppler shift. Therefore, decreasing the beam angle increases the frequency shift.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: only the velocity component parallel to the beam shifts frequency, so decreasing the angle increases Δf.

options.text: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the ultrasound beam causes a shift, so holding the probe at 90° maximises the signal.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses cos θ with sin θ; at 90° there is no velocity component along the beam so Δf = 0.

options.label: B
options.text: Changing the probe angle leaves the measured frequency shift unchanged because red blood cells scatter waves isotropically.
options.distractorRationale: Although scattering occurs in many directions, the Doppler shift depends directly on cos θ along the beam axis.

options.label: C
options.text: Decreasing the beam angle reduces the measured frequency shift because cos θ falls towards zero as θ decreases.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the behaviour of cosine: cos θ increases towards 1 as θ approaches 0°.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the blood velocity component parallel to the ultrasound beam produces a Doppler shift so decreasing the beam angle increases the frequency shift.

items.stem: Before placing an ultrasound probe onto a patient's skin, the sonographer applies a thick layer of water-based coupling gel. Why is this step essential?
items.workedSolution: Without gel, the large impedance mismatch between air and skin reflects over 99.9% of the ultrasound intensity. Coupling gel displaces air and closely matches the acoustic impedance of soft tissue, minimising reflection at the skin.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that displaces air so acoustic impedance closely matches soft tissue minimising reflection at the skin.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 595 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating ruled with 350 lines mm⁻¹. Determine the maximum observable diffraction order n_max.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 350 = 2.86 × 10⁻⁶ m. Since sin θ ≤ 1, n ≤ d / λ = 2.86 × 10⁻⁶ / 5.95 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.80. Taking the floor gives n_max = 4.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 4.80 and takes floor to get n_max = 4 (A).

items.stem: The coupled $y(x)$ and $y(t)$ graphs of a transverse travelling wave show a wavelength $\lambda = 24.0\text{ cm}$ and period $T = 15.0\text{ ms}$. What is the wave speed?
items.workedSolution: Converting to SI units: $\lambda = 0.240\text{ m}$ and $T = 0.0150\text{ s}$, so $v = \frac{\lambda}{T} = \frac{0.240}{0.0150} = 16.0 m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $v = \lambda / T$ in SI units to obtain $16.0 m s⁻¹$.

items.stem: Which statement accurately contrasts the structure and function of retinal cones and rods in the human eye?
items.workedSolution: Cones at the fovea have individual nerve connections for sharp colour vision in bright light. Rods share nerve connections for high sensitivity in dim light.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that foveal cones have individual nerve connections for sharp colour vision, whereas rods share connections for dim-light sensitivity.

options.label: A
options.text: Rods are concentrated at the fovea with individual nerve fibres giving colour vision while cones operate in dim light.
options.distractorRationale: Completely swaps the distribution, wiring, and light-level roles of rods and cones.

options.label: B
options.text: Both cones and rods share single optic nerve fibres equally across the entire retina.
options.distractorRationale: Foveal cones connect individually (1-to-1) for acuity whereas multiple rods pool onto one bipolar nerve.

options.label: C
options.text: Cones respond only to intensity without wavelength discrimination whereas three rod types detect RGB colours.
options.distractorRationale: Three cone pigments provide colour vision; rods are monochrome.

options.label: D
options.text: On the retina, cones at the fovea have individual nerve connections for sharp colour vision in bright light whereas rods share connections for dim light sensitivity.

items.stem: White light is incident normally on a transmission diffraction grating as shown. Which statement accurately describes the pattern observed on the screen?
items.workedSolution: At $n = 0$, all wavelengths constructively interfere at $\theta = 0$ (white); for $n \ge 1$, $\sin\theta = n\lambda/d$ puts shorter-wavelength violet inner and longer-wavelength red outer. Therefore option B is correct: central white maximum flanked by continuous spectra with violet closest to the centre and red furthest.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: central white maximum flanked by continuous spectra with violet closest to the centre and red furthest.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 650 nm illuminates two narrow parallel slits placed 2.2 m from a screen. Each slit has width 0.08 mm, and the centre-to-centre slit separation is 0.4 mm. Which positive interference order n is the first missing order due to single-slit diffraction?
items.workedSolution: Interference maxima satisfy sin θ = nλ / d and the first single-slit minimum satisfies sin θ = λ / b. Dividing gives n = d / b = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ / 8.00 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Selects the last bright interference order visible inside one side of the central envelope (d/b − 1) instead of the missing order d/b.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Counts the total number of bright fringes inside the central diffraction envelope (2d/b − 1) instead of the missing order index.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles d / b by using full angular width 2λ / b instead of first-minimum angle λ / b.

items.stem: A hydrogen absorption line has a laboratory rest wavelength of $\lambda = 656.0\text{ nm}$. In the spectrum of a distant star, this line is shifted toward longer wavelengths by $\Delta\lambda = 1.60\text{ nm}$. Using $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}$, calculate the recession speed $v$ of the star relative to Earth.
items.workedSolution: From $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}$, we have $v = c\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = 3.00 \times 10^8 \times \frac{1.60}{656.0} = 7.32 \times 10^5\text{ m s}^{-1} = 732 km s⁻¹$.

items.stem: Driven at 337.5 Hz, a 0.48 m stretched string (fixed at both ends) enters harmonic mode n = 3. Find how fast transverse waves travel along it.
items.workedSolution: Wavelength for n = 3 on L = 0.48 m: λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.48) / 3 = 0.320 m; hence v = f_n λ_n = 337.5 × 0.320 = 108 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes λ_n = 2L / n and v = f_n λ_n = 108 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ_n = L / n instead of 2L / n, underestimating wave speed by a factor of 2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the closed-pipe boundary relation 4L / n instead of fixed-string 2L / n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the harmonic frequency as the first-harmonic mode (omitting division by n).

items.stem: A stationary loudspeaker emits sound at 920 Hz while a detector moves directly towards it at 60 m s⁻¹. With sound travelling at 330 m s⁻¹ in still air, what frequency is heard?
items.workedSolution: Moving listener, fixed source: f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 920 × (330 + 60) / 330 = 1.09 × 10³ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 1.09 × 10³ Hz (C).

options.distractorRationale: Inverts the observer Doppler sign in f(v ± v_o) / v.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the moving-source denominator formula AND reverses the Doppler sign.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Places observer speed in the denominator fv / (v ∓ v_o) as if the source were moving rather than the observer.

items.stem: Calculate the slit separation when 460 nm light places the n = 4 bright fringe 15.8 mm from the central maximum on a screen 3 m behind two narrow parallel slits.
items.workedSolution: From y_n = nλD / d, solve for spacing: d = nλD / y_n = (4 × 4.60 × 10⁻⁷ × 3) / 0.0158 = 3.50 × 10⁻⁴ m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th bright fringe displacement as a single fringe spacing, omitting the factor of n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies dark-fringe factor (n − ½) instead of integer n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides total span by (n + 1) instead of n fringe intervals between n = 0 and order n.

items.stem: The displacement–position graph shows a progressive wave travelling on a stretched string. The wave has an amplitude of 0.06 m and a wavelength of 0.4 m. If the source oscillates at 85 Hz, calculate the wave speed.
items.workedSolution: From the displacement–position profile, wavelength λ = 0.4 m and frequency f = 85 Hz. Using the wave equation v = fλ = 85 Hz × 0.4 m = 34.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = fλ to obtain 34.0 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides wavelength by frequency (λ / f), confusing frequency f with period T.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the wavelength by misreading a two-cycle span as a single wavelength.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides frequency by wavelength (f / λ) instead of applying v = fλ.

items.stem: A class excites harmonic n = 4 in an open air pipe (0.54 m long, neglecting open-end effects) where sound travels at 338 m s⁻¹. Work out its frequency.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the first-harmonic frequency f₁ instead of the n-th harmonic.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses closed-one-end pipe relation nv / (4L) instead of open-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n.

items.stem: Normal-incidence 589 nm rays meet a 500 lines mm⁻¹ diffraction grating. Find the angle θ between the central line and n = 1.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 17.1° (C).

items.stem: Recorded on a displacement–time plot, a wave in a water tank has amplitude 0.045 m and period 0.2 s. At wave speed 1.2 m s⁻¹, find its wavelength.
items.workedSolution: Here T = 0.2 s and v = 1.2 m s⁻¹; applying λ = vT yields λ = 1.2 × 0.2 = 0.240 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = vT = 1.2 m s⁻¹ × 0.2 s to obtain 0.240 m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides period by wave speed (T / v) instead of multiplying vT.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reads the full two-cycle time span 2T as a single period when computing λ = vT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides wave speed by period (v / T), treating period T on the time axis as if it were frequency f.

items.stem: The sketch shows 633 nm light diffracting through a 0.15 mm single slit onto a screen 3 m behind. Calculate the full linear width of the central band.
items.workedSolution: From θ = ±λ / b, screen half-width is y₁ = λD / b = 0.0127 m; hence w = 2λD / b = 0.0253 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0253 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit width b and divides by screen distance D instead of 2λD / b.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates λD / b (the distance from the centre to one first-order minimum) instead of the full central maximum width 2λD / b.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 4 instead of 2 when doubling the first-minimum half-width.

items.stem: A plane-polarised radio wave from a Hertz transmitter strikes a receiving dipole aerial. When the dipole is parallel to the transmitter ($\theta = 0°$), the maximum emf amplitude is 160 mV. What signal amplitude is detected when the dipole is rotated to $\theta = 60°$?
items.workedSolution: The induced emf amplitude scales with the electric-field component parallel to the dipole: $A = A_0 |\cos\theta| = 160 \times \cos 60° = 80.0 mV$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Applies cos squared (Malus intensity law) instead of |cos theta| for dipole induced emf amplitude.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses sin(60°) instead of cos(60°).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies linear interpolation (1 - 60/180) instead of cosine projection.

items.stem: An oscilloscope trace of an amplitude-modulated (AM) $V$–$t$ waveform shows rapid carrier oscillations with a single carrier cycle period of $T_{\text{c}} = 12.5\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ inside a slower information envelope. What is the carrier frequency $f_{\text{c}}$ in kHz?
items.workedSolution: $f_{\text{c}} = \frac{1}{T_{\text{c}}} = \frac{1}{12.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}} = 8.00 \times 10^4\text{ Hz} = 80.0 kHz$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a carrier cycle period instead of a full cycle.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the period by the information frequency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Measures two carrier cycles instead of one.

items.stem: A plane-polarized beam carrying 32 W m⁻² leaves an ideal analyzer at 18.8 W m⁻². Apply Malus's law (I = I₀ cos²θ) here. Calculate the acute filter rotation angle θ.
items.workedSolution: Rearranging I = I₀ cos²θ gives cos θ = √(18.8 / 32) = 0.766, so θ = arccos(0.766) = 40.0°.

items.stem: Monochromatic red light of wavelength $640\text{ nm}$ in air ($n_1 = 1.00$) refracts into flint glass of refractive index $n_2 = 1.60$ as illustrated by the wavefronts. What is the wavelength of the light inside the glass?
items.workedSolution: Since frequency is constant across the boundary, $\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \frac{n_1}{n_2} \Rightarrow \lambda_2 = 640 \times \frac{1.00}{1.60} = 400 nm$.

items.stem: A 0.52 m air column closed at one end carries sound at 330 m s⁻¹ (with an ideal open end). What is the frequency of odd harmonic n = 7?
items.workedSolution: With L_eff = L + e = 0.520 m and odd harmonic n = 7, f_n = nv / (4L_eff) = (7 × 330) / (4 × 0.520) = 1.11 × 10³ Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the n = 1 first-harmonic frequency v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the prohibited even harmonic (n − 1) into nv / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies open-both-ends formula nv / (2L) instead of closed-one-end nv / (4L).

items.stem: A uniform vibrating string is clamped at one end. Its other end is attached to a light frictionless ring that slides freely on a smooth vertical rod. Why can this string sustain only odd harmonics (first, third, fifth,...)?
items.workedSolution: A displacement node at x = 0 and an antinode at x = L require L = n(λ/4) for odd integers n = 1, 3, 5,... This fits an odd number of quarter wavelengths, so only odd harmonics can form. Therefore option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: one displacement node and one antinode fit an odd number of quarter wavelengths, so only odd harmonics can form.

options.label: A
options.text: Because both ends act as displacement nodes so only even multiples of a half-wavelength fit along the string.
options.distractorRationale: The free ring is a displacement antinode, not a node, so the string fits odd quarter-wavelengths L = (2k − 1)λ/4.

options.label: B
options.text: A boundary pair with one displacement node and one displacement antinode fits an odd number of quarter wavelengths so only odd harmonics can form.

options.label: C
options.text: Because wave speed on the string doubles for even harmonics so they cannot reflect from the fixed end.
options.distractorRationale: Wave speed is set by the medium, not the harmonic number; even harmonics violate the node–antinode boundary condition.

options.label: D
options.text: Because standing waves on a string with a free end require superposition of three travelling waves instead of two.
options.distractorRationale: Standing waves form from the superposition of two identical travelling waves moving in opposite directions.

items.stem: In the microwave apparatus shown, a transmitter directs plane-polarised microwaves toward a flat metal sheet. A probe detector slides along a metre rule between them. Why does the probe meter reading rise and fall periodically?
items.workedSolution: Microwaves reflect from the metal sheet and superpose with the incident beam to form a stationary wave. Moving the probe detector along the axis detects adjacent minima separated by half a wavelength. Measuring across k consecutive minima (k × λ/2) cuts percentage uncertainty when finding λ.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: reflected and incident microwaves superpose to form a stationary wave with adjacent minima separated by half a wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: Along the axis between transmitter and sheet, microwaves reflect from a metal sheet and superpose with the incident beam so a probe detector moved along the axis finds adjacent minima separated by half a wavelength.

options.label: B
options.text: Adjacent minima detected by the probe are separated by one full wavelength because reflection doubles the frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Reflection preserves frequency and wavelength, and adjacent nodes (minima) are always separated by λ/2.

options.label: C
options.text: The metal plate absorbs all incident microwaves so the maxima arise purely from diffraction around the transmitter horn.
options.distractorRationale: A conducting metal plate reflects microwaves efficiently to create the returning opposite-travelling wave.

options.label: D
options.text: The meter reading drops to zero at every position whenever the probe moves closer to the reflector because microwaves are longitudinal.
options.distractorRationale: Microwaves are transverse electromagnetic waves; minima occur specifically at fixed nodal planes spaced by λ/2.

items.stem: While performing Required Practical 1 on a braided cotton cord ($\mu = 2.40 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹$, hanging mass 0.55 kg, $g = 9.81$ m s⁻²), a student plots first-harmonic frequency $f_1$ against $1/L$. What is the theoretical gradient of this line?
items.workedSolution: With $T = mg = 0.55 \times 9.81 = 5.40 N$, wave speed $v = \sqrt{T/\mu} = 47.4 m s⁻¹$, $f_1 = v/(2L) = 25.0 Hz$, gradient $= v/2 = 23.7 m s⁻¹$, and $\%\Delta \mu = 1.4 + 2(0.8) + 2(0.6) = 4.20\%$. Answer: 23.7 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Equates gradient of f₁ vs 1/L to v rather than v/2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by 4 instead of 2.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Forgets square root on T/μ.

items.stem: According to the Rayleigh criterion, when are two point-like stars of equal brightness considered to be just resolved by a circular telescope aperture?
items.workedSolution: Under the Rayleigh criterion, two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one pattern coincides with the first minimum of the other.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that central maximum of one diffraction pattern coincides with the first minimum of the other.

options.label: A
options.text: When the first minima of both diffraction patterns overlap at the same angle.
options.distractorRationale: Overlapping first minima leaves the central peaks completely superposed and unresolved.

options.label: B
options.text: When the central maximum of one diffraction pattern coincides with the first minimum of the other.

options.label: C
options.text: When the first secondary maxima of both patterns touch without any central overlap.
options.distractorRationale: This describes well-separated sources rather than the threshold of just-resolved images.

options.label: D
options.text: When the central maxima coincide and produce double peak intensity.
options.distractorRationale: Coincident central maxima appear as a single unresolved source.

items.stem: Suppose a loudspeaker on a car emits a 900 Hz note while receding from a stationary listener at 60 m s⁻¹. If sound moves at 332 m s⁻¹, calculate the frequency heard.
items.workedSolution: Substitute into the moving-source formula (away from): f' = fv / (v + v_s) = (900 × 332) / (332 + 60) = 762 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 762 Hz (B).

options.distractorRationale: Applies the moving-observer equation f(v ± v_s) / v instead of the moving-source equation fv / (v ∓ v_s).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the moving-observer formula AND reverses the sign of the Doppler frequency shift.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the wrong sign in the denominator, using v + v_s for an approaching source (or v − v_s for a receding source).

items.stem: At normal incidence, a 532 nm beam enters two narrow parallel slits spaced 0.6 mm apart. Find the fringe separation seen on a screen 3.6 m behind them.
items.workedSolution: SI conversion gives λ = 5.32 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m; bright-band spacing = λD / (slit separation) = (5.32 × 10⁻⁷ × 3.6) / 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.19 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) to obtain 3.19 × 10⁻³ m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit separation and divides by screen distance (λd / D) instead of λD / d.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the distance from the central bright fringe to the first dark minimum (½ λD / d) instead of bright fringe spacing.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2, confusing double-slit fringe spacing with single-slit central maximum width.

items.stem: An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) with word length 8 bits spans an input voltage range of 0 V to 5.12 V. Using the AQA ADC resolution formula $\Delta V = V_{\mathrm{range}} / 2^n$, calculate the voltage resolution in mV.
items.workedSolution: Number of levels $= 2^8 = 256$. Resolution $\Delta V = \frac{5.12}{256} = 0.0200\text{ V} = 20.0 mV$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides $V_{\mathrm{range}}$ by bit count $8$ instead of quantisation levels $2^8 = 256$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses $2^7 = 128$ instead of $2^8 = 256$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses $2^9 = 512$ instead of $2^8 = 256$.

items.stem: A sound wave exerts a peak pressure variation of $0.0500\text{ Pa}$ across an eardrum of area $60.0\text{ mm}^2$. The ossicles have a force lever ratio of $1.40$ and transmit to an oval window of area $3.00\text{ mm}^2$. Calculate the pressure amplitude acting on the cochlear fluid at the oval window.
items.workedSolution: Amplification factor $= 1.40 \times \frac{60.0}{3.00} = 28.0$. Oval-window pressure $= 28.0 \times 0.0500 = 1.40 Pa$.

items.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity 64 W m⁻² passes first through an ideal vertical polarizer P₁. It then strikes an ideal analyzer A whose transmission axis is rotated by θ = 70° relative to P₁. Using I = I₁ cos²θ for plane-polarized light of intensity I₁, calculate the emerging intensity.
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 32.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(70°) = ½(64) cos²(70°) = 3.74 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(70°) = 3.74 W m⁻² (A).

items.stem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.9 m, mass per unit length 8 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹, and tension 7.22 N. Determine the stationary-wave frequency in harmonic mode n = 3.
items.workedSolution: Wave speed along the string is v = √(T / μ) = √(7.22 / 0.0008) = 95.0 m s⁻¹. For n = 3, f_n = nv / (2L) = 3 × 95.0 / (2 × 0.9) = 158 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = √(T / μ) and f_n = nv / (2L) = 158 Hz (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts tension and mass per unit length inside the square root, using √(μ / T).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n, computing (n / L)√(T / μ).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the square root over T / μ, computing (n / 2L)(T / μ).

items.stem: Polaroid sunglasses reduce bright sunlight glare reflected off a flat lake surface. How do they do this while still letting an angler see fish below the surface?
items.workedSolution: Reflected glare from horizontal water is partially horizontally polarised and blocked by a vertically aligned Polaroid filter. Therefore option D is correct: reflected glare is partially horizontally polarised and blocked by a vertically aligned polaroid filter.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: reflected glare is partially horizontally polarised and blocked by a vertically aligned polaroid filter.

options.distractorRationale: Polaroid filters selectively absorb one plane of electric-field oscillation rather than refracting glare away.

options.label: C

options.distractorRationale: Light is already a transverse electromagnetic wave.

items.stem: In Doppler ultrasound monitoring of an artery, the frequency shift obeys $\Delta f / f = (2v\cos\theta)/c$. Why does the factor of 2 appear in this expression?
items.workedSolution: Moving red blood cells receive a Doppler-shifted wave as moving observers and then reflect it back as moving sources. Ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift, which doubles the frequency shift.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the correct explanation: ultrasound experiences a double Doppler shift as moving red blood cells receive and reflect the wave.

options.label: A
options.text: Because two separate piezoelectric crystals must transmit simultaneously from opposite sides of the limb.
options.distractorRationale: A single transducer probe transmits and receives; the factor of two comes from reflection off moving scatterers.

options.label: B
options.text: Because ultrasound undergoes a double Doppler shift because moving red blood cells first receive and then reflect the wave.

options.label: C
options.text: Because ultrasound waves travel at twice the speed in arterial blood compared with surrounding soft tissue.
options.distractorRationale: Ultrasound speed is nearly identical (~1540 m s⁻¹) in soft tissue and blood.

options.label: D
options.text: Because blood flows simultaneously in two opposite directions along the same uniform artery.
options.distractorRationale: Arterial blood flows in one bulk direction during systole; the factor of two arises from receiving and re-emitting the wave.

items.stem: How does a diagnostic B-scan differ from an A-scan when imaging internal body structures?
items.workedSolution: An A-scan plots echo amplitude against time for one dimensional depth measurement. A B-scan varies spot brightness with echo amplitude to form a two dimensional cross section.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that A-scan plots echo amplitude against time for one-dimensional depth, whereas B-scan uses spot brightness to form a two-dimensional cross section.

options.distractorRationale: Both A-scan and B-scan are non-ionising pulse-echo ultrasound techniques.

options.text: B-scan plots a single voltage spike against time while A-scan builds a full three-dimensional scan.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the definitions of A-scan (amplitude-mode 1D trace) and B-scan (brightness-mode 2D image).

options.label: C
options.text: B-scan operates without coupling gel because it sweeps multiple frequencies simultaneously.
options.distractorRationale: Every external diagnostic ultrasound scan requires coupling gel at the skin interface.

options.label: D

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 580 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 300 lines mm⁻¹. Including the central zero-order maximum, how many total principal maxima emerge across the forward semicircle (−90° ≤ θ ≤ +90°)?
items.workedSolution: d = 10⁻³ / 300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m, so d / λ = 5.75 and n_max = 5. Including ±1..±5 and n = 0 gives 2(5) + 1 = 11 principal maxima.

items.stem: A thermal imaging camera detects infrared electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $\lambda = 1.50 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}$ in vacuum ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$). What is the frequency of this radiation?
items.workedSolution: Using $c = f\lambda$, $f = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8}{1.50 \times 10^{-5}} = 2.00 × 10¹³ Hz$.

items.stem: How does an audiogram of age-related hearing loss differ from one caused by prolonged exposure to loud industrial machinery?
items.workedSolution: Audiograms distinguish the two mechanisms because ageing reduces high frequency hearing whereas excessive noise causes a characteristic dip near four kilohertz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that ageing reduces high frequency hearing whereas excessive noise causes a characteristic dip near four kilohertz.

options.label: A
options.text: Ageing causes a sharp notch near four kilohertz whereas loud noise reduces only low frequencies below fifty hertz.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the two classic audiometric patterns: noise-induced loss produces the 4 kHz notch.

options.label: B
options.text: Both ageing and loud noise produce an identical flat threshold shift across every frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Neither condition is flat across frequency; ageing progressively erodes high-frequency hearing.

options.label: C
options.text: Clinical audiometry shows that ageing reduces high frequency hearing whereas excessive noise causes a characteristic dip near four kilohertz.

options.label: D
options.text: Noise damage improves sensitivity near three kilohertz while lowering threshold at ten kilohertz.
options.distractorRationale: Excessive sound exposure damages cochlear hair cells and raises hearing thresholds.
